div.head: EDUCATION CCEIITTEE. THE QUESTION OF EXEMPTIONS.
div.p: EDUCATION CCEIITTEE. THE QUESTION OF EXEMPTIONS.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee v, as held at the To7n Ball on Monday evening. Ccurcillor J. Fulton-Smith presided and there were also present :—Mr. H. Roberts (deputy. chairman), Aldermen Bennett, Ellison and Forshaw ; Councillors Dickenson, Nield, W. B. Roberts, Singleton, and Wilkinson. Revs. James Davies, Canon Stevenson, N. Wilson, J. Yonge, Miss Williams, Messrs. C. Sawkins Burgess, T. P. Brads.haw, R. T. Fairclough, A. J. Jolley, H. Kingdon, E. Plinston, C. H. Unsworth, J. Upson, O. Walker ; with Mr. J. Moore Murray (director), Mr. R. B. Roberts (assistant director), and Mr. John Fairhurst (treasurer). ST. JAMES' SCHOOL. It wss intimated that the Rev. H. H. Corshie had been appointed a co-optative manager of St. James' Latchford, in place of the late Mr. U.N. Houghton.
THE SECONDARY SCHOOL ALTERATIONS. LAND WANTED FOR SILVER STREET SCHOOL
EXTENSIONS.

The Rev. Canon STEVENSON, in moving the confirm- ation of the minutes of the School Management Com- mittee, alluded to the fact that during the past season 800 toys from 13 elementary public schools in the Borough had attended at the public baths once a week, that they had all learnt to swim to some extent, 200 of them being able to swim at least one breadth, and the remainder at least half a breadth. The Canon said that that state of things was very creditable to the instruc- tors and a great gain to the boys. (Hear, hear.) A letter tad been received from the Board of Education in reference to the recent conference between the committee and H.M. Inspectors with regard to the pro- posed alterations to the Secondary School on some not -very important details which would not matter so much except that the work was being delayed. The com- mittee were gratified that a gift of a copy of Agencourt's "Story of Art by its Monuments " had been offered to the School of Art by Mrs. Pierpoint, daughter of the late Mr. J. C. Thompson. It was -fitting that the copy should find its home in the School of Art with which Mrs. Pierpoint's father had been so long connected. He was sure Mrs. Pierpoint bad the sympathy of all the members of the Education Com- mittee in her recent bereavement. (Hear, bear.) Alluding to the committee's recommendation that the Town Council should re-consider the application of the managers of Silver-street school for the purchase of land adjoining the school, in view of the Board of Education's requirements of increased playground and office accommodation, Canon Stevenson said the matter was a very important one. Unless the Council could see their way to allow the managers of the school to increase their land at a reasonable rate it would mean practically that the school would have to be closed and the town would have to face the cost of thel building of a new school in that district in its stead. The Rev. Father WIL`,ON seconded. Alderman i3ENNETT expressed his gratification at the results of the swimming instruction which, he said, seemed to emphasis, the great necessity which existed for further extending the the present facilities. The girls should have an equal chance. (Hear, bear.) The CHAIRMAN, alluding to the Board of Education's action with regard to the Secondary School alterations said he bad met the contractor (Mr. It. W. Collin) who lamented the fact that the delay had occurred as it was preventing men being employed during the coming winter. He looked upon it as a serious point as affect- ing the workingmen of the town. They had written to the Town Clerk asking him to write to the Board of Education with a view to facilitating the work and it was hoped it would have the desired effect. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then passed. FEEDING OF SCHOOL CHILDREN. The School Attendance Committee passed a resolu- tion asking the Board of Education to sanction the expenditure of a sum (not exceeding £100) out of the rates for the purpose of defraying the cost of the food required in order to carry out the Education (Provision of Meals Act) 1906. Alderman ELLTSON moved, and Mr. PLINSTON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman BENNETT asked whether there had been any response on the part of the public to the appeal for funds in connection with the Provision af Meals Act. Alderman ELLISON : I believe not.

_ The CIIAIRMAN : I am sorry to say there has not been any response. Whether that is owing to the monied men having gone to the suburbs to escape their share in supporting the town affairs I don't know, but the matter has rot teen taLen up, and we have to apply to the toard of Education. Mr. RonEnTs said he did not think the want of response was in any sense an indication of indifference on the part of the people of Warrington, hut there was a strong feeling that the n atter had been made the subject of legislation in order that everyone might pay his fair quota of the ccst, which should be a charge on the rntes rather than upon the individual.

SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS. Mr. UNON alluded to the following minute : "A Teturn with reference to the exemptions from school attendance granted by the committee daring the months of July, August, September, and October, 1308, was sub- mitted and noted, and it was resolved, that instructions be given for tbe exemption certificates of those chil- dren who are still of school age and are found to be not now in employment to he withdrawn, and for the children in question to be required to resume attend- ance at school." He congratulated the committee upon the minute. Although there was very little room to spare in the schools, he believed their action had been dictated in the interests of the children themselves. They would have to take into consideration the critical age between 13 ard 14, before the apprenticeship. 'rho committee had found that a large number who had been exempted for employment were not emplo3 ed, bet were merely running about the streets. It was the unanimous feeling of the committee that those children were far better in school than learning all sorts of bad inanners. Me School Attendance Committee ought to learn the lesson not to grant exemptions until they were fully persuaded that the children would be necessarily and beneficially employed. (Hear, hear.) Mr. FAIRCLOTJCII Said that if an exemption certifi- cate was given it ought to state the condition, so that there could be no mistake in case of a prosecution taking place before the magistrates. (Hear, bear.) Mr. PLINSTON said he entirely agreed with the resolu- tion. It had not been the fault of the committee that She children did not stay in the employment to which they had been sent. Alderman Er.msoN, in replying to the discussion, said youths went to work for a week or so (Ind then left off, and they bad, therefore, insttucted their officers to watch the cases, and the minute was the result. Now the committee had taken the bull by the horns,and they hoped to be able to put a stop to what was complained of.

The minutes were approved. CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS. On the proposition of Mr. Edwin Plinston seconded by the Rev. Father Wilson it was decided that all the schools in the borough close for the Christmas holidays the evening of Wednesday, the 23rd December, 1908, Itnd reopen on Monday, the 11th January, 1909.

McDOUGALLS Patellt SELF—RAISING FLOUR DENSTION. The Examineli Saturday, November 28, 1908 WOMAN'S REALM.
SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
MOSQUITOES AND COLOURS.

Mosquitoes are found to prefer negroes to whites, a black dog to a white one, and a dark-coloured resting-place. Careful tests have been extended to great numbers of the insects,- sliewing that they choose colours in the order of dark blue, dark red, brown, red, black, grey, and violet, and that azure, ochre, and white are distasteful, and yellow ex- tremely so.

div.head: DRESS-FASMON-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASMON-HOME.
WINTER BOOTS AND SHOES.

MI shades of brown are worn with tweed costumes, and, in fact, with short skirts of any colour sate black. High heels seem to be worn more with short skirts than with long ones. In fact. says a Globe writer, the shorter the skirt the higher the heels, and the effect is often more peculiar than beauti- ful. The gait is crippled, and any trace of charm or gracefulness necessarily disappears when the figure is bent forward as with the Infirmity of age. The mischief that results to the knees is serious enough, but worse re- mains behind. Displacement of internal organs is no trifle. Already there are coloured shoes to match green, blue, or purple costumes, a fashion that will be de- veloped immensely next season. We shall see shoes in almost every shade of colour, pale or dark, a possibility that has become fast owing to a new discovery in the art of dyeing.

div.head: SMART NEW BLOUSE.
div.p: A SMART NEW BLOUSE.

The remarkably attractive little lilouse pic- tured in our sketch is quite new and up-to. date in design. The original was carried out in silk cashmere of o particularly pretty and becoming shade of elderberry purple. The blouse was cut square at the neck, and opened down the front to display a vest of tucked net

dyed to exactly the same shade beneath. A roll of satin tubing finished the edges of the silk cashmere, and added a touch of bright- ness to the garment. At a distance of some 2in. from the tubing the blouse was cut up on either side, still following the square lines of the outer edge, to display beneath it another glimpse of the tucked net undervest. On the further side of this opening the blouse was set in three broad tucks, which were carried right down to the waist. Just above the line of the bust a little pointed tab projected over the tucked net vest and fastened across to the blouse, and two pretty buttons served to dc- curate it. The sleeves were very long, quite plain, and almost tight-fitting. They ter- minated in long points over the hands, the points being finished by a close ruffling of ivory Brussels net. A similar ruffling finished the top of the high collar.

FASHIOINS IN FANS. Although still small the fans this season are just a trifle larger than last. The handles are of gold, silver, and ivory, and are fre- quently inlaid with precious stones forming initials or mascots. Many are hand-painted, the handles decorated with a miniature of a (log or some other pet. For those with a Limited dress allowance there are some very attractive spangled silk-gauze fans in all the fashionable shades; it is de rigueur for them to be in harmony with the costume. The black fan, says Marjorie Hamilton in the Tatter, is having an unusual vogue, and al- though striking cannot be said to be pretty _ _ _

div.head: COSY FUR COAT.
div.p: A COSY FUR COAT.

Pictured in our illustration is a particularly smart and comfortable fur coat, cut on the very newest and must up-to-date lines, and quite an ideal garment for cold weather wear. The original of this desirable coat WM carried out in musquash dyed to exactly the shade of seal, and very difficult to detect from the more expensive pelt. The coat was elack-fit- ting in front and semi-fitting at the back and

sidos, the back being cut with the merest quepicion of a short-waisted effect. From the neck turned back big, wide revers and collar of the fur, the collar being 80 arranged that it could be worn up or down at pleasure. The fronts were single-breasted, and the coat fastened with three immense, handsome brown buttons aud loops of heavy silk cord. The sleeves were of the simplest coat shape, and were, of course, of full length. A thick soft lining of ivory satin completed this at- tractive model. METAL EFFECTS.

These obtain, says the Queen, in nets and tulle and on silks and satins, either as bro- cades or embroidery. On laces they are in. troclucecl with tambour stitehery. Steel, sil- ver, and gold give. importance, and the tinsel is often coloured mauve, green, or blue. Silver and gold nets are embroidered in antique designs. %me of the old Venetian laces, with designs in which animals appear, have been revived, and they are well in keep- ing with these metallic adornments.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

GROUSE ETU SALMIS.—Rost a brace of grouse, let them get cold, thea carve in neat joints the wings, the legs, and the breasts. Chop up the rost of the birds and putt them and 'the trimmings into a saucepan, with a small slice of bacon, a couple of Carrots, a shallot, one clove, a small sprig of thyme, and some whole pepper and salt to taste. Add a wineglassful of port wine, and fill up the eaucepari with stock. Put the saucepan at the side of' the fire, and let it simmer for a couple of hours; then strain the liquid, lot it reduce for twenty minutes, thicken it carefully with a max a flour and butter, and nid it. cm one side. Put the joints, dic., of the birds into a stewpan, pour the sauce over them, and let all slowly simmer until the contents are very hot: Dress them on a dish, pour the camp over, awl garuish with pippeto of bread fried in butter

div.head: LOFTY TELEPHONE LINE.
div.p: A LOFTY TELEPHONE LINE.

The highest telephone line. in Europe, which runs ,to the Regina Margherita Meteorological Observatory on Mont Rosa, at an altitude of 14,958 ft., is nearing completion. It was found impossible to run this line on poles, owing to the high winds and bad storms which prevail at these altitudes. It was also thought to be impracticable to lay an insulated cable, as it would gradually sink into the ice and would make repairs impossible. The final solution of the problem was to lay a bare Wire across the glaciers, and depend upon the insulating qualities of the snow and ice.

div.head: ORIGIN OF RAIN.
div.p: ORIGIN OF RAIN.

ACeording to the researches of H. Fritzsche, about three-quarters of the rain which re- freshes the continents of the earth is due to the vapours rising from the soil instead of to those coming from the oceans. Elaborate es- timates, based on all available data, shew that the -annual rainfall for the entire globe is equivalent to a layer of water enveloping the earth to a depth of about 3ft. The quan- tity of rain-water and melted snow, falling in a year is put at 111,000 cubic miles. More than two-thirds of this falls upon the sea. South America is the only 6ne of the conti- nents on which the annual rainfall exceeds that on the surface of the sea.

div.head: SUGAR AS A DISINFECTANT.
div.p: SUGAR AS A DISINFECTANT.

In many parts of. Europe it is customary among the people to burn sugar in sick rooms, a practice which is considered by physicians . as an innocent superstition, neither beneficial nor harmful. Professor Trilbert, of the Pasteur Institute at Paris; has, however, demonstrated that burning sugar develops formic acetylene-hidrogen, one of the most powerful antiseptic gases known. Five grammes of sugar were burnt under a glass bell holding ten quarts. After the vapour had cooled germs of typhus, con- sumption, cholera, smallpox, &c. were placed- in the bell in bpen . glass tubes, and within half an hour all the microbes were dead. If sugar is burnt in a closed vessel con- taining putrefied meat or the contents of rot- ten eggs, the offensive odour disappears at once. The popular faith in the disinfecting qualities of burnt sugar appears, therefore, as well founded.

div.head: ESQUIMAU'S KEEN VISION.
div.p: ESQUIMAU'S KEEN VISION.

Curiously enough, (recording to the greatest authorities, the best eyesight in man is found at the Equator and in the vicinity of the Poles. It is stated that good vision is meat commonly found in the country and On barren wastes broken by few objects in the line of sight. Eequimaux have been known to detect white foxes etealing along the snow-covered aete at incredible distances; and to be able to discern objects clearly in placca where the chance traveller would see only fields of blind- ing white. The Arabs of the desert are pro- vided with keenness of vision quite equal to their northern brothers. The plainsmen of Ainerica•have the beet eyesight• of Americans, inasmuch as the wide sweep Of the western plains develops their vision by reason of the absence of obstaelcs tending to shorten the range. The Indian's keen sight is, of course, proverbial; and it is doubtful whether- any white men have ever attained his remarkable proficiency in thie respect.

div.head: CALIFORNIAN CONDOR.
div.p: THE CALIFORNIAN CONDOR.

The Californian condor, otherwise the great Californian vulture, has been the sub- jeet of some interesting notes by Mr. W. Finlay in the Scientific Ameriettn. The writer points out that if not afforded some measure of pro- tection this remarkable bird will speedily be- come extinct. The stock raisers, having in. vaded ite haunts, exposed poisoned carcases for the panthers, bears, &T. Eating these large numbers of the condors are killed. And the Californian condor is e very slow breeder, laying only one egg at a time, and not always breeding every year. One pair, indeed, whieb had been watched, only bred three times in twelve yeare. It is stated in many ornithe. logical works that this species lays two eggy, but recent observations of collectors agree that there is only one. It was first mentioned by Shaw in 1779, and deacribed by Taylor in 1859. It is interesting to note that the egg m from which Taylor ad i e his description s now in England in the collection of r.s. J. H. Gurney. FISII THAT ARE POISONOUS.

There is, writes Professor Sir E. nay Lankester, 'a whole series of fishes which can- not be eaten by anyone without serious poisoning being the result, even when the fish are carefully cooked. Happily, these fishes are rarely, if ever, caught on our own coasts: They produce, when even small bits are eaten, violent irritation of the intestine, and death, the symptoms resembling-in many re- spects those of cholera. The curious bright. coloured, beaked fish of tropical seas and coral reefs, with two or four large front teeth and spherical spine-covered bodies, and the trigger fish of the same regions, are the chief of these poisonous fish. But there is a true anchovy on the coast of Japan and a small herring in the West Indies, and a goby on the Indian coast (Pondicherry), all of which are deadly poison even when cooked; and there arc many other, so that one has to be careful about fish-eating in the remoter parts of the world. The poisons of these fish with poison- ous flesh have not been carefully studied, hut they seem to resemble chemically the poisons produced by certain . putrefactive microbes.

div.head: "FATIGUE SENSE."
div.p: THE "FATIGUE SENSE."

Dr. J. H. Clarke believes that he cult et muscularity in this country is very Much overdone. In his'-hook, Vital Economy" (Unwin), he declares that "exercise" has be.. come a fetish word luring us to our perdition. Exercise is not, he says. for everybody or for anybody under all conditions, and the ind:s- -criminat-2 advice to take plenty of exercise is just as fatal as the indiscriminate advice to take plenty of fresh air. There are soma people in the world who "nevet know what it is to be tired " ; end they are generally very proud of this. They might just as well be proud of having no sense of smell or taste or sight. They are lacking in a very, neces- sary sense--that is all. Those people, Dr. Clarke says, will " over-fatigue themselve3 without being in the least aware of it, and I have often seen extremely serious results from this want of the fatigue sense. It is on the approach of old age that the evils of over- indulgence in excreiite in early life are most clearly seen, in inelastic muscles, a weakened, heart, and a liver which'rannot obtain its wonted stimulus.

SELF-ELECTRIFICATION OF THE BODY. Several years ago Professor A. Heydweiller observed the remarkable phenomenon of self- electrification of the human body. The needle of a quadrant electrometer having been charged to a potential of come hundreds o f volts, one of the pairs of quadrants was con- nected to the earth, and the other to an insu- lated metal . plate. The subject then raised one of his hands to about four inches from the plate,/ and holding it in this position stepped on an insulating stool, when the elec- trometer chewed a deflection indicative of a negative charge of the hand. The magnitude of this deliection and the interval of time occupied by its slow disappearance would vary according to the personal disposition of the subject and meteorological conditions. The same problem has been taken up, says the Scienti fin Ameriran, ,by two Russian physicists, Drs. Tereshine and A. Geor- gievski. Whereas the qualitative results of the first series are mainly identical with those of Professor Heydweiller, the electric • ten- sions (of 10 to 15 volts) found by the Russian experiments are much inferior, and experi- ments made on naked subjects gave very different results. And hence they draw the conclusion that the self-eleetriticatmn ot the human body is clue, not to the contraction of the muscles, but to the friction of the feet on the insulating stool and to thit of the clothes oa the body and on one an0t.1196

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
By Veronica
PRESS PHOTOGRAPHY.

Certain alterations in the conditions at present pre- vailing with reference to the payment of copyright fees for photographs that are reproduced in nevrspopers before permission has been obtained from the holders of the copyright,are likely to be shortly put into force. At a recent committee of the Professional Photo- graphers' Association it transpired that the newspaper society bad approached certain photographers to see whether some modification could be arranged from that, at present existing, and it was eventually arranged to refer the matter to a sob-committee of the 'Copyright Union. According to the present copyright law, a photographer can demand. his own price from any newspaper using one of his copyright photographs without having first obtained permission, but this has, in the past, led to many cases of extortionate charges being made. The necessity frequently arises of publishing a photograph of a person who, for some !reason or other, suddenly becomes notorious, and there is rarely time to first obtain permission to reproduce the photagraph,and it is to meet this difficulty that the present of the conditions is suggested. I happened to be in the office of one of the large photographic press agencies the day following the Lord Mayor's Show, and I was informed that they were simply inundated with photographs that bad been sent of this event. This is only an illustration of what not to photograph, for those who hope to get their pictures used by the illustrated press. An event of such notoriety as this you may be sure is very well catered for by the regular staff that is employed by the various Illustrated papers, and it is waste of time to send up photographs of such an event. Of course, there are times when any special feature, such as an accident in the procession or some other notable event, may be ' recorded by the stray photographer, that would give a special season for submitting a print.

div.head: LIVING PICTURE PHOTOGRAPHY.
div.p: LIVING PICTURE PHOTOGRAPHY.

We are all of us familiar with the various cinemato- graphic entertainments that are produced all over the country, but there has recently been put on the possible for any amateur to produce living pictures for his own borne entertainment. The new camera promises to have a most successful future, as by its meanskwe get apparently living pictures without having to go to the extent and expenses of costly projection apparatus. The idea is not entirely-new, as many of us have no doubt seen the thumb-books of living pictures which are retailed by the street hawkers in many places, and It is really this same idea which has been perfected for use in conjunction with the new camera which is called the Kinora. The Company that is handling this camera sell rolls of film in lengths from twelve to forty-two feet, which are p inserted in light-tight boxes. These light- tight bozos are in the camera and when exposed are sent bank to one of the Company's depots, when, for the price of a few shillings, they develop this roll of film, containing anything from between five and seven hundred exposures, and supply a bromide print from each negative, conveniently mounted up in book form ready far use in one of their viewing instruments. The viewing instrument in appearance somewhat resembles the stereoscope. It has a wheel attachment which mechanically liberates each picture in accurate rotation, and when these pictures are so viewed they have all the appearance of moving pictures. I am sure that in a shoat time a large amount of interest will be taken In this class of work, and, possibly clubs may be formed throughout the country for the interchange of these Kinora albums. For further information, I must refer you to the booklet that is supplied by Kinora Ltd., 21, Red Lion Square, London, W.

NIGHT PHOTOGRAPHY. I notice a letter in the illustrated press from Mr. A. H. Blake of the Blenheim Club, St. James, London, S.W. suggesting the formation of a society of those that are interested in night photography. "By night photography" he says, " I do not mean fakes or results obtained by combination of daylight and night exposures, but the results obtained solely after dark by natural and artificial light. This is, I am persuaded, a rew field for pictorial effect but little used, snd those who are trying to find out more about its conditions and extend its scope would gain much by co-operation with those engaged in a similar quest.' I have come across recently many photographer who have taken tip this branch of work, being interested therein owing to reading Mr. Dyke's book of "Night Photography," and so lam sure there is a good number of enthusiasts at present exist inn to form such a society. div.head: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
div.p: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
PUBLIC MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

Boys' Prank. There was a large attend,ince•at a public meeting held in the Co-operative Hal I, Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening unaer the auspices of the *Warrington Women's Suffrage Society. The Rev. C. Harvey Cook presided and there were on the platform Miss Boyden, of Man- chester; Miss Lucy Broadbent, Miss Massy, Miss Wilkinson, Miss Johnston,Miss Waring (secretary) and Mr. C. Plinston.

To guard against the possibility of disturbance, a large number of gentlemen interested in the movement occupied seats in various parts of the room. At the outset the CHAIRMAN' (the Rev. C. Hervey Cook) uttered a warning that he intended to conduct the meeting on strict linesornd said if there was trouble the .disturbers would have to deal with him,

The CrtAIRMAN said the question of woman suffrage was a very vital one. In his judgment the militant suffragists who were agitating so much were not the women who were seeking cheap notoriety or an easy fame. (Heal; hear.) The women were not playing at heroics, but they were being heroines. A woman did not take up her position on this question and ran the gauntlet of a term in Holloway Gaol simply because she wanted to make a cheap name for herself: It was not self-advertisement or self-glorification that the women were seeking. The jibes thrown at them were the jibes of the ignorant, and there were those who were trying to make a division between the sexes over this question. How far had the men studied the history of the women's question for the last two thousand years? 'The women of to-day were far different to those of years ago. The age of chivalry was great for women, but they had to make a greater age for her, and that .greater age was when she would stand side by side Nyith man as his-companion in enterprises open for her. (Applause.) He (the Chairman) looked for the day when he might greet his sister as a woman to whom would be open every door of learning and enter- prise that was now open ,to men and barred to her. Therefore, he drew no line, even at the House of Com- mons. The House of Commons could not be much more common than it was. (Laughter.) But, apart from that, he looked for the day when they would be , able to fight all their political, municipal and social 1 evils shoulder to shoulder, qualified exactly on the 1 same terms. The women's cause was also the men's, for Ithey rose or sank together. (Applause). Miss ROYDEN said there could be nothing more , deplorable than to increase sex antagonism. A more , disastrous disease could hardly attack society. Class !antagonism was bad enough, but sex antagonism wonld ibe much worse. There was really no fear at all, from 1 the point of view of women suffragists, of sex , , antagonism. The men's league for women's suffrage, 1 which was doing a good work on their behalf, was , I surely proof that men and women were not going to ho I absolutely eivided on this question. It was true there was a certain element of sex antagonism, but that was not due to any political question. It was born in a much more complicated world. It was born through 1 the industrial cenditions. Women were told that they 1 , were the worst enemies of the men in the labour market. ; There was a certain element of truth in it. There was , 1 a disastrous influence which made women the Involun- tary blacklegs of the market by undercutting men. ; ; That was disastrous to both. They were fighting against, each other instead of side by side. The state of affairs 1 was not the fault of the women. There seemed to be an idea that women worked and took lower wages because it amused them, and that by some extraordinary 'perversity in the female character they delighted to think they would be paid an average wage of 72. 3d, per t week. She supposed there was a small percentage of 1 women who worked for amusement and extra pocket r money. There were 51 million women of the "working classes" earning their living to-day. Did they really i , wish to support those women n idleness? Was it the wish when the men complained that the women were Iflooding the labour market that they should , remain at home, able bodied women? The 1 gentlemen would not all go round. (Laughter.) ' There were two million women who could not get 1 • married. Did they propose to support them in idleness? I The right to work was the right to be honest. The , men had at present before the Government a" Right to I work" Bill. The women wanted their "Bight to I work "Bill. (Applause.) No healthy human being had Ithe right to live on the fruits of the labour of other , people. There were too many people doing it already. It was as much the duty of the women to work as the ; men. Women who were bringing up children for the ; State were doing the noblest work any woman could do. and it, was a monstrous injustice that any woman should be called upon also to work in factories. (Applause.) But for the women who were not married and had no children it was an absolute duty to work, and if the work was only organized properly there was enough to go all rourd. In fact, there was too much work. It was owing to the extraordinary stupidity of our social arrangements that women were taking work from the men. How was that going to be affected by the women having the franchise ? Any class that had no political rights would be, exploited by the classes that had. (Applause.) The women wanted the men to ' give them the power to help themselves. They " did not want, charity, they wanted justice." The gift of the vote ,raised the whole level of the class or sex to which it was given. They were told that the way to raise the status of woman was through trade unions. She admitted a good deal could be done by trade unions, but by no means everything. To many miserably paid women workers it was a mockery to talk of trade unions ; for the sweated class trade unionism was a hopeless impossibility. 'flan, again, the sphere of industrial strife was being removed from between • masters and men to the House of Commons. If the men desired to be just, the only way they could do it was to give the women a chance of speaking for themselves. In this country they had suffered from class legislation long enough. They should not be guilty of sex legisla- tion. The women were confident wages would gradually rise, and that the status of women would rise by the granting of the vote. One of the first things they would do if they got the vote would be to insist that the biggest employers of labour in the country—the Govern- ment—should pay equal wages for equal work in the Government departments. If the women got equal pay for equal work it would be generally worth an employer's while to employ men because in the vast majority of eases the men were the better workers. (Applause.) She appealed to everybody not to be indifferent on this question. It VMS almost criminal to stand aside. She demanded that either they should be opposed to them or join them. (Applause). During Miss Bovnee.'s address, a peculiar incident occurred. Mr. J. If. \Yardman, a Socialist who was in the Audience, suddenly exclaimed "They are using chemicals." He was seen to be remonstrating with some well-dressed youths who, it appears, bad been saturating rags with the contents of a bottle and throw- ing them tmder the seats. The smell was most offensive and Mr. Wardman remarked, " It is impossible to sit here, Mr. Cook." Mr. Wardman immediately eat down amidst laughter. Be, however, seized the bottle, whioh was found to contain bisulphide of carbon. The CHAIRMAN uttered a stern rebuke to the youths who, after Miss Royden's sreecb, made their exit from the hell.

....... Miss (rex Iluo Anurgr addressed the meeting. She did noVadvocate violent methods but if every woman taxpayer bad the courage of Mrs. Despord and refused to pay taxes without representation, they would have the vote to-morrow. (Applause). She referred to the good results of women's suffrage in Australia, pointing out that women did not vote as a sex any more than men did and in the main their politics were much the came as the politics of the men. They might emphasise one side of progress more especially,such as temperance- reform, but in the main their presence was indicated more by the discovery of new unbjesk, matter than by defection of opinion on present subjects. Sccial problems in Australia were being dealt with in a far more satisfactory manner and there was far less improvidence and misery than in England. Australia might well Ku to the mother count', : " Trust the women mother, as I have done." (Applause). Questions were then asFed by members of the audience and replied to by Miss Royden. One question was : So long as the social system continues, which is responsihle for the impossibility of all who want work to find it, is it not desirable or is it not favourable to the majority of workers that men I should have the prior claim to work, in as ranch as a I much greater sum would be received as wages in con- I sequence ? Miss ROYDEN said the right to work belonged to every human being and she did net at all admit that men had the prior claim. If it were true that a man received larger wages hecauses he had a wife and children the wife ought to have a legal claim on half his wages. It was a perfectly appalling thing to put a woman at the mercy of a men for a livehibood. Mr. NIGHTINGALE asked Miss Roycicu if she was prepared to support a plan for compelling the Govern- ment to grant State aid to women who were rearing families, where it was necessary. Miss ROYDF,N said she did not see any other way of doing justice to mothers than by the State endowing them. The mother was doing the noblest, most sacred, and most dangerous work any human being could do, Asked whether she was advocating votes for all women or only for women householders, Miss Royden said that as a member of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies she was asking for the vote

snd for that reason she was deprived of the power of supporting herself. Another question was whether if women got the vote they would run a political party of their own and cause ill feeling between the sexes by having their own candidates at elections. Miss 110YDEN said that in Australia and New :;ealand no sex antagonism had resulted from women's suffrage. On the contrary men and women had been drawn closer together by the fact that, they had a common interest and the women had become more public-spirited and intelligent on the subjectof politics. to be given to women on the same basis as it is or might be given to men. The Rev. %V. BRACECAMP said be knew something of the work women did thrnughout the country and he was anxious they should have the vote as soon as possible.. Mr. JOHNSTONE proposed a vote of thanks to the

Mr. W. MASON in seconding said he had been requested by the Committee of the Women's Suffrage Society to try to form a branch of the Men's League for Women's Suffrage in Warrington. After all, it was from the men that the women were going to get this modicum of justice. One wondered sometimes how men with all their accumulated experience and education could face a question like the demand for women's suffrage in the cool and ignorant way in which it had been faced in the last, four or five years. If one had a feeling predominant in one's mind at present as a man, it was that of absolute shame that one was a member of a sex which had faced the subject of women's suffrage from such a weak and vacillating point of view. He was glad the best men in every party were coming round to the position that votes for women were bound to come because the demand was just. The vote was heartily accorded. A similar compliment was passed to the Chairman on the proposition of Mr.,C. PLINSTON seconded by ,the Rev. W. BRACECAMP.

DISTRICT NURSES. A Year's Work in Warrington. Another admirable year's work in the service of the sick and suffering was under review at the annual meet- ing of the Warrington District Nursing Association which was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Alderman Smethurst (deputy Mayor) presided and amongst others present were The Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, W. Bracecamp and John Yonge ; Miss Turnell (the superintendent nurse) and other nurses, Mr. F. W. Monks, Colonel J. D. Fairclongh (hon secretary), Mr. H. Roberts, Alderman Burton, Mr. John Fairclough,Mr. C. S. Burgess,' Mr. H. Hope, Mr. George Walker, Mr. Fargher (in'quiry officer), and Miss Peterkin (the inspector of the Queen Victoria's Jubilee Institute for Nurses.) LETTER FROM MR. MONKS. _ _ _ _
The SEcn—Ei,iiii-ietietie-follOiviiiiif;ii;i (addressed to Alderman Smethurst), from Mr. Monks, the hon. treasurer of the association.

"24, Lancaster-road, 13irkdale, Sontbport, 22nd November, 1908. My dear Sir,—l regret I shall not be with you on Tuesday next, but I hope you will have a good meeting with an enthusiastic determination to carry on the good work without the everlasting diffi- culty of finance. My own view of the work and its beneficent results are well known to you all, and my Interest in the association is as keen as ever, and although eleven years has passed it has only proved the necessity for its continuance. I had hoped to see it free from any debts before resigning my treasurership, but that satisfaction I must forego. I have, however, the satisfaction of knowing that the Nurses' Home is paid for, and the only debts are for current expenses. As to the future I have no fear. lam confident that my fellow townspeople will not allow it to fall away for want of financial support. I need not dwell upon its usefulness and value to the poor who require all the comfort and consolation such visitation as the nurses affords them, nor tha educational value it is in the art of nursing, where only relief from pain and suffering is possible. Although no longer able to take an active part in the administration of this and other kindred institutions of the town, I still continue to take a deep interest in their success, and all that pertains to the welfare of my native town." (Applause). THE REPORTS, The itth annual statement of the late hon. treasurer pointed to the neessity of a more permanent source of income adequate to the needs of the association. If it had not been for the special effort made by Alderman Smethurst they would have been face to face with a large debt requiring a considerable sum for interest alone. As it was they owed the bank £62 14s. id., and unless their subscriptions were considerably increased, they would gradually get behind again. They could not expect special subscriptions every year. The Working Men's Committee had done very well, and a more systematio collection would help matters. It was a matter for regret that congregational collections showed a continued failing off. Leaving out the special collec- tion of £358 4s. Gd., the total InCOMA had been £465 Gs. 4d., against an expenditure of £BB3 16g. Gd., showing a net loss on the year of .£llB 108. 2d. The Committee's report stated that the committee were glad to give assurance that the need and value of the insti- tution were as great and as good as ever.lt was intended to adopt early measure in bringing the institution more cogently before the various people and societies in the tovrn,so as to secure a more widespread interest and more adequate and general support. The hopes were cherished that upon the appeal they presented, the response would bOcome more commensurate with the requirements. The report of the Superintendent Nurse showed that the totarnumber of cases nursed was 487 and the visits paid 12,777. ELECTION OF OFFICERS. _

The following officers efeerii:—President,Lord Lilford ; vice-presidents, the Rev. Canon Willis, Mr. Ziba Armitage, Mr. J. J. Bleckly, Mr. W. H. Bleckl7, Lieutenant-Colonel J. D. Bucktcn Mr. J. Smethurst bnd the Mayor, Lady Greenell, Lady Walker, Mesdames Armitage, Buckton, Crosfield, Frost, 11. Greenell, Long, Lyon,. Parr and Willis ; hon. treasurer, Mr. Henry Roberts ; hon. secretary, Lieutenant-Colonel J. D. Fairclough ; committee of management, Mrs. Broad- bent, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Fairclough, Mrs. Jchn Fair- dough, Mrs. Harrison, Miss Massy, Mrs. Monks, Mrs. Roberts, Mr-. W. P. itylands, Mrs. R. Smith,Lieutenant Colonel Buckton, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Mr. J. Fair- dough, Mr. J. Fargher, Mr. Hope, Dr. Joseph, Dr. Langdale, Mr. G. Walker, Rev. Father Wilson, Rev. John Y one and Mrs. Yonge, Alderman Smethurst ; superintendent, Miss 'Purnell; Nurses, Miss McGregor, Miss Rennie, Miss Leake, Miss Foster. , NEW RULE.

_ The rules were approved with the exception of role 14, which WEIS altered to read as follows :—" That the services of the nurses are free of charge to the really poor, but those who are in more comfortable circum- stances, and who have appreciated the services of the nurses, are expected to contribute to the funds of the society." WORK EXPLAINED.

Miss PP:TERI:IN then delivered a highly interesting address on the work of the institution, and the Mayor and several other gentlemen also spoke most highly of the self-sacrificing labours of the nurses. In answer to the Rev. W. Bracecamp, Mr. HOPE said that anyone sending to Miss Turnell could have a curse, but the Superintendent would decide if it was a suitable case, and would take steps to see that a doctor attended. The SECRETARY: The cases must be attended by a doctor. Rule 12 states :—" All new cases should be sent to the Lady Superintendent at the Nurses home. The cases may be sent by medical men, clergy and ministers of all denominations, and other persons and societies working amongst the poor."

div.head: 'TUE iVORINGMEN'S COMMITTEE.

The annual meeting of the. Workingmeh s Committee was held at the Town Hall on Monday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) presiding. LIVING ON STILTS. The people live on sixteen-foot stilts in the rentarkahle turpentine-growing count ry of France. They don these stilts after break- ' last. They do not remove them again till -it is time for bed. There are two reasons for the wearing of these stilts. One is the tur- ,Pcntine gathering. The other is the herding -of the great flocks. The turpentine comes -from the maritime pine. The tree is tapped, 'l,l shingle is inserted, and from the shingle is ,hung a tiny bucket, into which the turpentine Young pine trees are tapped low, but with each year's passage the incision is made higher up, so that it is not long before most 'of the trees are tapped twenty or thirty feet from the ground. Hence the huge stilts of the workmen. On these stilts they traverse the flat country, covering five to six yards Avith one stride.

div.head: HOBBY-LIOIt6/1 IN A PULPIT.
div.p: HOBBY-LIOIt6/1 IN A PULPIT.

A curiosity which never fails to excite the interest of all visitors to the old parish church of Berkewell, near Coventry, is a very high saddle shaped stool, known as the pul- pit hobby-horse, to be seen in the vestry. It seems that about the year 1750 the rector of Berkswell was wry fond of riding, and it is said that he was far more at home in the saddle than he was in the pulpit. So he had s stool made with the seat padded and shaped like a saddle, which could be placed in the pulpit efore he ascended the steps, and on which he could sit whilst delivering his sermon, instead of standing. By this means he hoped to infuse more life and spirit into his sermon.

div.head: POTATO BILLIARD BALLS.
div.p: POTATO BILLIARD BALLS.

The potato is used in France to make tistioa meerschaum pipes and billiard-balls. Aire er the potatoes are peeled they are kept for thirty-six hours in an eight per cent. eolu. tion of sulphuric acid. They are then dried and pressed hard enough for use in making pipes. Under strong pressure they become solid enough to be turned into billiard-balls.

CRADLE OF CORNISH CHRISTIANITY.

In the obscure Cornish village of Perran- '2abuloe, lying almost amidst the sandhills •that stretch from Perranporth to Newquay, 'there may be seen the now fast disappearing l'ernains of the earliest Christian Church in ugland. It is known as St Piran's Qira- tory, and was built somewhere at the close of -the sth century, A.D. At an early datek, which 'cannot be fixed with any degree of certainty, iolent sandstorms swept over the church it rid buried it. In 1835 a violent storm swept a Portion of the sand away and uncovered a •e, orner of the Oratory. Interest was then "Atm in preserving the remains, but the Wind and rain have nearly demolished the urch, and what was the cradle of Cornish tvhristianite is in danger of becoming a rub-. uish heap.

div.head: nu lIRTII-11TING HABIT.
div.p: nu lIRTII-11TING HABIT.
An investigation of geophagy, or the earth- .eiting habit, has shown that its eXCUECS in- 'elude a liking for the odour and taste of the Irztriety ,of clay eaten, an unnatural craving

to aisease, an attempt to sansvy nunger, the force of example, and supposed medicinal virtues. The habit seems to exist all over the world. Fine clay, or stone butter, is eaten on bread in Germany, and earth is baked in bread in Sweden and the Kola peninsula, and is found in the markets of parts of Italy. The Persians use it in sweetmeats; the Nubians as medicine. Gray shale is much eaten in Northern India. Another great delicacy is soil containing white ants and their net.

The queerest house in the world is pro- bably the famous Bone Cabin in Wyoming, near the Medicine Bow river. This cabin's foundations are built of fossil bones. Bones of dinosaurs—jaws of the diplodocus, teeth of the brontosaurus, knuckles of the ichthyosau- rus, vertebrae of the camarasaurus, chunks of the barosaltrue, the eatiasaurus, the brachiosaurus, the stegiosaurus, the ornitho- lestes, or bird - catching dinosaur all entered into this wonderful cabin's foundations. This hut was built by a Mexican sheepherder, who had kap- pened by chance on the grandest extinct animal bed in the world. This was a plot about fifty yards square, wherein lay in rich profusion the bones of all the animals of the Ileptilian Age. The place was evidently once a river bar, and the dead bodies that floated down the stream were arrested to lie there for hundreds of thousands of years.

div.head: CHRISTIANITY AND SOCIALISM.
div.p: CHRISTIANITY AND SOCIALISM.
REV. DR. BALLARD'S INTERESTING LECTURE.
Sharp Criticism of Mr Blatchford's Views

"Christianity and Socialism" was the subject of a highly interesting lecture delivered in Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Monday evening by the Rev. Dr. Frank Ballard. There was a large attendance and for two hours Dr. Ballard held the close attention of his audience by a masterly exposition of a 15ifilcult and controversial subject Mr. E. J. Guest presided and was supported by the Revs. E. Blanshard Keeling, T. Miller, F. Walwvn Kernick, and J. B. Buglass and Mr. J. C. Holland "(president of the Circuit Bible Class League.) Mr. Frank Hickman was at the organ. The CHAIRMAN said it was a high privilege to have a man like Dr. Ballard, who was an expert and bad given special attention to the subject, in their midst that evening. The problems which perplexed all thoughtful minds were many and perhaps there was no problem greater than that of Socialism. He must frankly say that he was not a convert to Socialism 1.9 he knew it, but he was ouite willing to sit at the feet of Dr. Ballard and hear at that could be said in favour of it. They had reason to thank the Socialists for bringing before them very prominently the great evils which existed in society at the present time. But he did not think Socialism would pnt an end to selfishners, neither did he think the capitalist had a monopoly of selfishness. It was in human nature through and through and there was only one things° far as he could see which was going to put an end to selfishness in any heart, and that was the religion of Jesus Christ. It was only as the mind of Christ was taken hold of and brought into our minds that we became self-sacrificing and self-denying. He held that Christianity was alone able to remedy the evils that existed amongst us.fre did not think that Socialism would tend to improve the material well-being of this country. Competition was necessary to bring out the very best that was in a man. He quite admitted that the workingclasses did not at present receive a fair share of the profits which were gained in manufacturing and they ought to share more fully in them. lie believed that if the habits of the workingclasses were better, we should all rejoice if their wages were considerably greater because if the increased money were spent judiciously and wisely it would tend to their own comfort and to the well-being of the community at large. The competition in our midst was often-times very cruel and tyrannical and , unfair and be would like, if it were possible, to make it criminal on the part of any capitalist to unfairly crush out the life of smaller tradesmen. (Hear, hear.) He was willing and anxious to he taught by Dr. Ballard and if the lecturer convinced him that Socialism was right, he would join the ranks. (Applause.) The Rev. Dr. 11.kr.t.krtn said that what the Chairman took for granted was very mildly expressed hut he was afraid there were some Methodists who would think it was very dreadful. (Laughter). Next week in one of the large cities of our land he (Dr. Ballard) had to take Tart in a number of Christian services with a view to trying to help his fellow-men to become better, and there were some very devout and godly Methodists there who had absolutely declined to give a half-penny towards the expenses because he was such a dreadful man, known as a Socialist and revolutionist. (Laughter) They in Warrington took that for granted with equanimity. They roust be larger minded in Warrington and he was very glad to know that, for it was time some Christians were larger-minded. There were repre- sented in the title of his lecture what he thought they might all without any risk agree to call

THE GREATEST FORCES OF OUR AGE, At all events of the land in which we lived. There were some on either side whose policy appeared to be-little those who differed from them. There were some Socialists who thought it was their wisest plan to be- little and do other things to Christianity. They said it would soon be over and they could afford to despise it. On the other hand there were some Christians who regarded Socialism as just a passing wave and thought that if they would only let it severely alone it would, to use their not very classic expression, fizzle out. (Laughter.) The marvel to him was that they did not see that all the time it was fizzling in. (Laughter.) Whether they agreed with Socialism or not, they had to consider it and the first thing they had better do that night was to understand their terms. The Chairman dropped that little parenthesis which was very important and significant—he did not agree with Socialism "as he unders' ad it." That he (Dr. Ballard) was inclined to think was the crux of the whole matter, for out of twenty people who talked about Socialism, he was inclined to think there were at least seventeen who did not understand it, judging by the remarks they made, especially amongst Christian people. He would ask them to distinguish in Christian AS in social matters between the- principles of the Christian faith and the practice of it as they might perhaps observe it in SOMA of its devotees. Ho was not responsible for ecclesiasciciarc, traditionalism, or Churchianity, or any of those representations of Christianity with which Church history made them fAmiliar. Ile spoke to them of the Christianity of the New Testament and it was sufficient for their purpose that night to define that as being the mind of Jesus Christ as set forth in the New Testament when the New Testament was honestly interpreted by itself. To use n shorter formula, it would be sufficient to define it as " The mind that was in Christ." They might also take ths Christian Church as being composed of a body of men who accepted the teaching and the revelation of :testis Christ as to the character of God and His laws for social service. Dealing with

div.head: SOCIALISM
div.p: SOCIALISM
Dr. Ballard qaoted a -n-u-r-aTwO-f anthoritles, suel as

Professor Graham,Professor St:baffle and Nir.Tl.G.Wells, to arrive at a definition. Professor Graham pointed out that it was impossible to give a single definition that would and general acceptance because the word was used by writers of authorityjn distinctly different senses. In the widest sense of the word, said the professor, Socialism was any scheme of social relations which had in view a more equal distribution of wealth or the pre- vention of two great inequalities, in whatever way effected. That, remarked the lecturer, would no doubt be the sense in which the late Sir lVilliarn Harcourt said "We are all S mialists now." Bat Professor Graham pointed out that there was a sacond sense which was perhaps the most used sense, in which the word was applied only to the aim and endeavour of the State to secure by laws or constitution gretter equality of con- ditions or to prevent too great inequality. There was also a third sense, in which Socialism was the system, economic and political, under which the production of wealth was carried on solely by the State as the collective owner of the land and instruments of produc- tion, instead of by private capi'. list employers or companies, while the distribution in like manner was made by the State on principles of justice. This, the only true Socialism according to its a Therents, was now generally called collectivism, to denote the collective ownership, or the ownership by the State as representative of all, of the land and instruments of production. Professor Schaffte said " The Alpha and Omega of Socialism is the transformation of private and competing capitals into a united collective capital." Dr. Ballard also quoted from the manifestoes of the Independent Labour Par.y, the Fabian Society, and the Social Democratic Federation showing that each aimed at the emancipation of land and capital front individual and class ownership and vesting it in the community for the general benefit. The lecturer remarked that

div.head: ONE OF TUE COMMONEST OBJECTIONS
div.p: ONE OF TUE COMMONEST OBJECTIONS

to anything savonring or Socialism was that it would be the death of the individual and his initiative, but that was only one of many misconceptions. As a lead- ing Socialist writer pat it : "It is the aim of a rational Socialism to regulate, co-ordinate and strengthen individual action." The aim of Socialists was in a very real sense a revolution—not necessarily anarchical and cataclysmic, not accomplished by dynamite or bombs, but none the less real for being gradually an alteration of ths present conditions. As regarded the motive and aim which Socialists had in view, there neither ought to be nor was there any contradiction or conflict what- ever between Socialism and Christianity. Taken in its broadest sense, every man who was a Christian, if he deserved the name, ought to feel exactly as Socialism did in regard to the sicutalities and facts around us and the desirability of substituting for them something very much better. He did not think it was necessaiq to harrow their feelings or span] time in reminding them of the things which were unsatisfac- tory. The facts were tragic enough. Mr. !Coble, a young Wesleyan minister and a real Christian Socialist, wrote : " There is in the modern world the grossest inequality of means and unfairest distribution of wealth. Nothing can justify, no service can make fair, the aggregation in the hands of a comparative few of more than two-thirds of the wealth of this richest country in the world, while the nruaining third is thinly spread over the whole vast surface of the toiling millions upon whose backs is reared the stupendous super-structure of industry, and commerce. Nothing can justify the facts that 42 out of 43 millions of people in those islands are practically at the mercy of one million wealthy men , and half of our entire income is the property of one- ninth of the population. One-third of the working ' classes of this incredibly wealthy Empire and kingdom never attain a rerurneration sufficient to keep them and their families in a condition of physical efficiency, let alone civilized decency and comfort, and over against this exists a mess of luxury and wealth surpassing the dreams of Crossus—roulti-millionaires living in incon- ceivable grandeur upon the proceeds of the labour of the whi`e, black, and yellow slaves, and all this in a I nominally Christian land and in a so-called Christian I civilization in Christendom." C3ntinninv, the lecturer pointed out that we had some 40 or 11 millions of people in these islands and out of those it was a fact that 10 millions at least were living on the poverty line, if not under it. They k lew his views on

There were millions of our fellow men in this land of whom it could not honestly he said that such a life was worth living. Every man, whether he was unbeliever or Christian, if he was a citizen or an Englishman ought to he most pronounced and deter- mined not merely in his judgment, but in his purpose that so far as in him lay, everything possible must be done to bring about a better state of things. (Applause) The chief aim of Socialism was to produce a great economic change. in that regard. there was no possibility of conflict between modern Christianity and Socialism. Where they came to the parting of the ways was as to the method by which the better conditions were to be brought about. Were they to part with mutual curses and recriminations ? Were they to differ as dogs differed over a bone, or were they to differ rationally, thoughtfully sensibly and kindly? The

div.head: si;iTort Twri "CGARfON"
div.p: si;iTort Twri "CGARfON"

said: "T shall oppose Liberalism and Toryism and Caristianityas long 119 I have the use of my hands. hut I hope that we shall have courtesy and toleration." But this was what the writer considered to be courtesy and toleration: 'lt is not the lack of ideas in the Liberal party that has made the Labour men begin to move" he wrote "It is the Liberals' utter lack of principle and sincerity." That was to say they were all rogues together. (Laughter.) He (the lecturer) most confess that he did not appreciate that kind of couresy, nor did it comport with his ideas of toler %- than when the writer went on to state: " Socialists will light for Socialism and will relentlessly attack and ruthlessly smash any and every party that opposes them." He thought there was a better way than that. Discussing the methods, the lecturer said he did not suppose any Socialist now would endorse anarchy and revolution. But there was

A :NEW SOCIALISM AND AN OLD SOCIALISM. Tie belonged to the new school in Socialism just as he did in Christianity. When writers on the " Clarion" found it such an easy business to twit Christians on the difference between modern and ancient Christianity, they must not be surprised if he turned gently to them and reminded them of the difference between new Socialism and old Socialism, because it was distinctly a part of old Socialism that there should be the employment of dynamite and bombs, anarchy and revolution —"Down with everything that's up "—and it was carried out in ce.rtain quarters in a very lurid fashion. Nowadays Socialists, with very few excep- tion., were net apostles of anarchy. Another way by which it was suggested the objects they had in view might be attained, was by Liberalism and philanthropy. That was a matter for thought and investigation and those who held that view had a perfect right to their opinion. There was a third way which he did not quite know how to .characterise unless he called it "Clarion" Socialism. At all events, ittiging by the attitude of the responsible editor of that p*er during the last few years, it came in the end to downright and even bitter

_ . ANTI-CITRISTIAN SOC lALTS M. A fourth wav,.which to his mind was the best, was what he called Christian Socialism—that was to say the adoption of the principles of Socialism and the carry- ing of them out on Christian principles and by Christian means. The lecturer characterised as absolutely false Mr. 11/atchford's statement that the churches had always been banded together to oppose the forces of reform. There hnd been cases of Christians who had been untrue to their Christianity in history just as there had been all kinds of freaks in human nature, hot that was no justification for so sweeping and wild a statement. The writer went on to say " The Churches must he fought and defeated. Tha people must be delivered from superstition and priest rule." Those representations were as utterly unwarranted as they were unhelpful and unfair. The Churches, whatever their faults might be—he did not deny that they were many—were not banded together against social reform and were not hindering it. Was any Christian to be branded as a narrow-minded obscnrantist simply because he did not echo all the sentences found in the "Clarion "? That was

TTRA.NNY GONE MAD. As to superstition Rn 3 tpriest rule, he sunnased there were some people in •orne Churches which were in danger of those things, tuft he must leave them to speak for themselves. For his part, and as having had to do with the Free Churches now for more yeors than he liked to think about, he was bound to sty he had never yet met in the vast body of Cnristianity represented by the Free Churches either superstition or priest rule. (Applause.) Mr. Blatchford said." I have been asked why I have gone out of tny way to at'ock religion. I reply it was because I found religion in the NVIV that I attacked it as a Socialist." Yet in " Britain for the British " Arr. Blatchford said dis- tinctly again and again that Socialism had

TIENTOTANCs To TEE,. riEvEr.IPNIENC TRUE SOCIALTiNt in this country as C., editor of the " Clarion." (Applause.) it was proba'Ay vain to hope that Mr. Blatchford would go back to his own better writings bet he (the lecturer) said this carefelly,end he spoke of what he knew—thet this propegan t of bitter and anti- Christian spite and ererlastingly talking about smashing the churches would do more harm than anything to the cause of true Socialism and the benefit of the community as a whole. Mr. J. Rernsay MacDonald rightly wrote " If we examine the personnel of the Socialist move- ment we shall see how absurd is the statement that Socialism and Secularism are one and the same thing." Some of the noblest workers not merely in the cause of moral and social reform, but of Christian Socialism, Reid the lecturer, were members and leaders of the Cnristian Churches. The Rev. J. H. P. Peilii, in the course of a Barnpton lecture at Oxford, said there was that in Socialism that came from Christ and made for his cause. its Peals were truly and profoundly Christian. Canon Wilson, late of Rochdale, expressed a similar view. All the attempts to set Socialism and Christianity by the ears, said Dr. Ballard, and mike fighting between them were unwarranted and unworthy and hindered the very developments they professed to desire to bring about. There was no religious reason why every Christian should not also be is Socialist granted that his judgment was convinced. There was no social or Jonomirs reason why every Socialist should not also be a true Chiistian. There was every rc.son for the benefit of both why every Socialist sheuld be a Christian and why every Ciaristiae, so far -as in him lay, should set before himselP the ideal of Socialism. Even when they found they differed in judgmaent they should at least go together as far as they coil I. He took it they were all agreed as to the unsatisfactory state of things ; that there should he more justice in the land and then there would he less need of charity that the way of progress was in evoletiel, not revolution : that "if any man will not work neither let him eat" and that as a corrollary there must be work for all to do; that in this country it ought not to be is crime or a source of ceaseless misery and shame when a working- man was permanently disabled; that ineteed of 53. e week there should be it minimum pension of If: a week,as in New Z.seland,for everyone who had worked until he was fifty and could show an honest rener I. C,omnetition and the accumulation of wealth mist be checked. MILLIoN: kr rays WERE MONSTROSTriSs, and it did not matter how much they gave away. Tee cmesLion was:how hal they made what they gave away? It ought never to be possible for a mae to become millionaire and it never would b 3 possible in a properly conducted crynnannity, tie did not rely crass re-plenty ; that would be unthinkable. There were ma :Lads of men and women in our land who never had a chance. Every man had a right to thie degree of equality—to make his life worth living as a child of God as well ae a hercten being and a citizen. ( Anplanse.) Socialism was an idial and if people said it wag a dream be replied "So is Christianity." There had never been a Christian country yet. There was no , Christian city anywhere, lie questioned if there was al Christian Church anywhere, although there were plenty with the name. Mr. Blatchford in "God and my neighbour " told ne that the present state of all airs I had come to pass because our nleirs were being run on anti-Christian lines. If al: this misery arose on that, account, was it not ti tie we tried Christian lines instead ? (Applause.) The difficulties in the way of I the Socialistic ideal were so real, so deep-seated, so enormous and complex, that he ventured to say earnestly that without the principles which were embodied in the religion of Jesus Christ, that ideal would Dever he reached—and more than that it was not worth fighting for. Apart from the Christian faith Socialism was an economic scheme and simply meant a larger possession of this world's goods to eveny man. What good wnel,l that do ? Mr. Ramsay Macdonald said "I candidly confess to you that I can see no hope for the future unless we can armeel to the char- acter of the people, unless first of all character is established like a bulwark in our midst. You cannot have things done for you and be men of character. The I man of character is the man who believes in self-help and self-respect. He insists on taking responsibilities upon his own shoulders, so that he shall not be the recipient of good things merely, but the doer of geed things." Mr. illatchford said man had no responsi- bility. If ha were not responsible, there was an end of character, and if cheracter was gone, where would we get reform from ?—Nowhere. 'Lee truth would be illustrated in human beings—which God forbid—that they might take a pig out of a stve and put him in a drawingronm but unless they altered his neture,he would turn the drawineroom into a stye. Unless Ym got human nature altered, we might alter all the condi- tions of environment and have men of the ape and tiger type still living. We !nest appeal to character and say that the rubbish about what was called determinism, instead of being a channel of social reform or ofSocialism was the greatest conceivable hindrance. Dr. Ballard quoted some telling words of Mr. Blatchford in which he pleaded the spirit of altruism—" Christ's glorious gospel of dove against man's dismal science of greed." Mr. Blatchforl said altruism was more important than Socialism itself and given nelversel love of man for man they would have something better than Social km itself. Then why in the name of Socialism. asked Dr. Ballard,talk about opposing Christianity ? The lecturer concluded with the following hymn which he s•vegested should be adopted as the song expressing the ideal of the Christian Socialist. These things shall be ! A loftier rat , Than e'er the world bath known shall rise With flame of freedom in their souls And light of knowledge in their eyes. They shall be gentle, brave and strong To spill no drop of blood, but dare All that may plant man's lordship firm On earth, find fire, and sea, and air. Nation with nation, hand in hand Unarmed shell live as comrades fre3 ; In every heart and brain shall throb The pulse of one fraternity. New arts shall bloom of loftier mould And mightier music thrill the skies And every life shall be a song When all the earth is Paladise. (Applause.)

div.p: MTNiSTERT VIEWS.

The Rev. T. Mii,r.F.n, in moving a vote of thanks to the chairman and lecturer, said no thoughtful Christian man, whether minister or layman, could be indifferent to the great question of Socialism. Ire personally ng,reed with what Dr. Ballard had said hut he wanted to know how the better day would he brought ahent. If property had to be bought from the present owners the price would be enormous and if it were not to ha purchased it seemed to him an ininstice to COnfr.Pate it. If the property were purchased, the wealth would n into bands which would make permanent the great class distinctions and since there was no assurance that all who were bought out would become Christians, they would still hive corruption and vi6P. If only that question could be cleared up his tendencies were in favour of Socialism as it anneared to be the only politics to-day which had an ideal worth aiming for. (APPlauso-) The Reg. P. ITA.r.wvN KPRNTC:i seconded and said he was glad to recognize that in a historic chapel of Methodism like that the question of Socialism could he faced and such sentiments could be uttered so plainly and emphatically by Dr. Ballard. Ever since he listened to one of the P ..napton lectures referred to by Dr. Bullard, a gradual impression had been growing upon him. At that time if he had any political con- victions at all, they were strongly on the Conservative side. While he would not at ',resent care to take the responsibility of calling himself a Social ist,his thoughts have been tending to one issue whilst Dr. Ballard was sneaking, and he had felt in the strongest sympathy with Dr. Ballsrd's presentment not only of Socialism but .also of Christianity. (Anplansa), _

The Rev. H. Br. 4NSIL.IIIII KEELING in snpporting he had been learning from Dr. Ballard that night that he was really a great deal more of a Socialist than he thonqht he was. (Langhtor). The vote was heartily passed. A BATCII OF QUESTIONS.
Dr. BALL:kno then answered questions submittoi by members of the audience.

The first one called forth a warm protest fro-a the doctor for, alluding to the previous night's address, it expressed a doubt if Dr. Bullard would have spalcen in the same way about Mr. Blatehford if be had been present to defend himself. The questioner said he would be glad if Dr. Ballard would publicly assure the audience that he was prepared to meet Mr. Illatchford at any time or at any place and make the same state- ments before his face,

Dr, BALLIIIII said there was not a vestige of a shadow of foundation for any sunh question. lie did not say anything against Mr. Blatchford, not a syllable. He was prepared to stand by everything he said but not by what people chose to say be said. (Apnlansel. 119 ANT 9 really sick at heart of this nonsense. If Mr. Blatchford would come and meet him he would shake his hand and talk with bins as he would with anyone. He bad nothing to say against Mr. Blatchford : never in his life had he written a word against him. Tie challenged the questioner to find in his (Dr.l3l.llard's)writines a single unkind personal word against 'Air. Blatchford. All be

hai June was to criticise his writings and he believed he was warranted in doing that. (Applause). I Another question ran : Socialism according to the Encyclopsdia Britanuica is a form of Government, held by certain people to be the best for this country. If S), what has it to do with religion ? But as in my opinion it certainly contains some elements of religion, can you point out any line of demarcation where Socialism ends and Christianity begins." Dr. BALIAIO3 said he could not, unless the questioner cionld point out in a water pipe the line of demarcation where the water ended and the pipe began. (Laughter.) fie regarded Socialism in one sense as an economic system but he contended that it was the only economic system which had in it the potentiality of expressing the mini of Christ as given to us in Christianity. The modern system of unchecked competition never could express the mini of Christ for it set men against men and ma le fighting the basis of social life. Another question was : "03 you endorse the Principles of the indeponilent Labour party ns a ! political force ?" Dr. Ballard said his business there was not politics but sociology. fie left his hearers to form their own opinion politically.So far as by politics they might help on the Socialistic ideal, he would certainly follow the gene-al political ideals of the Independent Labour Party. The question continued " Don't you think we should bring about better condi- tions more quickly if Christian people joined the Labour. Party and educated those of that party who do not believe in personal responsibility ?" There was a groat deal of truth suggested in that. He would have no objection to it, and if a Christian man thought he was able to do that, lie (Dr. Ballard) could scarcely give him any other advice than to follow his own conviction. He had not found the members of that party particularly open to that kind of influence, but leavening was a good principle. He below' there were net many of the independent Labour Party who did not believe in personal responsibility. He bad thought that the people who did not believe in personal responsibility were rightly confined in the places called asylums. (Laughter.) Another question was : "If Christianity and Socialism are identical, what is the need for Socialism?" Dr. BALT. um slid he had not said that. Christianity was a religious ideal ; Socialism was an economic ideal. They were not ident'cal, but one was the channel or the expression of the other. Christian principles stood for co-operation rather than competition, brotherhood rather than fighting. Socialism embodied that more than any other system Another questioner asked : "Is there any danger that if we call ourselves Christian Socialists nor, the outside world will come to the conclusion that Christianity itself has been a failure ? " Dr. BILLUM said be thought not, for the reason that Chriatianity was not a creed or a coat-iron I theological system, but a life. Some of their friends appeared to associate with the Christim faith a sort of ' crystallisation which found expreesion in the old formula " As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever I shall be." That was the rankest heresy conceivable. It never was true sod never would be. We were learn- ing mere and more of the mind of Christ every year. We had a purer and truer conception of the mind all f meaning of Christ to-day than the Christian Churches ever had before. (Applause). One question road : " Why should there not be millionaires ?"

Dr. flAr.r. tun sail for many reasons. In the Rrst place, because as a rule they had bettor say nothing about the way in which millionaires' money was made. Even if they held there was no dishonesty involved in it, there was a rotten condition of commercial and civil life which made it possible. He did not under- stand how Christian Churches count so demean them- selves as to go cap in hand and ask millionaires fJr money. _ _

" How is it the parsons are only just connecting themselves to Socialism ?" asked one questioner. Dr. Elam. tRD lam a afraid, to begin with, they are not doing that. (Laughter.) I wish they were. Some lof them are, and I say it is bectuse some parsons are learning more quickly than others. The question continued "Es not this a matter which reflects on them and their previous honesty in the leadership of their congregations ?" Dr. B tr,r,t.ran : No it is not. It is a rattter which shows their personal honesty acknowledging they I have something to learn, and setting themselves to learn I it. I wish all our friends outside the Churches would Ido the same. (Applause.) It >plying to the Rev. T. Miller, Dr. B tr.rAtto said there were economic difficulties in the way which were lenormous. No Socialist proposed that there- should be one magnificent coup by which everybody should ho robbed of everything and all things should be dis- tributed. They proposed to proceed by evolutionary steps. As instancing the lines on which Socialists would proceed, Dr. Ballard referred to the successful management of puhlic undertakings and conveniences by the municipalities. He hop,: Ihe would live long enough to seethe railways nationalised. It belonged to the very essence of Socialism that there should be a gradual development. There were not nearly so many and great difficulties in the way of Socialism as a com- munistic or social scheme, as there were in the way of Christianity as a scheme of moral character. They all acknowledged that the social millennium was distant, Ibut there was something immediate, and that was what Christianity stood for. Personal character was never lost, hut was the best and utmost that any man could contribute to social evolution.
GOLF.
