NEW CMTDE TO THE HOLY I. AND. The Rev. J. W. Miller. 8.A., of L.icester, who has conducted many partios to the Holy Land, has just issued " The Uniryne Guido to the Mediterranean, the Holy Land and Egypt." Mr. Miller's experience has convinced him that many of the regular guide books are practically useless owing to the facts that they are over-,,urdened with matter, their maps are too large and flirosv,and difficult to consult. Mr. Miller's guide is of a handy, pocket size, the maps are all on separate , pages with descriptive matter alongside or below, and could easily be studied while the tourist was on horse- back. Moreover Mr. Miller has drawn his maps so , that instead of conveying a useless bird's eye view they bring historical and other features of the landscape to the attention of the traveller in the sequence in which he approaches them. The guide is strongly- bound, clearly-printed, and should be invaluable for future tourists.

div.head: ITCHING TORTURES YIELDED TO CUTICURA

"While I was doing missionary work In the lower portion of several cities I found it necessary to know a little of the efficacy of a few medicines and after a white I found that a little knowl- edge of Cuticura was about all I needed. One of the very bad cases I had to deal with was that of a young 'woman who had come to us not only broken ixt spirit but in a most awful condition physically. Our doctor examined her and told us that she had scabies (the Itch), incipient paresis, rheumatism., etc., brought on from exposure and the effects of her ragged-edged life. Her poor body was a mass of sores from scratching and she was not able to retain solid food. We tried many things, a good tonic was prescribed and baths with a rubbing of lard and sulphur. We worked hard for seven weeks and you can imagine how discouraged we were when, after all that time, we could see so little improvement. One day I hap- pened to see a Cuticura advertisement telling how a little baby had been cured of a bad case of skin eruption, and although I had but 97 cents (four shillings) with me, I bought a cake of Cuticura Soap and a bottle of Cuticura Resolvent. When I reached home I was like a child with a new toy, and we bathed our patient well and gave her a full dose of the Resolvent. She slept that night better than she had since she had been with us and the next day I located the price of a box of Cuticura Ointment. I am not exaggerating when I say that in exactly five weeks this young woman was able to look for a position, being strong enough to work and full of ambition. In another month she left the home, strong and well. Laura Jane Bates, 85 Fifth Ave., Nevr York, N. Y., U. S. A.. Mar. 11, '07." The adage which declares PEACE AND that "It never rains, but it WAR. pours" found a new justifi-

cation in the Parliamentary proceedings of Wednesday. In each House there was what it is usual to speak of aa a " full dress" debate. The Lords were engaged in doing what was in days long past commonly described as Jeddert (or Jedburgb) justice. They were trying the Licensing Bill with all the duo formalities after they had sentenced it to death. Such proceedings can, of course, have no importance and, apart from what may follow, little public interest. What was more remarkable than the speeches was, we are informed, the presence of many members whom the oldest habitues of the Press Gallery failed to recogoise. "There are books that are no books," said Cusrmns LAMB. Similarly there are Peers who cannot properly be described as Peers of Parlia- ment, for they attend the meetings of the House of Lords only when it has been determined that something shall be done in contravention of public opinion, and in open defiance of tho House of Commons.

In the representative Chamber Mr. RUNCINIAN moved the second reading of his Education Bill. The circumstances are probably without parallel. This young Minister has sat silent on the front bench since he was advanced to Cabinet rank. He has been content to remain an enigma. Whether the PantF. MINISTER had good reasons for raising him to a position so exalted was a question that was left wholly without answer until Wednesday. Such resolute self-repression is rare, even if it is not unprecedented, and indicates remarkable powers of self-control and, as appears from the result, still more remark- able powers of keeping steadily at work in a predetermined direction, whilst pre- serving the appearance of inactivity. For whilst Mr. Ruszormax has seemed to be an inarticulate Minister, he has been conducting negotiations of the most difficult character, and, as it would for the present appear, has been con- ducting them to *a successful conclusion. In this instance silence has undoubtedly been golden, and now that it has at length been broken Mr. RIJN-or:wax will be recognised as a Parliamentarian of distinguished powers, and with the gift of eloquent and convincing speech. The Minister of Education frankly told the House that he does not consider his measure an ideal Bill. In fact, he abandons ideals in connection with a subject so thorny and complicated. He regards himself as a means of bringing about an arrangement in which there must be necessary impetfections. As he says of himself (recalling a phrase of Lord PALMERSTON'S) he is partly an arbitrator and partly "an honest broker." Both the brokerage and the arbitration have been most competently done. It was a great thing that Mr. RufscrAfesT should be able to announce to the House that be had not only won over the Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury,but the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Westminster. The leaders of Nonconformity, he said, had come to him of their own accord. They are so desirous of the settlement that they were eager in urging him to a compromise. This shows, we are bound to say, great nobility of spirit, for the Noncon. formists know quite well that, to use the plain phrasing of Dr. CLlFFortn,they are giving eighteen- pence in order to secure a shilling. The prospects of Mr. RIINCIMAN'S Bill must not , be judged from the discussion of Wednesday. It was unavoidable that all the most hostile opinion, from whatever quarter, !post at once come to the front. We have already heard the worst that can be said against the new measure, and it was all anticipated by the author of the Bill. Mutual forbearance and respect, as he says, are the only conditions on which a settlement can be made in existing circumstances. The settlement must be by mutual consent. There must, of course, be consideration of the House of Lords. It is a part of the Constitution, and it is better—much better —to arrive at an educational settlement which will pass the House of Lords, as this Bill will do, than to hinder education and to keep the whole education question in the cauldron of political controversies, than to wait for twenty years or more for the undoing of the evil'wrought by Mr. Bassoon. If the new settlement fails to last, then we hope no more time will be expended on com- promises,but that the Government of the day will go straight for the secular solution of difficulties which bristle round the question of religious education.

The evidence of Mr. Rocke- JIISTIFYIN'iI THE feller in the Standard Oil TRUSTS. case, now being tried in New York, reveals the mind of modern America. The suit of the Government against the Trust is taken on the plea that it is "a combination in restraint of trade." The leading note of the oil king's evidence was pride of wealth and achievement. The pride of the self-made man was apparent in the first replies to counsel. He started in the oil trade nearly fifty years ago with a capital of £5OO. Ten years later the business had grown so that the capital was raised to £203,000. What the capital may be at the present time it is not possible to compute, nor probably can Mr. Rockefeller him- self compute the wealth that has come to him from its operations. Wealth in itself is not immoral. Mr. Rockfeller holds that the Oil Trust has succeeded because it was able by the possession

of great capital to effect economies which smaller men were unable to adopt; and he adds another reason, which in his case is probably fully justified, that" I WR9 an able business man, my competitors were not." What does all this lead to ? It is the apotheosis of the iron doctrine ' that the weakest goes to the wall. Small competitors, having paved the way for business by the expenditure of capital and labour, found themselves confronted suddenly by a vast corporation which, by its " economies " and its power, was able to undersell them, to filch the business they had created, and ultimately to compel them to "come in "or "go under." From the point of view of a strict cold business man like Mr. Rockefeller, that was perfectly legitimate,and, indeed, it would be hard logically to dispute it. But whether it is good for a community that such power should rest in the hands of a single corporation is another matter. The significant fact is that tho view which Mr. Rockefeller takes of the means by which competitors were "bought out" is that which prevails among the great business men of the United States. It is the doctrine of power in excelsis, and it sets up wealth as a law unto itself transcending the humane creed.
Since the ascendancy of MR. BiaaELL's Liberalism in Warrington VISIT, we have been favoured with

visits from numerous promi- nent politicians, including two members of the Government—Mr. Lloyd-George and Mr. Sydney Buxton. To-day, a third Minister, the Right Hon. Augustine Birrell, K.C., M.P., is announced to speak at a Liberal mass meeting in Parr Hall and we have no doubt that he will receive a hearty Lancashire welcome. As the author of the first of the three Education Bills to which the present Government his addressed itself with energy and purpose, as the present Secretary for Ireland, and as a writer and speaker of distinction Mr. Birrell is au interesting and prominent personality. Few men in the Ministry have had heavier tasks to face, and none have succseded in earning greater respect, or have made fewer political enemies, than Mr. Birrell. It is Warrington's additional good fortune that he comes at a critical moment in the history of Liberalism, awl when a pronouncement from a Cabinet Minister will be especially welcome and, we trust, helpful and inspiring. Not only is the nation to day deep in the consideration of the latest attempt to bring about a settlement of sectarian differences in regard to education, but a crisis has arrived on the licensing question. After seeing the pluckiest measure of modern times—for remedying intemperance, curbing the power of the drink traffic and restoring monopoly values to the public purse,—successfully piloted through the House of Commons and backed by a huge majority, the nation is once more face to face with that grim fortress of reaction and class privilege, the House of Lords. It will need something more than a blast of the trumpet to bring down these walls, but a broach must be made in them somehow. They have too long frowned darkly on the Liberal Govern- ment's efforts to advance social progress. Govern- ment "of the people, for the people and by the people" is be coming a mere empty shib- boleth. The people elect their representatives to the legislature merely to see them produce legislative measures which are vetoed by an Upper House of Peers who represent nobody but them- selves. The situation might be farcical were it not so tragic. Here is the Licensing Bill, a measure which has occupied ax weeks of Parliamentary time and been hailed with delight by all the forces of reason and reform in the country, unceremoniously thrown out by the Lords at the dictation of one Trade and a few millionaires pledged to uphold the sacred (?) rights of property. It is time the nation settled the question as to who shall rule : the peers or the people ? Almost with his dying breath the late Premier said in tones which rang through the land : " The people shall prevail ! " It is time they exerted themselves to that end. Mr. Birrell has a grand text for to-night, and we hope he will raise the battle cry with no uncertain voice.

The trouble with regard to THE Goa:souNs' this interesting detail of PRIVATE ACCOUNT. Poor Law administration in Warrington has been described as a storm in a tea-cup, but it seems to us, on looking into the matter, that some of the ingredients which go to fill up the cup are not without interest, and merit some attention. The Private Aocount—which was euphemistically known by a select few as the Nemo Fund—is rather an old institution and was objected to by a Local Government Thud auditor so far back as 1882, but the Board never pursued the matter and the Guardians found the fund too useful to be readily relinquished. It has been maintained by the bank interest on the General Account of the War- rington Union, and for the five years ending June last the revenue from this source has amounted to .£556 17s. and the expenditure to .14!-.) 2s. A statement has been privately circulated among the Guardians, showing the disbursements during the period mentioned, and from a study of this document which we have been privileged to make, we have *drawn certain conclusions. There is evidently considerable justification for a large proportion of the payments ; they are legitimate expenses which have been sanotioned by the Guardians, but which might not have passed the fastidious eye of a Government auditor if included in the general accounts of the Board. But other- items seem to testify to the convenience rather than to the propriety of the fund. For instance, the entertaining of four deputations from other Unions and the "pioviding refreshments on Board and Committee days for Guardians and outdoor officers for over a year" is included in the statement, at a cost of £lO. There are also numerous periodi- cal payments for " spirits " during the five years, in all numbering sixteen, and totalling £4O 13s. In what way all this spirit has been dissipated is not revealed, but we may perhaps conclude that the administration of Ithe Poor Lsw is such dry work that it calls for fairly frequent refreshers. Luncheons and dinners, 'buses and waggonettes—doubtless on Poor Law , service—also bulk largely in the accounts. We notice, too, that when the Guardians have desired to express in tangible form their grief at the death of an old member or official there is an item for " wreaths Ells." charged against the uncomplaining Nemo Fund. The Guardians doubtless made a sacrifice when they decided at the last meeting to close the account. It seems to us that they took the only course open to them when the searchlight of publicity was directed towards the Nemo Fund. We do not suggest that the moneys have been wrongfully used, but it is quite obvious that such a fund is open to abuse and actually invites that suspicion which all public authorities should avoid like the plague. Let the interest on General Account be added to the Union balances. It will be more to the credit of a businesslike Board than the maintenance of a Nemo Fund, however elastic land convenient.

Death of Warrington's Oldest Butcher. A familiar figure has been removed by the death of Mr. Michael Finnerty, Green-street, at the age of eighty years. He was Warrington's oldest butcher, commencing business in the town over fifty years ago, and had had a stand in the Market Hall ever since the erection of that building. About forty years ago Mr. Finnerty opened a shop in Green-street and sub- sequently acquired another establishment in the same street. Latterly he had not taken an active part in the business but he was one of the best known inhabitants of the neighbourhood and will be much missed. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Tuesday,the Rev. Father Walshe,Church of the Sacred Heart, officiating. A large number of local butchers attended, including Councillor Singleton (President of the Butchers' Association)

div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
[FROIt OUR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.]

"History being made with almost breathless rapidity "—that is the chief impression created by the events of the last eight or nine days. The New Education Bill has been introduced, and has been welcomed by almost every one, except a few extremists on either side, as a very hopeful endeavour to effect a settlement of the controversies that have so long been obstructing educational progress. It is impossible to exaggerate the magnitude of the results involved in a successful pacification of the sectarian feuds that have made the schools their battlefield. Scarcely less momentous is the decision so lightly and confidently taken by the Lords, in a Party meeting at Lansdowne House on Tuesday, not to give the Licensing Bill a. second reading. For that decision is equivalent to a declaration that for any Temperance Reform the way is permanently barred by the House of Lords. An important measure to remove the financial and other difficulties which hamper the working of Land Purchase in Ireland was introduced by Mr. Birrell on Monday, and on the same day the Upper House dis- cussed a motion by Lord Roberts in regard to tba number and equipment of our military forces.

THE NEW EDUCATION BILL. It is not difficult to realise the motives that inspired the compromise upon which the new Education Bill is founded. The deadlock between two opposing views was felt to have brought about a situation that was becoming intolerable, because of the injury it was doing to the cause of national education. And it was at last quite evident that, if Nonconformists and Churchmen remained incapable of adjusting their differences, the secular solution was inevitable. Mr. Runciman's measure, which was read the first time on Saturday,goes a long way towards providing unity of administration, and while it is not feasible to dis- pense with contracting-out altogether, the danger that these untransferred schools will be inadequately staffed and equipped is reduced by the provision of a larger grant than was conceded in Mr McKenna's Bill. At the same time we are taken further away from the secular solution. At present it rests with the local education authority whether any religious instruction should be given in provided schools. The new Bill directs that Cowper-Temple teaching shall be given in every school to children whose parents desire it. GRIEVANCES REMOVED. The grievances of the Passive Resister are removed by the withdrawal of rate-aid from sclr,ols that are not under public control, by the abolition of religious tests and by the stipulation that, where denomina- tional teaching is given in the schools under the local education authority, the whole cost of this teaching must be furnished by voluntary effort, and that no child shall be compelled to attend a non-provided school. It is natural that the teachers, as a class, should feel some anxiety lest the permission given to assistant teachers to volunteer to give religious instruction may leave the way open for an indirect application of tests, and a preference, in some schools, for teachers who are prepared to give this instruction. But there are too many safeguards against such a violation of the spirit and letter of the new measure for the danger to be more than infinitesimal.

div.head: GREAT ADVAN rAG ES.
div.p: GREAT ADVAN rAG ES.

Some disadvantages are incidental to any settle- ment of the education controversy. But the advantages of Mr. Runcinaan's solution are very ptriking.. Public control, abolition of tests, and unity of administration, will be established in a large majority of the elemen- tary schools. If, as there is every reason to anticipate, the compromise is loyally accepted by the main body of English Churchmen, the number of Church schools contracting out will not be large. The increased grant, as compared with that fixed by Mr. McKenna's Bill, to the schools which do contract out, will, if there,is no great falling-off in voluntary effort, remove a great blot upon our educational system—the great discrepency in equipment and efficiency between pro- vided and non-provided schools. As grants will be allocated in a block to associations representing whole denominations, there will be a special inducement to denominationalists only to maintain schools in areas where there is a special demand for them. A GENUINE COMPROMISE.

That the -jonTqTr-oini-se is On a sound basis seems to be indicated by the fact that both sides are making substantial concessions. The Church gives up the religious atmosphere; Nonconformists accept the right of entry into Council schools. Certainly there are details which still call for careful consideration and the exercise of the same conciliatory spirit which has presided over the constructive work so far. The conditions of transfer especially are indicated, on the side of the Church, as calling for modification, though on the face of them, they seem to be both equitable and practicable. But it is scarcely possible to tolerate the idea that a plan which has been so successful in winning for itself general support on broad principles. should be wrecked on any comparatively unimportant detail. Mr. Runciman has accomplished a wonderful feat of tact and statesmanship in finding common ground for claims that have so long been in hopeless opposition. _ GOVERNMENT FROM LA.NSDOWNE HOUSE. It used to be a commonplace of Conservative denunciation that the educational policy of the Liberal Government breathed a spirit of pure malice against the Church of England. The absurdity of such a suggestion has been completely demonstrated. It will not be long before public opinion recognises, if it does not recognise already, that a similar imputation against the Government's policy of Temperance reform is equally absurd. All the moral forces of the nation have declared themselves in favour of the principles on vihich the Government has founded its licensing legislation. But such a declaration carried no weight at all with the gathering of Conservative peers who decided on Tuesday not even to give the Licensing Bill a second reading. The Government had deblared that the length of the time-limit was a matter for negotia- tion and adjustment. The House of Lords will not consider any time-limit. So far as it is possible to discover any intelligible ground for the attitude of the Opposition, it seems to have been dictated by the assumption that Mr. Balfour's Act of 1904 had gone to the utmost limit in reducing licences, and that the Licensing Bill of 1902 had gone to the utmost limit in regulating clubs. " Not another inch," was Mr. Balfour's motto. A great constructive measure which passed through the House of Commons with an impressive majority in its favour has been condemned without reprieve by a private gathering at Lord Labsdowne's house ! The second reading debate in the Lords, which began on Wednesday, is, of course, reduced to an empty farce. THE DEADLOCK IN LAND PURCHASE.

The tranquillity and well-being of Ireland, it is agreed by all who know the conditions of life in that country, depend upon the satisfaction of the widely- prevailing land-hunger, and the enlargement of uneconomic holdings. Mr. Wyndhatn's Act haa broken down through a miscalculation of the sum that would have to be advanced. Mr. Wyndham calculated it at f-100,000,000. As a matter of fact, Mr. Birrell told them in the House on Monday £180,000,000 woad. have been a more accurate figure. The heavy loss at which Irish land stock has been issued, and the waste of money involved in the payment of bonuses to land- lords who sold flourishing estates, where there was no , agrarian trouble, at high prices, account for deficiency. Mr. Birrell's measure proposes to guarantee .£10,000,000 instead of £5,000,000 a year for the working of the Act ; to increase the interest on Irish Land Stock from 21 per cent. to 3 per cont., and to defray the loss on flotation from the British Exchequer ; to raise the rate of interest paid by future purchasing tens on the advances made them for purchase from 3} to 31 per cent. ; to adjust the bonus on a sliding scale, giving a smaller bonus in proportion to the ntimber of years' purchase; and to reorganize the Congested Districts Board, and empower it to acquire land com- pulsorily outside as well as inside congested districts. The only hope for the West of Ireland is to be found in the breaking up of the large grazing lands. But this does not mean that the cattle-rearing industry will suffer. Mixed farming has produced the best results in countries like Denmark, and there is no reason why it should not in Ireland. A DANGEROUS RESOLUTIONI _ _

Lord Cromer pointed out the unerisdom of such a resolution as Lord Roberts moved upon the state of our national defences. It was liable to do great harm when there is so much nervous tension amongst European Powers. The motion, too, if it dissipated as it was intended to do, the belief that the Navy gives us practical immunity from invasion, would throw cold water upon the enthusiasm that prevails at present for the maintenance at all costs of our naval supremacy. Lord Crewe very properly refused to accept a motion that might afterwards be used to suggest that the Government had accepted in principle a proposal for increasing our land forces to an enormous extent. But the Lords were impervious to argument, and passed a resolution that would do infinite harm at the present moment if it were taken seriously.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Royal ceremonial is generally well stage-managed, and mischances are rare, but the " Manchester Guardian " relates an amusing episode in connection with a visit of the Prince of 'Wales to a certain Yorkshire city. There were some presentations to be made, and at the appointed moment the people to be presented were not ready. The Mayor, a hearty Yorkshireman of plain manners and homely speech, was much distressed. "Oh, my Prince, my Prince," he exclaimed, "there's been a nitch !" * * * Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, has long ago gained the reputation of being one of the busiest coroners in the country. On Tuesday be started work at half-past eight in the morning, and journeyed to the neighbourhood of Wigan, where he held two inquests in different places. Hastening back to Liver- pool, he reached Lime-street Station about quarter- past one, and after snatching a hasty meal he hurried bff to the Exchange Station just in time to catch the ten minutes to two train for Bootle. There he resumed the murder inquest at two o'clock, and did not finish his duties until after five. This is a typical and not an .exceptional instance of Nsf,r4.,P;righouse s working day. Alderman Bennett baying resigned the chairman- ship of the Finance Committee the " Observer" suggested last week in its pleasant way that as a -strong man was required the chairmanship would be offered to Councillor Fulton-Smith, notwithstanding that Councillor Wilkinson had been deputy-chairman for a year. We are glad to see that the Committee has a better sense of the fitness of things, and has this week promoted Councillor Wilkinson to the ,chairmanship. A man's strength is often an unknown -quantity until it is tested, but we should be incliiied 'to back Counciilor Wilkinson if it came to a wrestle with his deputy, Councillor Fultou-Sintth. * * * "The Dawn" is broken or about to break! In the • current number of this brig'it and cultured little periodical appears the announcement that the December issue will be the last. Like its predecessor Sunrise," "The Dawn" has only been able to flash tits radiant beams acros§ the community for a brief number of years. For many reasons we regret the failure of Alderman Bennett's little journalistic enter- •prises. They have had a distinctive character and considerable literary quality. On other grounds we can find a certain amount of satisfaction in " The Dawn's" approaching eclipse, dissolution, fading away —or what you will! Its brightness, in our view, has for some time been clouded by a high-flown Imperialism bolstered tip by Tariff Reform. The "cartoons for the people" have fortunately had only a small circula- tion. They misrepresented facts with a shamelessness which ought to have made even "The Dawn " blush. Then there is "Harold Wolfgang" a novel which has 'wandered through the pages almost since the dawn of time. We note that the hero has this month decently died and been cremated, and that the story is " to be concluded" next month. We had feared that the story might have contrived to continue its tiresome triviali- ties for another year or two. "Harold Wolfgang," a novel, and The Dawn," a monthly magazine of progress, have however decided to die together. With fervour we say : Requiseat in pace ! There is one malady which has defied the skill of of all the physicians in the world. They can alleviate it in some cases, but they cannot claim to cure it or to prevent it. This is the common cold in the head, which afflicts millions of us annually.—" The Weekly Dispatch." div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. The Right Hon. Augustine Birrell, K.C., 11 P., will address a great Liberal meeting at the Parr Hall this (Saturday) evening. A. limelight lecture on " Emigration " will be delivered at the Salvation Army Barracks, Academy- street, this (Saturday) evening by Adjutant Pinchen Of London. Herr Backhaus, the eminent pianist, and Madame Ella Russell, the great prima donna, will give a concert at the Parr Ihll on Monday evening. An admirable and high-class programme has been arranged, and there should be a crowded audience to enjoy this rich musical treat. The Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Porshaw) will hold an " At Home "at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon. The annual concert in connection with People's College will be held in the Parr Hall on Thursday, December 17th. Launch of a Coasting Steamer. The steamer " Agnes Ellen " about 350 tons dead- weight built to the order of James Henry Monks (Preston) Limited, was successfully launched from the yard of Messrs. Scott and Sons, Bowling, Glasgow, an Tuesday, the 24th inst. The ceremony was per- formed by Mrs. J. H. Monks' the wife of Captain J. 11. Monks, one of the managing directors of the company. The vessel is constructed to Lloyd's highest class (100 Al.), and will be fitted with machinery of 550 HP. by Messrs. Ross and Duncans, Glasgow. She a also equipped with the latest improvements. and is constracted so as to attain a speed of 111 knots. Warrington Grocers' Association. A highly successful social promoted by the Warrington and District Grocers and Provision Dealers' Association was held at Atkinson's Cal 4 on Thursday evening. The attendance numbered about 'forty and included the President(Mr. W. J. Kay) and Mrs. Kay and ether officials and members of the association. The prize-winners were : ladies, 1, Miss Carter ; 2, Mrs. Wm. Monks. Gentlemen : I, Mr. J. Be.id; 2, Mr. Dutton. Songs were given and an enjoyable evening was spent. Before the party broke p a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies /or tho support they had given to the function, on the Proposition of Mr. J. Gandy seconded by Hr. W. Monks. Wedding at Penketh. A pretty wedding was solemnized at the Wesleyan Chapel, Penketh, on Thursday at 1.30, when Miss 'Florence Annie Wood, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. David Wood, Mount Pleasant, Penketh, was married to Mr. Laurence Martinius Pedeston,of Blackpool. The . ceremony was performed by the Rev. John Gunnell. The bride was charmingly attired iii a pretty white Crepe de chine dress, directoire strle,with a white felt hat trimmed with white wings. She carried a bouquet of Choice white flowers. Her two sisters, the Misses Mary and Elsie Wood, acted as bridesmaids and wore pale blue dresses trimmed with white lace.T hey also wore gold pendants and chains, the gifts of the bridegroom. After the ceremony a reception was beld at Sankey Schools. Many handsome presents were received. Old Age Pensions. A. meeting of the Warrington Pensions Committee was held at the Town Hall on Thursday, Alderman t'ilethurst presiding. Additional cases to the nnmber or 222 were dealt with, making a total of 32 con- '3idered by the committee to date. LI 161 cases Pensions of ss. per week were allowed, eight of 4s. eight of 35., one of 2s, three of is. Piventy-one 4Pplications were adjourned owing to Poor Law ?elief having been received, ten on account of the l'lcome being above the statutory amount (one applicant as receiving 30s. weekly), three because they were "der the pensionable age,and three because they had tot resided in the United Kingdom for the necessary Period. Two applicants had died since their claims ere sent in. In accordance with the Act, no claim !a,rt be refused immediately but must first be :uiourned and the claimant given an opportunity of t‘',l3Pearins before the committee. The total amount of .1,; 'ea Pensions allowed by the committee is £BO ss. per iullE and they will become payable from January let
Parsonal. Sir Gilbert Greenall has been invited to accept the presidency of the Federation of Lancashire and Cheshire Agricultural Societies in succession to Sir Lees Knowles. _

We are pleased to learn that Mr. John Sutcliffe was elected last week to the office of Borough Surveyor of the Metropolitan B irough of D.3ptford. Mr. Sutcliffe occupied the p )sition of Assistant Borough Surveyor of Warrington from 18.1)3 to 1991 under the present Borough Engineer and Surveyor, Mr. T. Longdin, and left Warrington in the ' latter year on obtaining the appointment of Assistant Engineer and Surveyor to the Metropolitan Borough of Lomb3th. Mr. W. J. Ball,formerly assistant in the Warrington Rural District Council °Toes, and now deputy Engineer under the Crewe Corporation, has just been admitted a member of the Institute of Civil Engineers. Ur. B. S. Newcombe, surveyor to the Warrington Rural District Council has been admitted a member of the Royal Sanitary Institute.
Bnkss AND COPPER lIEARTR SVITES, see window dispky for now and artistic pitterns.—J. S. GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Town Council.

The monthly meeting will be held at the Town Hall at six o'clock on Tuesday evening.—Sub-committees have been appointed to consider the provision of more bowling greens, the formation of open spaces and recreation grounds, and the question of unemployment. Fire In Bridge-street. _ _

Afire broke out in the shop of the Queen Tea Co., Bridge-street, at 639 last evening. The firemen, with the engine "Captain," were soon on the spot and the are was put out in about half an hour. A quantity of Christmas goods was destroyed, but the loss is covered by insurance. Women's Chicle.

Mrs. Dunn presided at the meeting of the Warring- ton Wornen's Circle on Sunday, Mrs Hamer, Misses Croft and Tynan also taking part in it. The speaker was Mrs. Letheren, who took as her subject " God wants the girls, the happy-hearted girls, the loving girls, the best of girls, the worst of girls. He wants the girls to bo His pearls, and so reflect His holy face, and 'bring to mind His wondrous grace." Mrs. Peart's solos, "Peace and rest," and " Life's lullaby" were much appreciated: also a recitation from Miss Shaw entitled "Found dead."

Bold-street Wesleyan Band of Hope. In connection with the re-orgtnising of the above Band of Hope, a social gathering of members and friends was held in the schoolroom on Wednesday evening. A short programme consisting of recitations, songs, and dialogues was given by the members of Stockton Heath and Ellesmere-street Bands of Hope, and Mr. Hamblen addressed the children on the work of the Band of Hope movement. Refreshments were provided by the members of the carninittee and a profitable evening was spent. A strong Committee has been appointed to carry on the work, the officers being: Rev. T. Miller, president ; Mrs. Sutton, superintendent ; Mr. Miss, treasurer ; Mr. Wilmot Ashton, secretary ; Mr. A.. Brocklehurst, registrar ; and it is hoped that the Society will have a very successful session. Comlng of Age.

On Monday evening the coming of age of Miss Lily Boyle, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Alban Boyle, was celebrated by a dance at the Winmarleigh Cafi?, Sankey-street. There was a good assembly of friends, and hearty congratulations were freely indulged in. —Daring an interval in the proceedings the Rev. Fathers Roche and Marrs made some congratulatory references to the interesting event, which were responded to in suitable terms by Mr. and Miss Boyle. Another pleasant feature of the evening was the excellent singing of Miss Florence Brown, Ur. J. Rabbitt, Mr. James Bibby, Mr. Fieldhouse and Miss Boyle, their efforts being most enthusiastically acknowledged by all present. Mr. John Gibbins kindly acted as MC., while Mr. Underwood- ably presided at the piano, and dispensed some of the latest music during the dancing. A xery happy evening was brought to a close about 13), all having thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

A Builder's Chancery Action. At the Lancashire Chancery Court held at the Assize Courts at Manchester, on Tuesday, bef.fre Vice- Chancellor Leigh Clare, the case of Collin v. Itowcock was heard. Mr. Eastwood (instructed by Messrs. Spencer Wellhead and Co., Warrington), appeared for the plaintiff, Mr. Henry Collin of Warrington and the defendant, George Bowcock, and the infant defendants were respectively represented by Mr. Bennett and Mr. Abbott (both instructed by Mr. J. A. Bradhnry, Man- chester). Counsel explained that the plaintiff and his two brothers carried on the business of builders and contractors in co-partnership at 'Warrington. With moneys belonging to the partnership they purchased certain plots of land in Warrington and Stockton Heath, which, in accordance with their usual custom, were conveyed to their threo wives as tenants in common. The plaintiff's wife dted, and by her will left all her property to the plaintiff and the defendant, George Bowcock, in trust for the infant defendants at twenty-one. The plaintiff claimed a declaration that he was absolutely entitled to the one-third share of the plots of land vested in his wife at her death. The Vice-Chancellor made the declaration. A Pair of " DOULTON " ORNAMENTs make a choice and acceptable present. Stock ranges from ss. to .£5 per S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: Warrington School Attendance Officers' " Defection."
div.p: Warrington School Attendance Officers' " Defection."

- The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Branch of the School Attendance OXicers' National Association was held at St. Mary's Schools, St. Helens, on Saturday, Mr. Thomas Bromilow (president) being in the chain—Mr. Clough (hon. secretary and treasurer) submitted the annual report, which stated that the membership had been reduced by sir during the year, chiefly owing to the defection of the War- rington members, and with Ur. Rutter's resignation, received that dry, not a single Warrington officer remained a member of the branch, which they them- selves started on November 3rd, 1900. Now, owing to the formation of a new branch, for all officers serving under the Administrative County of Lancaster, which the county officers were in honour bound to enthusiastically support the Warrington Branch was further depleted, though even now there was no pros- pect of disbandment. The St. Helens men had been absolutely loyal since they joined. The accounts sbowed a small balance in hand. The old officers who remained were re-elected, with the substitution of Mr. Ainison, of St. Helens, as hon. secretary and treasurer for Mr. Clough, who is on tke executive of the new county association. During the year Mr. Martindale (Earlestown) attended the National Con- ference and was one of a deputation to the Minister of Education.—Mr. Clough was thanked for his services as secretary, and the Vicar of St. Helens for the use of the room for the meeting. Memorial to a Schoolmaster.

On Sunday last special services were held at Risley Presbyterian Church in connection with the unveiling of the stained glass window which has been placed in the church to the memory of the late Mr. John Wightman, who for 32 years was headmaster of Risley Presbyterian School, and for a very long period an office-bearer in the church. Mr. Wightman was held in the highest respect and esteem throughout Risley and district, and the window has been subscribed for by old scholars and friends. The unveiling ceremony took place at the afternoon service, when the church was filled to its utmost capacity, the pulpit being occupied by the Rev. J. J. Glover, who took for his text Hebrews, chap. xii, verse 1, and referred in feeling terms to the late Mr. Wightman's work. At the conclusion of the sermon the hymn " Nearer my God to Theo " was sung, after which, while the congregation remained standing and turned towards the window, Mr. Thomas Stringer, of Warrington, an old Risley " boy" who takes a keen interest in all that concerns his native village, unveiled the window, and read the inscription as follows,ve.. : —"To the glory of God, and in loving memory of Thomas Wightman, 32 years headmaster of Risley Presbyterian School, and an Elder of this Church. Erected by old scholars and friends as a tribute to his personal worth, Christian character and example. Died 13th, November, 1907' After the unveiling, the hymn "Peace, perfect peace " was snug, and the Rev. James Leas, Manchester, offered the dedicatory prayer. The musical portion of the service was under the charge of Mr. James Henshaw, organist, while Miss Clare sang the solo " Oh, trust in Him," in a fine clear voice. At the evening service the church was again well filled, the preacher being the Rev. J. Lees. The window, which is a beautiful specimen of stained glass work, has been supplied and placed in position by Messrs. Wragge, Ltd., of Salford. It is in two parts, the designs representing respectively " Faith," and Love."

div.head: EDUCATION COMPROMISE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMPROMISE.
THE GOVERNMENT'S NEW BILL.
Some Local Opinions.

A number of local gentlemen who take special interest in Educational matters have kindly responded to our invitation to favour us with their views on the new Education Bill drafted by Mr. Runciman (Nlinisttx for Education) and issued last Saturday. The following are the contributions we have received : REV. E. BLANSEIARD KEELING
(SCYPERTICTKNDENT WESLEYAN .IINISTE11).

"I see no way at present out of the Education Controversy. The present proposals will not, in my view, ensure Educational peoce. I would consent alinoq to anything that would do that. While the Secular solution would, lam convinced, only tend to strengthen and entrench those political and social forces which make for unrighteousness, and which are a standing menace both to freedom and purity, and as long as the so-called followers of Jesus Christ refuse to admit that there are simple elementary truths of religion on which they can all agree as the basis of religious instruction ; so long must the mischievous strife continue, with its disastrous results on the national life."

CANON MORLEY STEVENSON. "I do not like to give any definite opinion upon the new Education Bill until further light has been thrown upon some points which are at present obscure or uncertain. We must all wish for a peaceful settlement and a great responsibility will rest upon those ycho frustrate this desired end ; but, on the other hand, the settlement to quite be permanent and satisfactory must rest upon sure foundations and I do not feel convinced that this new Bill ga rantees this. The most I can say, at present, is that it may form a basis for negotiation which, I trust, may lead to a settlement that may put an end to the present state of unrest."

div.head: MR: E. J. GUEST, 13. A., IP.
div.p: MR: E. J. GUEST, 13. A., IP.

" My time is very much taken up this week with business and other matters and I am not able to investigate with sufficient care the many points which occur in the compromise on the Education Question which I trust will lead to a settlement. I only hope that the settlement will not tend to endow the Roman and Anglican Catholics and thus help them to propagate teaching which always restricts religious liberty and prevents the development of national life. But the controversy over this Education question has done much harm to true religion and any settlement that is come to on reasonable terms will be heartily welcomed. The vast majority of the people are standing aloof from all the churches, and I believe that tho bitterness engendered by this controversy has much to do with this attitude of aloofness. What the people know of Christ draws them to Him, but the beauty and grandeur of His character are obscured by the strife of tongues. Far too much time is taken up in fighting over details, and the things which are of chief import- ance are neglected."

MR. A. J. JOLLEY. "Those who really care about educational progress know that the Act of 1902 marked the greatest stride forward in English education since 1870. And most, if not all, who realise that upward evolution is a gradual process, would prefer to abstain from drastic legislative changes for another dozen or score of years in order that the great improvements inaugurated by local authorities under that Act might develop and ripen undisturbed. Unfortunately educational development is being hindered by the squabbles of fanatical sectaries and the Bill now' before Parliament is a praiseworthy attempt to secure peace. Should it become law in its present form it will enable local authorities to carry out still greater improvements, especially in towns, and in some cases to effect economies also. The financial proposals of the Bill seem to be fair in dealing with existing interests, and it is to be hoped that the Bill may soon become an Act and a period of rest from theological strife—at any rate in the field of education—ensue. No one who has carefully studied the developments of thought in England during the past half century will dream that this Bill represents finality in education. It marks another step tiowards universal system of free,compulsory elernebtary educa- tion, a system which, if not in the generally received sense secular, will be at any rate undenominational and non-clerical; the basis of a wisely co-ordinated super- structure, national and democratic in the hest sense, enabling bcrys and girls of ability, unhindered by poverty, to pass from the primary, through secondary, to technical schools and to the Universities.

div.head: REV. J. F. IkIATTHEVGS.
div.p: REV. J. F. IkIATTHEVGS.

" I entirely agree with my friend the Rev-. .T. Hirst Hollowell, Secretary of the Northern Counties' Educa- tion League, that the new Education Bill is the worst which the preseat Government has so far introduced. True it establishes universal Council schools ; but it permits contracting-oat. It makes Cowper-Tenipleism generally operative ; but it makes the right of entry statutory in all schools. It further removes tests for teachers ; yet it permits teachers, who volun- teer therefor, to give special dogmatic instruction Where an education authority is biased, preferential treatmeqt will be meted out to those teachers, who are more disposed to give denominational teaching. The whole thing Sir,is pernicious. It is no cure for passive resistance. We have not been fighting to secure a far more deadly compromise than anything which took place in 1870. Besides, compromise always leaves a rankling injustice somewhere. Moderate men who cannot believe that religion can be safely left men, the churches, but must call in the aid of the State, are in a pitiable condition. How the high Anglicans must laugh up their sleeve at the further state establishment and endowment of religion by Nonconformist ! Cock-a- doodle-doo ! Away with the whole thing ! To you tents 0 ! Israel !" 1 REV. C. HARVEY COON. 1 "Reviewing the Bill from the standpoint of freedom I from doctrinal and dogmatic subscription, whether I implied or written, the Bill stands in my judgment 'justified as a most reasonable effort of reasonable men lanxious to meet the reasonable (not unreasonable) demands of totally opposed theological schools of dog- matic theological thought. I agree that this Bill is not ideal, but I protest it is reasonable. Its regulations for avoiding tests (religious), its interpretations of school areas, of Elementary Schools, of all the points lunder the 12 Clauses and the Schedules, do strike ;me as conceived in a judicious and equitable temper. I held no brief for the Government, but as I read the I Bill I cannot but be struck with the larger charity and magnanimous concern the framers of it exhibit for the theological susceptibilities of Trinitarian Churchman, Trinitarian Chapelman, as well as for outsiders (Unitarian) like myself and for those who hold no Theistic belief at all. We have all been remembered. 'And as a citizen I greet this Bill with considerable pleasure. It seeks not to Hollowellise, or Cecilise, but to Humanise our Educational machinery, and make it adaptable to the heterogeneous needs of our cosmo- politan society. Unfortunately the greatest common measure acceptable to one theological party in the educational strife is the least common measure accept- able to the other theological party, so it is no wonder that Agnostic, Atheist and other non-theological believers, as well as many devout Church and Chapel folk are crying out :—" A plague on both your houses." I greet this Bill because it La at least an attempt to legislate for the citizen. I will be no party even though Ibe a parson to having my theology or anybody else's pumped into other people's children without the parents' consent. Education is the concern of the State,theology of the Divinity schools, religion of the religious, whether in the organised Churches or outside them, for I would remind those who need it, that there is a great Church in the world and of the world which has no ecclesi- astical organisation or architectural structures, and yet is of that spiritual order " not made with hands " eternal in the stuff we men are made of. To that Church, I believe this Bill will be acceptable—not as a final settlement of the theological squabble in educa- tional matters, but as offering a via media for this generation and an opportunity for the yeasting of the pre- sent hubbub to subside,that Se years hence:other men may be able to take a calmer view by having larger vision.l' MR. JAMES BALL. " I suppose most of us will agree that the term " Education " Bill is rather a misnomer, and the Government's present effort is another form of the everlasting religious disputes question. Frankly, on the whole, Ido not like the Bill. It is an armed truce, not a settlement, and will not in practice be any better than the system at present in vogue. The " Right of Entry " and " Contracting out " provisions are objec- tionable. The former cill weaken the discipline and unity of school life and be an unnecessary interference with the authority of the usual teaching staff. It also provides an insidious opportun- ity for religious tests for teachers who may or may not volunteer to give denominational instruction. Teachers should be just as free from catechism on personal belief as any other public servants. " Right of entry "involving varied denominational instruction in the same school to groups of scholars will confuse the child mind by accentuating differences of creed and church polity which are suffioiently troublesome in later life..

Contracting out sets up a dual system of finance and supervision, and provides a rather cynical test as to how far denominationalists are prepared to replace rate aid by voluntary subscriptions to keep their schools in an efficient state. The difficulty of supervising scholars' attendances will be increased.

The good points of the Bill are the increased grants from the Exchequer, the provisions for single school areas, appointment of teachers by the one authority, and the facilities for transfer of voluntary schools. The Bill could. I believe, by amendment be moulded into serviceable shape, but I have no expectation of it becoming an Act It is too Laodicean. REVS. E. C. E. CARLETON, AND J. B. BUGLASS. div.head: GUARDIANS' PRIVATE FUND
div.p: GUARDIANS' PRIVATE FUND
INTERESTING DISCUSSION AT THE BOARD MEETING.
I` Not Imitating West Ham."

There was an interesting discussion on the private fund account of the Warrington Board of Guardians at the meeting of the Board on Wednesday. It will be remembered that the Local Government Board auditor called attention to the fund in June last and the Guardians decided to terminate it, but since then there have been several suggestions that full inquiry should be made into the matter. At Wednesday's meeting Mr. 11. Bolton submitted the following resolution : " l'hat so much of the resolution adopted by the Board on the 2nd September last as refers to the time fixed for the consideration of the return showing the receipts and expenditure on the private fund account during the five years ended 30th June, 1908, he rescinded and that the return he considered at any time convenient to the Guardians." Mr. R. LEE seconded and the resolution was carried without a word of comment.

The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Mather) : All the members have been supplied with the return and if they wish to enter into the matter now they are at liberty to do so. MIS. COILING WOOD said that as she raised the question at the last meeting she would like to say the was perfectly satisfied with the report she had received. The CLERK explained that there was an item : Mr. Shearer, £l6 3s. 2d. of which no details were given. Since the return was forwarded, Mr. Sutton had supplied him with the particulars as follows :-22nd September 1903, deputatron to Whittingham Asylum, £3 las. ; deputation to Lancaster Asylum, LI 145.; expenses of inquiry rc settlements in Chorlton, Bury, Manchester, and past Derby Union, £2 15s. The CHAIRMAN (after several minutes' pause) : As there is no comment we will pass on to the next business.
Mr. EVANS : Do I understand the matter is finally close 4

- The. CITAIRMAN : Nothing is finally closed as long as there is mortal man on earth. (Laughter). Mr. EVANS : I don't want it quite so broad as that. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said he understood the resolution meant that Mr. Bolton had something in his mind which be wished to say. lie (Hr. Evans was not of all satisfied that such a resolution should appear on the agenda and nothing should be said. It left the Board in a worse position than before. He did not wish to remain there under any brand of dishonesty. Mr. FURNESS said that in introducing the resolution Mr. Bolton had taken upon himself some responsibility and the Board were entitled to an explanation from him.

Mr. BOLTON said he prc posed the resolution to give other Guardians an opportunity of speaking about it. The matter had been so largely discussed among the Guardians and the outside public that the time had arrived when it should be cleared up. The CHAIRMAN: Are you prepared to go into it this morning, or what are you going to do ? blventually Mr. BoLTON moved that the question be considered at the next meeting. Mr. GILL seconded. Mr. JOLLEY moved an amendment that it be con- sidered that morning. It was an undoubted fact that a, great many insinuations—so far as he knew, completely baseless and ungrounded insinuations—had been made and by associating himself with the resolution Mr. Bolton had made himself responsible for those insinua- tions. He said not a single word in justification of them but had deliberately associated himself with the tone or notion lying behind them by saying there was something to be cleared up. Mrs. Collingwood who raised the question at the last meeting, now said ske was perfectly satisfied. Mr. Bolton apparently was not satisfied or he had not the manliness to say so. Mr. RITCHIE seconded and the amendment was carried by 19 votes to 3. The CHAIRMAN : Now, Mr. Bolton, will you lead oft the discussion ?

Mr. BOLTON : I have nothing to lead off for. Any Guardian should point out anything in the accounts he thinks is not right. I think there is a lot wants discussing. The CHAIRMAN Well, discuss it now. Mr. BOLTON : We have got some money unaccounted for.
MIES BROADBENT said she thought that ,e hen a deputa- tion was sanctioned by the Board, the expenses came out of the general fund.
The CHAIRMAN :
In some cases.

Councillor EVANS said he was not going to enter into special criticism of any amount, but he did say that seeing that misrepresentation or misunderstanding had gone abroad, he was most anxious that the full facts should be given to the public and the public mind set at rest that the Board had not been imitating West Ham or anything like it, but had been setting aside money in a legitimate form for the purpose of using it in the best interests of the ratepayers and of the institution of which they were Guardians. How long had the account been in existence?

Mr. JOLLEY : More than twenty years. , Mr. EVANS : May I ask whether the auditors have had knowledge of this proceeding? The CLERK explained that in 18S2 the Local Govern- ment Board auditor pointed out the account to the Clerk and told him that in his opinion it was an illegal expenditure. The Clerk brought the matter before the Guardians and they intimated in a letter that they were prepared to fight the Local Government Board if the auditor made a surcharge. The Local Government Board replied that they would not give a decision but would leave the matter, seeing that the auditor had taken it up and they had been appealed to aft &wards, although in their opinion they considered the Guardians were the custodians of the ratepayers' purse and all moneys given to them should be accounted for in the same manner as all other moneys they had to deal with. The Local Government Board referred the matter to the auditor to deal with. He came round the following half year and the correspondence was shown to 'him but he said" Well, lam going to leave it alone" or words to that effect. From that day to this, no auditor had taken exception to the account until last June and the Guardians immediately dispensed with the fund. Mr. EVANS said that although a lot of the money might appear to have passed through the hands of officials, he recognised the fact that as the officials were only servants of the Board, the Guardians must be responsible. The late Clerk had been their legal adviser , all along the line and he (Mr. Evans) did not believe Mr. Sutton would have had anything to do with the, fund if he was not satisfied that it was a legal and honourable procedure. The CLERK : He has been prepared to fight it at any time and so were the Guardians. Mr. EVANS : What is our position now with the Local Government Board in this matter? The CLERK: I think we have settled it with the Local Government Board. A few months ago they sent a letter, and I was instructed to forward a reply. I pointed out exactly what I have stated to you this morning, and I have had no reply from them. Mr. EVAN'S : I have heard again and again, strong expressions of this kind : that there are ratepayers in this Union who are prepared to combine to ask the Local Government Board to make an inquiry into the matter. What I say is that the public should know the exact facts and so let it end. _ .

..„ Mr. GILL: Why should expenses of deputations come out of private funds? Mr. JOLLEY : Why shouldre.t they ? The CH A IRMAN : I cannot tell you that. Mr. FURNESS said he had gone carefully through the report and he must admit that there were very few if any accounts to which, as a Guardian, he could take exception. On the face of it, the money had been spent in the interests of the institution and of the ratepayers. The weakness of the matter was that as far as he could make out, the account had been operated upon by three or four individual members of the Board. Had their predecessors been careful enough before granting cheques on the account to have taken the whole Board into confidence,there would not have been the suspicion which had arisen. There was really nothing in the account to which they could take special exception. The money had been spent in a judicious, legal and honest manner. Certainly there were items, perhaps covering five years, that they might have taken some little exception to, but they were of such a character that he did not think the Board would be dignified or discreet in discussing for a moment. He believed the private account was originated by the treasurer of the Board presenting to the Board the interest which had accumulated. He as treasurer could have kept the principal entirely in his own hands without banking it but he had not thought fit to do sl. He said the account was worth so much per snnum and they could have the interest as a separate fund on which to draw cheques for any purpose the Board thought Eft. He (ilr. Furness) was strongly of opinion that no good purpose would be served by further discussing the matter. Had there been cheques for anything of an illegal character, he and other members of the Board would have been the first to have taken exception to it. To his mind, it was a storm in a teapot, but the Board had caused suspicion by allowing the account to be drawn upon in a very narrow way.

BACKHOUSE : Do I understand the private fund is now at an end? The CHAIRMAN: Yes. The CLERK : Mr. Furness says they are all legal payments. I would like to mention there are two or three that cannot be considered as legal payments. Mrs. SIMPSON asked why so much had been spent on spirits. She thought the Guerdians always paid for their own but money seemed to have come out of the fund for that purpose. No answer was given to the question. Mr. W. C. BROOKS asked whether there were any minutes on the books covering the expenditure? The CLERK : I cannot say that. I think there will be minutes for a lot of the items. In regard to the deputation expenses, they are all legal payments if they have been authorised by the Board and 1 should take it for granted that they have been authorised. The reason they have been paid from the private account is because the amount was getting large and Mr. Sutton has made payments out of the fund instead of going on to the general fund. I should say the Board authorised the deputation expenses. The other matters are not on the minutes, and if they had been they are certainly items which the Local Goveratuent Board auditor would not have passed. Mr. W. C. BROOKS : Would it not be wise if we sent all these particulars to the Local Government Board ? The CLERK : I have replied to the Board and told them exactly'how the payments have been made up and. I think they must be satisfied. Mr. FURNESS formally moved that the matter be closed. Mr. COOK seconded. Mr. EVA.NS said he took it that the resolution would not debar any member from giving special notice of motion if he desired tore-open the matter. The Cif AIRMAN : I don't think it warild. Mr. Houghton expressed regret that there was not a private fund in existence at the present time for one specific purpose. Nothing would have pleased him better than to spend £lO or £2O on some memorial to the late Sir John Hibbert, to decorate the New Infirmary and Padgate schools. fle would be glad if they could raise the money for that object even now, by some means. Mr. JoLLEv said there MS one point which had not been alluded to by any speaker and that was the main reason, from what he had learnt from Mr. Sutton and his late father, as to why the account was originally established. Anyone who knew anything about their work as Poor Law Guardians was aware how in many respects they felt themselves tightly bound by the con- solidated or 'ers and regulations under which they carried on their work. There were some public bodies, such as Town Councils, which bad a great deal more elasticity in their operations than was allowed to Boards of Guardians. Thee had been a tendency in recent years to relax the stiffness of the orders in some directions and some things were practicable for Guardians now which wore not practicable ten years ago, much less more than twenty years ago when the fund was established. One very important purpose of the fund was to give more elasticity to the work of the Git adians and provide a perfectly legitimate fund which, however, did not come within the purview of the auditor, to enable the Guardians occasionally In deserving cases to give relief to persons outside the strict limits of the regulations governing relief. There was another point as to the legality of certain payments. Amongst the regulations controlling their work was one which prevented them paying an account after a certain date, although it might be a just debt. On several occasions through some laxity or carelessness, accounts had been sent in after the specified period, and had been quite rightly and properly paid from the fun I. It was not a question on which any member of the Board need feel any hesitation in speaking frankly. Personally, he regretted the action of the Board in discontinuing the fund. If the Board had chosen, as it did in 1882, to stand up to the Local Government Board, the fund might have continued and it would have served in the future, as it had done in the past, a useful purpose in helping the Board to carry on its work with greater efficiency and economy. They must not think they were going to save money by discontinuing the fund. They were not. The resolution was then put to the meeting and I carried without dissent. '

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Love that IVomen Desire."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Love that IVomen Desire."

In "The Love that Women Desire" Mr. G. Carlton Wallace, a very popular dramatist, has given us a play of more than ordinary merit. It compels one's attention by a powerful plot, the sensational side is not overdone,and there is plenty of sparkling humour. The chequered story of Philip Carnaby, the dashing and impulsive yeoman farmer, and his sweetheart Sybil Thornburn is designed to illustrate the truth of the adage that "The course of true love never did run smooth" but, notwithstanding all that villainy and misunderstandings can do, everything comes right in the end and the couple are happily re-united. The joyous consummation is not achieved without trying adventmes and hair-breadth escapes for the hero in the wild regions of Brazil, and the many tight corners ! in which he finds himself rouse interest to fever height. Mr. Carlton Wallace's Company give an altogether satisfactory representation of the romance. ! Mr. Sydney Leyton takes the part of Philip Carnally with considerable dash and enthusiasm, while Miss ! Aimee Grattan Clyndes is a charming and winsome Sybil Thornburn. Mr. J. 0. Stewart as Squire Abingdon acts the stern, unbending autocrat to the life. Mr. Morris Mand as Richard Abingdon and Miss Jessie Elvin as Madge Abingdon are a capital pair of conspirators, always trying to compass the hero's downfall. The village constable rejoicing in the uphonious name of Salve rhurry, is pourtrayed with are skill by Mr. J. W. Wilkinson, while Mr. John Hignett as the irrep-essible Dennis O'Rourke c,uld not be improved upon. Miss May Neilson also con. tributes a great deal to the laughable side of the play as the pert Patty Swift. All the minor parts are in capable hands and the performance goes with a capital swing from beginning to end. The scenic effects are unique and strikingly beautiful, the Virgin Forest in , Brazil being one of the fiaest stage pictures ever seen in Warrington. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Local playgoers are promist d a treat next week when Mr. William Greet's chief company, now in its eleventh year of tour, will present Wilson Bareett's , great play " The Sign of the Cross." It is doubtful! whether any play has enjoyed greater popularity, and although it has been played over 13,000 times it is always enthusiastically welcomed, An excellent com- pany will appear next week, including Mr. Cyril Austen-Lee as Marcus Superbus and Miss Constance Little as Mercia. As most people..knoav, the play has for its theme the persecution of the 'early Christians, and the scene is laid in Rome.
Next week the theatre orehe3tra will be enlarged.

Visit of the " Hunger-Marchers." A band of thiity-eight " hunger-marchers " on their way from Birmingham to Liverpool visited Warring- ton on Monday evening. They left Manchester i shortly after ten o'clock n the morning calling at several places for rest and refreshment and arrived at Warrington at 7 p.m. A short open-air meeting was held at Bridge-foot when the principal speaker was Mr. W. Terrence Mitchell, the leader of the men, who spoke on the defects of the present poor-law system. The men, whose ages ranged from 25 to GO yeare of age, subsequently, sat down to supper at the Bridge-street cocoa rooms the cost of the meal being defrayed by the money which had been collected on the march. Nt ten o'clock a procession was formed and the men proceeded to the Workhouse where the night was spent in the casual ward. On entering the institution each man after giving his age,address, and occupation was supplied with a liberal quantity of I bread, but some of them returned it as they said they "did not need it " after the supper which had been provided for them at the cocoa-house. Their break- fast 03nsi5ted of tea and bread. They asked for butter but it was not supplied. The men, however, appeared to be very satiefied with the treatment accorded them and before leaving for Liverpool the next morning they gave cheers for the master (\lr. J. F. Awbery).

The Clerk reported the receipt of permission from the Local Government Board for the subscription by the Guardians of £3 3s. per ann,trn to the funds of the Chester Home Teaching of the Blind S3ciety. RELIEVING OFFICER'S SALIRV,_

The Clerk read an application from :klr. Pearson, relieving officer for the Fradsham district, for an increase of salary. Two years ago the Board increased his salary by £lO and he now hoped they would be able to see their way to give him a similar increase, making his salary .M 0 per annum, which was the amount his predecessor received. In support of the application he need only remind the Board of the exacting and onerous duties of the office which he trusted he had performed to the satisfaction of the Board. Several members of the Board having expressed them- selves as favourable to the application, it was decided on the proposition of nr. Woodword seconded by Mr. Hallows to refer the nutter to the Finance Committee.

div.p: AN F.XPiN- SINE SN-WER-IG,E. SCHEMN._

The Clerk reported that at a nieeting of the Halton Parochial Committee the tender of Mr. B. Oxley, of Ilelsby, amounting to £2,911 for the Halton Sewerage work was accepted. Mr. Wright moved the adoption of the minates. Mr. Stokes asked how much the rates would be increased by the scheme. The Clerk said he had laid estimates before till Halton Committee and he believed they involved Is. in the 2 for the year. Mr. Stokes : Will that include way leaves ? The Clerk : Way leaves will be very small. There is no question of way leaves with District Councils. If you do any damage in going across property, you have to pay for that. Mr. Stokes said the matter was a most serious one to the ratepayers of the district and there was a strong feeling about it. Ile moved that the matter be deferred until the next meeting. Mr. IVo9dward considered that the Council having delegated powers to the Parochial Committee, it was unfitting thit they should revise a decision of that committee which was anything like unanimous. Mr. Stokes : I hope this Council will always safe. guard the interests of the ratepayers and the public at large. lhe Chairman : That is our intention. The Council decided to adjourn the matter for a fortnight.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
BASELESS CEIARGE AGAINST A POLICE INSPECTOR. EARLESTOWN WOAAN'S ALLEGATION.

Before the Newton magistrates on Monday, Lewis Innes, inspector of police at Barlestown, was charged by Isabella Hope, a married woman, with criminally assaulting her on two occasions.—The defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. J. J. Dootson, who appeared for the complainant, said that on the 30th May last year his client was a single woman, and was in a certain condi- tion. She went to Newton Police Station to take out a summons against her present husband. She arrived at the Police Station too late to get a summons, and she saw Inspector Lanes, who afterwards arranged to go to , Warrington with her in order to get the summons. They went together the next day by train to Warrington, and the alleged assault took place. On their arrival at Warrington they separated, and met later at the magistrates' clerk's ofßce. • The clerk to the magistrates was not in, and defendant gave the complainant 3s. to get some refreshment. The complainant was severely cross-examined by Mr. A. Smith, who defended.—Asked why she did not pull the communication cord in the carriage, she said that she had no money to pay the floe, had she been con- victed for doing so. In addition to receiving 3s. from the defendant he bought her ticket, and had given her various sums at regular intervals since. She had told no one or the offence—not even the magistrates' clerk; and made no communication to anyone until some two or three months later, when she told a male friend named Shirley. After a brief deliberation the bench dismissed both charges, the Chairman remarking that the inspector " left the court without a stain upon his character."
CAPTAIN 11. RICO Al AN ODDFELLOWS ANNIVERSARY.

The annual meeting of Viaduct Lodge of Oddfellovvs (Manchester Unity) took place on Saturday at the Wellington Inn, Earlestown, and was attended by a member of the Board of Directors, namely, Captain Richard Rigg, M.A., P.P.G.M., and ev-lkf.P. for West- morland, who spoke on " The principles and present position of the order." Bro. \V. Sutton, P.P.G.M., presided, and Bro. Thomas Seddon, N.G. was in the vice-chair. In the absence of Bro. T. S. Steel, the toast of" The Manchester Unity Grand Master of the Board of Directors " was proposed by Bro. J. Grace, of St. Helens, and enthusiastically received. Captain Rigg in reply said they in the Manchester Unity were always prepared to hold out the right hand of fellowship,and say , " Let 'em all come, the more the merrier." (Laughter and applause.) They had accumulated funds closely approaching to £14,000,000, they had a membership of over a million and their lodges were spread over the four quarters of the globe. He had been in Oddfellows', lodges all over the world and he had found brethren standing side by side through prosperity and adversity, always ready to help one another. (Applause.) The Manchester Unity rested on a sound and popular basis and recognised equality of opportunity for all. As every private soldier could work his way to Field Marshal, so could the humblest of their members work himself up to the highest and most responsible position in the lodge. The great aim of the unity was to get the noblest and best from the members. (Applause.) He regarded it as a valuable training ground for men who had to take office in public or municipal life, as it was impossible to work without business methods in any capacity. (Applause.) He bad had the honour of eing a member of the House of Commons, but he

looked upon it as a much greater honour to be one of twelve directors of one million of OddfeHOW% the cream of the artizan population of this counoty (Applause.) A mu3ical progranarne WAS viz) thrviz.z

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
GASWORKS BOYS' STRIKE.

PROCESSION TifROUGli Sr. HELENS SPREErs. Some inconvenience was caused at If essrs. Pilkington's sheet glassworks, St. Helens, on Monday, when a number of boys employed as" block minders " and in other capacities struck work. These lads work in eight. hour shifts. and during the afternoon they asse nbled near the works with the object of preventing the lads who start at 4 p in. from going to work. The firm employ large numbers of boys and young men, and it has been the practice for years to pay a standing wage and' plus " money, but now the firm, it is stated, have decided to modify the system of p tyment,and announced to the boys that instead of the ptynsent for overwork a fixed sum would be paid for various grades of work, whereupon the boys struck work. Late in the after— noon the strikers formed in procession with concer- tinas, mouth-organs, Stn., and" demonstrated " through the principal streets. The number of boys who are affected is stated to be even as large as 20) or 300, but it is not clear that the disaffection is so general as this.

div.head: WANTED TO GO LIONfE.
div.p: WANTED TO GO LIONfE.

Richard Hifi, lshonrer, of 13)1d-street, St. Helens was very penitent at St. Helens Police Court, on Mon- day, when charged with disorderly conduct and damaging the wood bed, &c., in the police cell. When asked by the officer on duty why he had done this, the man said he wanted to get out and go horns. He was fined 103. and costs for the disorderly conduct and 10s. and costs for the damage.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A LOCAL DEALER. Alleged Bdylng Stolen Gods.
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A LOCAL DEALER. Alleged Bdylng Stolen Gods.

At the Warrington Police Court on Nfonday, Zichariah Z tremski, senor' !hand dealer, of Nfersay- street, WAS charged with feloniously receiving sixty- three glasses knowing them to have been stolen. The Chief Constable stated that on Saturday last a man named George Postlethwaite was sentenced to six month's imprisonment on two charges of stealing clothing and a number of glasses from the pavilion orr the Waarington cricket. The magistrates, on hearing the case, thought the purchaser of the glasses (Mr. Zaremski) ought to be charged as they were bought at such a low price. The defendant, who was in Court ea S-itiuday, was then arrested, The man Postlethwaite took the glasses to the defendant's shop on Sunday, November 8, and asked for four shillings for them, but this offer was refused, and he finally accepted two shillings.

It was pointed out by Mr.T. S. Steel, who defended, that Zaremski, being a Jew, may not have acted with the same discretion as an Englishman. With regard to the purchase taking place on Sunday, it should be remembered that Saturday was the Jewish Sabbath. The defendant was a man of previous good character, and it was unlikely he would risk his reputation for the sake of a paltry few glasses. The magistrates dismissed the case, the chairman (Alderman W. Forshaw) remarking that defendant had better be more careful in the future.
