div.head: CLASSIC RECIPE.
div.p: A CLASSIC RECIPE.

There has been much talk lately about a new rreparation for the cure of oh3tinate fatness —a simple harmless mixture that any of our readers can make up at home, after procuring the ingredients at any chemist's. This is it :—One half-ounce of Marrnola (in a sealed packet), one ounce of fluid .extract of Glycyrrhiza. B.P , one ounce of pure Glycerine 13. P., and Peppermint Water to make six ounces in all. This wonderfully successful recipe has become classic. The dose is tr-o teaspoonfuls after each meal and at bedtime. Stout men and women are by no means required to half starve themselves when they go in for this simple treatment. Let them rather increase their strength and fortify the nervous system by a little indulgence in wholesome and enjoyable dishes. Fatiguing physical exercises are likewise quite unnecessary. Nourishment and repose are as essential to health and beauty as is the elimination of the excess of fat, which, in the form of internal depositss is really dangerous and always injurious to health.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Presentation to the Rev. T. W. and Mrs. Barber

The dedication festival was celebrated at St.Clement'a Mission on Sunday and Nionday (St. Clement's Day).— Mr. J. J. Firth (Police Court missionary) delivered an address to the Sunday School children on Sunday afternoon and the Rev. Canon Stevenson preached in the evening.—On Monday evening the Lord Bishop of Liverpool preached an impressive sermon on the words "-Cast thy bread upon • the waters ; for thou shalt find it after many days."— After the service a social was held in. the schoolroom,

at which there was a very large attendance. The Bishopi having inspected the St. Cloment's Lads' Brigade, Mr. C. Gandy asked him to make a presentation to the Rev. T. W. and Mrs. Barber.—Elis lordship then handed Mrs. Barber a gold watch, and to the Rev. T. W. Barber a purse of gold and an illnininated address, and said he had great pleasure in doing so in the name of the people of St. Clement's. It showed how their work was appreciated. The address bore the following inscription : To the Bev. T. W. Barber, B.A. We, the undersigned, on behalf of the congregation and friends of St. Clement's Mission, Warrington, desire to record our hearty recognition of your services as curate-in-charge of the Mission for the past four years. It is impossible here to fully and sufficiently express how your services have been valued and appreciated. Let it suffice to say that you have established for yourself during the time you have been in charge of St. Clement's Mission, a place in the grateful and kindly remembrance of those who have been associated with you. This slight token of appre- ciation together witk a purse of gold, we beg you to accept with our hearts' best wishes for long years of health and happiness. November 23rd, 198, St. Clement's Day." The address was Signed by the follow— ing sidesmen :—Messrs. C. Gaudy, H. Broadhurst, T. W. Davies, J. Gray, J. 11. Houghton, J. C. Rhoden, G. H. Warburton Steel, J. Wainwright and Edwin Warburton. Speeches having been delivered by the Rector and Mr. H. Houghton, The Bishop said he was grateful they had done him the honour of asking M:. and Mrs. Barber to accept those presents. The Rector had reason to be thankful that he had such good workers as Mr. and Mrs. Barber, and he, as Bishop, was thankful that he had such good people working for hint in the diocese. (Applause.)— The Rev. T. W. Barber, in returning thanks, said he would ever keep a warn, recollection of the people of St. Clement's in his heart. He heartily thanked then for their kindness towards his wife and himself. (Applause).

div.head: Rev. Dr. Ballard at Bold-street Church.
div.p: Rev. Dr. Ballard at Bold-street Church.

At Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday sermons were preached by the Rev. Dr. Frank Ballard, the eminent preacher and lecturer, whose discourses were much appreciated by.the very large congregations which assembled. In the morning Dr. Ballard took for his subject' Saints" and in the course of a fine sermon he said that everybody was afraid of the word saints. Boys and girls did not %ant to be saints and young men thought more about football than about being saints. The notion was that holiness was dreadful. True holi— mess was not. Dr. Ballard showed how the life of the saint was the truest happiness and that if there were more saints the state of the world would be much better than it is. The choir rendered the anthem "The Saviour of the World," Mr. Frank Hickman presiding at the organ. I In the afternoon a united meeting in counee..ion with I the Bible Class League was held in the church when [ Dr. Ballard lectured on" Environment."

Arr. JOHN IiPsON presided and said that was a red letter day in the history of the League. The organiza- tion was only formed at the beginning of 1967 and already it had done much to justify the high expecta- tions of its founders. They were endeavouring to encourage those who were upholding the banner of truth in the district and to promote the cause of purity and temperance among the men. They counted it as perhaps the greatest of their achievements that they had secured the services of Dr. Ballard who by his tieetings and lectures had already helped many of those who were responsible for the leadership of the classes. The subject of " Environment" was one upon which entirely different views prevailed. 'L'here were those who regarded environment as having no weight on character and destiny, and that view was shared by those whose environment was all that could be desired. On the other hand others maintained that environment was everything. Dr. B kLT.ARD quoted from one of Mr. Illatchforcrs books " Not guilty, a defence of the bottom dog," and taking the writer's definition of environment, to which he had devoted a chapter, he strove to prove how hope- lessly in error the writer was, and how he contradicted himself. Dr. Ballard also quoted from IL G. Well and Henley, in support of his contention that men was above heredity and environment, and that while these forces played a certain part in his life, man was not the sport of chance and circumstance. At the evening service Dr. BAI,LATLO spoke ore " Sinners "and in the coarse of his remarks maintained that if a man could not sin be could not love.
The choir sang the anthem "Thou, whose- Almighty Power." After the service a meeting was held when Dr. Ballard answered a number of questions from his sermors•

SHOCKING NEGLECT CASE.
A Mother Sent to Gaol for Three Months.

Margaret Forrest, last from Wrexham, wra charged at the Borough Police Court on Saturday with neglect- in. her children and causing them unnecesrary suffering. She pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Browne prosecuted for the N.S.P.C.C. He stated that the prisoner was the mother of the boy who was charged with stealing a shirt from the market a short while ago and stated that his mother had told him to steal it. A detective was dispatched to the mother's house and she was told t 3 attend court the following morning. Instead of doing that she decamped to Wigon, taking two children with her, the youngest 12 months old. She afterwards returned to Warrington and went roaming about the town instead of going home. While in Warilngton the youngest child died and an hquest was held, the jury recommending that the mother should be severely censured.—Mrs. Eliza Hill was called and she statea that when the woman went away she took charge of the other children. They were in a filthy concution and she had to burn all their clothes.—Charles Forrest, husband of the defendant said he gave his wife all his wages except a few pence for r )cket-money. His wife 'rag addicted to drink.—Mrs. Plinstor wife of the licensee of the Bay Horse Hotel, and William Fiddler of 13, fireball-street. also gave evidence. Dr Hodgkinson stated that he made an examination i of the body before the inquest, and found that the child had been neglected, but he was not in a position to say ' that the neglect hastened death.—lnspector Cox, of thel N.S.P.C.C.,stated that he had the woman under observa- tion for four years. The husband was a bard-working man but was very simple, and she could do what she liked with him. They had six children. He found that defendant had been staying in a very small house in Wigan, where three or foot families lived together. The atmosphere was very unhealthy. The ether child who was taken to Wigan by the defendant said that they walked all the way from Wigan to Warrington.— After much delireration the Bench decided to send defendant to goal for three months with hard labour. div.head: WARRINGTON LAW CLERKS SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LAW CLERKS SOCIETY.
Visit of the Lord Mayor of Liverpool.

The members of the newly.formed Warrington and District Law Clerks' Society were honoured with a visit from the Lord Mayor of Liverpool (Mr. J. Chaloner Dowdall) at their first general meeting held at the Winrnarleigh Cafe on Wednesday evening. The large attendance augured well for the success of the organ- ization,the objects of which are in every way commend- able. Mr. H. B. Heughton presided and the following solicitors were present :—Messrs. E. A. White, H. J. Westbrook, T. S. Steel, IV. IT. J. Jenkine and F. G. Taylor. Tne secretary (Mr. Samuel L. Collis) annoriced that he had received letters of apology for non- -1 att mdance from the Mayor (Aldermen Forshaw), the 1 Town Clerk (Mr. .1. Lyon Weittle), the denuty Town I Clerk (Mr. A. T. Hallaway), Messrs. Henry G reenal I, H. .1. Longton, Herbert Woods,T. Ridgway and Herbert Hatton. The CHAIRMAN extended a very hearty welcome to the Lord Mayor of Liverpool and said they esteemed his presence all the more when they considered how great the calls must be upon one of his lordship's pro- fersion who had been elected to the high honour of Lord Mayor of one of the finest cities in the world. I -He hoped the aims and objects of the Society would Icommend themselves to the whole of the legal profes- sion in Warrington They were in no way antagonistic or likely to cause the slightest friction between !employer and employed, but rather to increase the ' friendly relationships between them. Moreover their work would tend to the benefit of the employer be u-e it nos the aim of the Society to educate by lectures and discussions those lesser lights of law who were pre- cluded by circumstances from improving their legal education, except by means of a Society like that. They were proud to think they were part and parcel of a great and honoured profession to the talents of whirl: the highest offices in the land were open. (Applause). The LORD MAYOR Of LIVERPOOL said he accepted their invitation with great pleasure, firstly because the 1 Mayor of Warrington was president of the Society and , it was common among all the Mayors and Lord Mayors of this part of the county that whatever one pet his hand to,another would support it if he could. Secondly, he was very much in favour in every trade, profession, business or group of societies such as that. He thought that people's interests held together ranch more than was commonly supposed. What was good for each was good for all—with certain limitations—and that was the side of this question which was more overlooked than the other. People saw quickly enough where their interests conflicted hut they did not always see where they jumped together and what a great accession of pleasure, efficiency and profit wee derived from asseciatiors like that. Lastly, it was a pleasure for him to come, because they were ruem- hers of his own profession, that of the law. The Chairman had alluded to the dignity of the profession. The position that English law sers held was difTeren• from that which lawyers held in many other countries. They were one of the three great effective powers of the State end it had "pen to the profit of the country that they were so. They had proved themselves worthy of their trust. The law was a profession which was full of human, political end practical interest. It was full of human interest, most strikingly in its most exceptional phases. The law hal an increasing interest in the politics' world. The interference of the State in all relations of life was growing every day and it was small wonder that those who took part in public life included an ever-increasing number of lawyers. Their profession was a very practical one because we lived and moved in relations that were determined by law and further the law had the particularly practical aspect to them that it was their business. His lordship then referred to the progress of the Liverpool Law Clerks' Society founded seven years ago and spoke of the value of social interconrse. He pointed out that the constant social intercourse of the bar had always made for its efficiency and had not detracted in any way from the tenacity with which counsel looked alter the interests of his client. Sergeant Buzfuz conducted his case none the worse because he had said " Good morning " to Sergennt Snnhhin. (Laughter.) In conclusion the Lord Mayor addressed the gatheiing on the subject of " Evidence "which he handled in a highly interesting and informing way. Mr. E. A. WHITE in proposing a vote of thanks to the Lord Mayor of Liverpool, said it was a somewhat extraordinary thing that until societies of that kind were formed no system seemed to have been attempte I for training lawyers' clerks and yet perhaps there was no class of men from whom in after life more successful men had arisen. Possibly to some extent the lack of a system of education, inducing self-reliance and a spirit of inquiry and observation, had brought that about, and another reason was that the inefficients were weeded out early. Moreover lawyers' clerks haul always helped each other a great deal, in fact, without the assistance of each other they could not get on. Mr. IL J. WESTBROOK in seconding said the society would establish a status which had long been wanting among solicitors' clerks. If there was a profession in which knowledge was novrer it was the law and every- body connected with the law must rocognize that fact.

.. .. .. ... , —. 1 The.vote was heartily accorded and the LORD IVIAYOR briefly responded. . A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman on the pronosition of Mr. T. S. STEET„ seconded by Mr. NV. H. J. JENKINS and supported by Mr. F. G. TAY-LORI

div.head: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.
(By PEDo).

Strange and varied opinions have already been expressed, anent the secession of the Southern Associa- tion and its probable result, in view of the decision of the N.C.C.U., also the understanding to confine Inter- national honours to those runners who represent their clubs in the National Championship. The clubs forming the " Southern " have not been unanimons from the outset, and it is rumoured that steps are being taken to alter the representation of that body. If this is not satisfactorily accomplished the dissentients have a remedy at hand, and the probability is that several much strengthened teams from the South will contest the " National."

-....---- So far the Southern representations (by sulking when they could not get their own way) have acted the part of a spoilt child and they are at present being treated as such ought to be. The sporting instinct of those who place finance and local matters before National and International considerations can scarcely be commended the result of this policy in connection with the Marathon Race, at the Olympic Games, did not satisfy the man in the street. It is generally conceded that a cross-country runner represents the purest form of amateurism in sport, also that in connection with any branch of amateur sport profit should be secondary and the primary object of a club or promoting body, should be to obtain the best athletic results from the com- petitors, with suitable wards or momentos for the deserving. " Putting a little bit away " is alright, when used right, but even in the ordinary walks of life people with miserly ideas generally let the rain in to-day in their efforts to keep it out to-morrow—self-sacrifice truly, but to b 3 of value it shoull be international. We may be dying to live, but as nature has a limit and and provides the handicap we should try to put up the best record in our time.

Ev'uthel rofessional pedestrians, whose commercial desires may resent starting from scratch, realises the necessity for making a concession to provide competi- tion. In cross-country running eveigone goes the full course and the csompetit6r, who accidentally or other- wise, fails to follow the trail is excluded from the awards; lethargic individuals who permit others to dominate their interests in commerce usually suffer, and if the sporting section of the Southern Association will allow the shrieking commercialists to lead thorn off the trail they must be debarred from taking part in the "International "which is deservedly cousidered the best fixture of the season. Club handicaps and novice races were plentiful last Saturday and it is plessin,g to note that new hands at the game acquitted themselves well.

Housewives who do this, generally come out well in the end, and are known as clever cooks, excellent managers, women who always ad a way out of a tight coiaer.

div.head: NCERNING CHRISTMAS
div.p: NCERNING CHRISTMAS

Perhaps some of you think that it is somewhat early to be printing Christmas Stories in our columns. But you must remem- ber that it is only about a month to the Festive Season, and high time to be arranging holiday matters. I do want specially this Christmas to help seine of our poor little children—to give some a little pleasure. I am sure my members will give me a hand in this matter. So many require warm clothing that it is im- possible to help all, but this fact need not hinder us from helping a few. It is worth doing if only one little child can be made happy by our efforts. Will my members read carefully the article by William 11. Farrar further down these columns, on "The Poor Children's Christmas," and then think out the problem of what they intend to do this Christmas to help those who have hardly the necessaries of life? Don't forget the Competitions. First.—To the sender of the best article of clothing for some poor child I will give a P.O. for ss.
Secon4/y.—For boys only. I offer prizes for the best essay on "Cricket and Football. Which I prefer, and why? " ThiPdly.—For boys and girls. The best 6tory or anecdote connected with Christmas.
Fourthly.—The best essay •on the difference between the Christmas cf a poor and rich child.. With love, UNCLE NED.

Once more Christmas is approaching us. I can hardly realise it, but, nevertheless, it is true, and we are not nearly ready for it, for there is much to be done before we can give this most joyous of all seasons the welcome which it demands. There are presents for father, mother, and our friends, all to be made or bought; mysterious little journeys to be made to the village, and even more mysterious little packages smuggled into the house and secreted in some place where no one but their owner can find them. Then on Christmas Day we shall have great. pleasure in presenting cur friends with such trifles as we have bought, and receiving from them endless gifts which delight our youthful hearts. Then, perhaps, some of us will be fortunate enough to have a Christmas party, where the pleasures which that affords will bring the healthy flush to our cheeks and lend a merry sparkle to our eye. Christmas is indeed a happy time, but why is it co? The true answer is this: Because it is the birthday of Jesus Christ, Who wishes us to be happy on that occasion. Besides being happy, He wishes us to be both humble and unselfish. " What has that to do with Christ- mas?" I hear you MEL'. A very great deal. If we were to take a trip on Christmas night to some of the poorest parts of London, we should be horror stricken at some of the sights we should witness. Pcor little children, half naked and uncared for, are to be seen sitting or lying about in the dark alleys or doorways. Perhaps some have fallen asleep, worn out with fatigue and hunger. Perhaps some have brutal parents, who do not trouble how wretched ths little ones are, and who spend their money in that baneful drink and their spare hours in the tap-room, instead of buying food for their children and making a comfortable dwe:ling- place for them. Now, this is where the humbleness and unselfishness must come in. Do you not think that we who have good homes and loving paren's could well afford to give up some little pleasure or cosifort to make such little children as I have mentioned a little happier? Let us picture ourselves in their places. How should we feel? Should we not like to be thought of just a little? Of course we should. So I say, "Why try to find the best of our Christmas happiness in selfish amusements? Why not strive to bring bright- ness to the darker lot of others?" It is only the humble who are happy in themselves, and who make others happy around them. Let us remember the lowly birth of our Lord, and, if we want this Christmas to be the happiest we have ever spent, we must think most of others, least of ourselves. BEATRICE ARNOLD.

div.head: WELCOME TO
div.p: WELCOME TO
V. Russell and Philip Colwill. A Mirror has been sent to Ida Bow. THE POOR CHILDREN'S CHRISTMAS.

A cold, cheerless clay, and hardly a, piece of wood or coal in the house. No wonder the children look pinched and hungry as they scramble down from their scantily-covered beds. .Christmas Day and Santa Claus had forgotten to come! The tears stood in the little 011SS' eyes, but they brushed them away quickly when they saw mother's pale, worn, but brave smil- ing face. Times have been very hard this year, but mother gives the little ones a plateful of hot porridge each, and then sends them out for a, run so as to warm their little limbs. How they would have liked to give her a present They had tried singing carols, but had been ruthlessly banished from the first door, and had a dog set on to them, so that they were too frightened to try again. They watch the people streaming out of a church close by, and wonder whether the little girls and boys so richly clothed are going to have a nice Christ- mas dinner. Memories of last year's plum pudding flash before them, but funds are too low to have one this year. Mother meets them at the door, and there is a bright smile on her face as she tells them that the people from the mission have just delivered a small hamper, in which is ft nice piece of beef and a real plum pudding. And not only that, but an invitation for two of the children to go to the Christmas treat, to be held the next week, when they would each be given a warm garment and an orange and a bun to take home. But there are many who spend a cheerless Christmas in this , England of ours, just because someone has tor- gotten our Lord's words:—" Inasmuch as ye have done it unto the least of these my little ones, ye have done it unto Me." WILLIAM R. FARRAR. THE RICH CHILDREN'S CHRISTMAS.

Was there ever a gayer time in all the year! House parties, dances, and pleasure galore! For weeks every member of the party has been scanning the shop windows, choosing presents for their near and dear once. And then the dresses! How many hours have been spent in choosing materials and styles, and being fitted? But at last the day has arrived, and the family and guests. all arrayed in their lovely gowns, are assembled together round the well-laden table. After dinner they all depart to the draw. ing-room, where there is a huge Christmas tree, upon which is suspended a present for each guest from the host. and hostess. What delight is expressed as each parcel is unfolded, and what surprise that it is just what was wanted! Then follow games for the children, and many shrill shrieks are heard from coma timid little maidens as the crackers are pulled. At last bed- time comes, and, happy and tired, the little ones are taken off to their dainty little nests. The fr oo rn is then cleared and dancing com- mences, interspersed with games and music and kissing under the mistletoe. At last, when all are tired out with the gaieties of the day. the party asserableè in a circle, and, all joining hands, sing the good old ballad. "For Auld Lang Syne." WILLIAM R. FARRAR.

There are many stories told about kindness to animals. And one is about the owner of a vegetable garden, who •one day noticed that a basket which had juet been filled with new turnips became suddenly empty. He questioned the gardener, who likewise could not under- stand the matter, and proposed, as a certain means of discovering the thief, that they should hide themselves behind a hedge. This was done. After a few minutes, they saw a dog go to the basket and take a turnip, and went to a stable. The men followed the thief, and discovered that the horse was also con- cerned in the affair—the dog gave the horse the turnip. The gardener angrily seized his knobbed stick in order to chastise the dog, but his master held him back. FRED. FURGREAVES.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to tell you that I have received the watch safely, and to thank you very much for it. It came to the. house yesterday morning, after I had gone to school, and, as I was at school all day, I did not see it until the evening. At I had not received it before, I began to feel very anxious about it. as I thought you might have Eent it to the wrong address. Once more thanking you, I remain, your loving Niece, VIOLET SANDY.

A certain prince wont into his vineyard to examine it; and he came to the peach tree, and he eaid, "What are you doing for me?" And the tree raid, "In the spring I give my blossoms and fill the air with fragrance, and on my boughs hang the fruit which presently men will gather and carry into the palace for you." And -the prince said, "Well done, good and faithful servant."

And he came to the maple, and he said, "What are you doing?" And the maple said, "I am making nests for the birds and shelter for cattle with my leaves and spreading branches." And the prince said, "Well, done, good and faithfill servant."

And then he came to a little daisy that was growing in the hedgerow, and he said, " What are you doing ? " And the daisy said, " Nothing! nothing! I cannot make fleeting- place for the birds, and I cannot give shelter to the cattle, and I cannot send fruit into the palace, and I cannot even furnish food for the sheep and cows—they do not want me in the meadow; all I can do is to be the best little daisy I can be." And the prince bent down and kissed the daisy, and said, " There is none better than thou."

div.head: WIDNES v. ST. HELENS.
div.p: WIDNES v. ST. HELENS.

The League fi stare took place at Widnes, before 3,000 spectators. The play in the first few minutes was very fast and exciting. lace got away for Widnes, with the ball at his feet and scored a fine try, Jones improving. St. Helens then attacked, and a cross kick by Hill enabled H. Greenwood to score. Lee failed at the place. ,From a scrummage on the home line the visiting backs showed some good passing, and J. Greenwood crossed the line for Lee to place a goal, Half-time score—St. Helens 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points). Widnes 1 goal,l try (5 points).—The play in the second half was of a very scrappy character, there being no addition to the score. Results :—St. Helens 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points), Widnes 1 goal, 1 try (5 points.)
L.tNCASHIRE SENIOR CUP. SECOND ROUND. Warrington 0 9 6 *Swinton *Oldham *Leigh Runcorn

Warrington In the Semi-Final. The Warring ton men realised expectations on Saturday when they won at Swinton and reached the semi-final round of the Lancashire Cup. Both teams were as selected and a very keen game was witnessed under the worst conditions. The ground was like a swamp and rain fell almost continuously. There was a crowd of P bout 3,090, a couple of hundred coming from Warring- ton. Teams :

Swinton—Townson, back ; Wharton, Wallwork, Rewin, and Gartrell, three-quarter backs •, Fairhurst and Jones, half backs; Barnett, Simistor, J. Preston, W. Preston, Pomfret, and Lloyd, forwards. Warrington—Tilley, back ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor, and Bradshaw, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins, half backs; A. Boardman, P. Boardman, Naylor, Belton, Hewitt and Chesters, forwards. Referee, Mr. A. Smith Halifax. Touch judges, Messrs, H. Ball, Wigan;andT. Smith, Rochdale Hornets.

Warrington started operations but the home team at once got On the attack through a run and kick by Wall- work, which took play to the line, and Fairhurst smartly dropped a goal. This early success did not do the homesters much good, for Warrington buckled too with energy and had rather the best of matters. Fish and Jenkins were tackled near the line, but there was no more scoring before the interval. On resuming, Warrington au ads great efforts, and the forwards gradually wore the home pack down. Brad- shaw rushed to the line, and from a scrum near the corner Taylor got hold and punted right across to Fish. The latter fielded finely and raced over at the corner. There was some desperate play after this, but Warring- ton were safe and held the home lot in check. Fish distinguished himself again by fielding a Swinton kick, and after an exchange with Dickenson, running in a second try which was not converted. The match was nearly over when the Swinton forwards dribbled the ball to the Warrington line, and hot work followed under the posts. Brooks finally cleared to half-way, and end came with the score : Warrington, 2 tries (6 points) ; Swinton, one goal. BARROW v. RURCORN.

This Lancashire Cup tie was played at Barrow, before 2,000 spectators, in wet weather. In the first half Run- corn played with the wind, and good passing and fine work by Jolley culminated in Butterworth being tackled in possession, and Barrow quickly changed the venue. From a combined movement Coutts secured, and returned the ball to Friend, who scored Barrow's open- ing try. The same player failed at goal. The Cestrians retaliated gamely, and Jolley seizing a pass from an opposing half back scored a try and kicked a goal. Half-time score—Runcorn, 1 goal 1 try (5 points) ; Barrow, 1 try (3 points). Barrow were expected to reap an advantage from the wind, and rain in the second half, but they met a resolute defence. Haney and Mclienny were repeatedly tackled in possession, and Jolley played an especially fine game for Runcorn. Result :—ltuncorn, 1 goal 1 try (5 points) ; Barrow,l 1 try (3 points).
• MONDAY'S MATCHES. WIGAN V. LEIGH STILL UNSETTLED.

Wigan and Leigh re-played their Lancashire Cup tie at Wigan before 14,000 people and the home side won by 11 points to 5. During the game Johnston of Wigan left the field without the perrnibsion of the referee, and then returned. This being directly against the rules, Leigh lodged a protest after the match and the protest was upheld by the Lancashire Union. The Clubs were ordered to play the match again at Wigan on Monday next.
WARRINGTON'S GREAT VICTORY. UNBEATEN OLDHAM OUTCLASSED.

Remarkable interest was shown in the visit of the unbeaten Oldham team on Monday, as the recent form of the locals had been such that high hopes were enter- tained of them being the first to lower the Oldham colours. A most brilliant and exciting game was witnessed. Warrington played as if their lives rested on the result, and by really superior football they beat the Oldham men by the huge score of 27 points to nil. A large number of people came with the visiting team, and Warrington people rallied so well for a Monday match that there were fully 6,600 present, and the gate realised 1:”.1. Beautiful weather prevailed and the ground was in excellent order. The teams turned out at full strength rs.follows _ _ .

Warrington ; Tilley, back ' • Fish, Dickenson, Taylor, and Trehearne, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins, half-backs ; Neill, Dowell, A. Boardman, P. Boardman, Thomas and Chesters, forwards. Oldham : Wood, back ; Tyson, Smith, Llewellyn and "Birdie '' Dixson, three-quarter backs ; White and W. alf-backs ; Ferguson, Avery, Longworth, Nansen, Dixon,du-ens and Wilkinson, forwards. lieferee, Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton. Warrington won the toss and had the sun and a fair breeze at their backs. Avery started and for a time the Oldham men held a slight advantage. Gradually, how- ever, the Warrington forwards found their feet and began to get possession of the ball. Play was soon transferred to the Oldham half and Fish had a fruitless shot at goal from a penalty. Oldham managed to force matters to the home quarter where Wood failed at quite an easy shot at goal. This was the visitors last chance of scoring for some time. Warrington at once rushed the game to the Oldham half and a judicious punt by Taylor set Treharne going on the right. The Welshman made a fine run and passed inside at the right moment to Taylor who opened the scoring amid a hurricane of cheers, which were renewed when Fish added a goal. This success seemed to endow the locals with confidence, and their subsequent play was delightfully clever and dashing. After a spasmodic ru,:th to the Warrington quarter which was repelled by Tilley, O'Neill and Dowell led play to the railway end again. Brooks got away smartly and threw to Fish. The wing man broke past Tyson with a desperate effort and passed back to Jenkins a ho had no difficulty in piercing the Oldham defence a second time. Thomas this time took the kick and a good shot placed the visitors ten points in arrears. Oldham could make no headway against the Warrington forwards, who were seen to the best possible advaritage in close and loose work. P. Boardman led them splendidly in one dangerous raid, and after realizing the attack the ball was worked across to Fish with rare strategy, and this player, find- ing himself baulked of an opening, cross licked to Trehearne, who took the ball splendidly and dodging "Birdie " Dixon and Wood he raced over for a good try, which Thomas improved upon.

Any attempt to force matters Si the Warrington end was met by Tilley and Dickenson. and the latter with his lofty kicks and quick following up was always a source of trouble to the visitors. White in saving was tackled and hurt and compelled to retire. Handicapped now, Oldham fell further in the rear, and their goal had several narrow escapes. Taylor drew the defence again and then screwed the ball to Trebarne who raced behind the posts, Thomas adding his third goal. Half- time score : Warrington, four goals four tries (20 , point) ; Oldham, nil. The Warringtonians were heartily cheered at the interval on what had been so far a great display. Turn- round, Warrington early made play at the Oldham end, only to be driven out by Smith and Dixon. Tilley met the invaders splendidly, and kicking with judgment the East Lancashire men were not allowed to become dangerous. Play for a little while was at the home quarter flag until Jenkins threw to Brooks, and this player, drawing on Smith, simultaneously gave to Dickenson, who immediately sent on to Fish, the latter dribbling well into the Oldham half before B. Dixon dropped on the ball. Before Warrington were repulsed, Dickenson got hold and dropped a beautiful goal. The forward ought to have increased the score a minute later, but Dowell made the mistake of passing on the line, and the ball was charged down. Smith then improved Oldham's prospects with a long run. Tyson was in attendance but fell a victim to Tilley's fine tackling a couple of yards from the line. Fish led the way back with another great dribble, and then came the try of the match. Brooks took a pass from Jenkins when on the run. His dash carried him clean through the Oldham centres and pursuit was hopeless. When faced by Wood, the Warrington lad swerved beautifully and completed one of the finest tries seen on the ground, right behind the posts. Thomas kicked the usual goal. In the last five minutes Warrington almost scored again, Jenkins being held just outside the line. Final : Warrington 6 goals 5 tries, 27 points ; Oldham nil.

HALTON VILLA. V. WARRINGTON A LBIONS.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. Albions started and immediately made for the visitors' goal, but were pulled up for offside. Albions had a good opening, but the final effort failed, while Wyatt saved a simple shot at the other end. Both Connor and Mather had attempts to give the home team the lead, but both shots went over. The Villians, after leading by one goal, added two goals on in the second half, and thereby won by three goals to nil. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT JUNIOR LEAGUE.

A tine 'game reulted fiOm the meeting of the undefeated Heathside team and Arpley-street. Both teams were exceptionally keen. Heatbside to retain their unbeaten certificate and Arpley-street to be the first to lower the colours of their opponents, and so the game was fast from beginning to end. The result, a pointless draw, was a fair reflex of the game'. It is needless to single out any boy for special praise, as the whole 22 played well. Parochial continue on their way rejoicing, and on Saturday defeated the Beamont boys by five goals to one. They now have the advantage of Heathside, and when the two meet on December sth the game should be worth going a long way to see. div.head: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
div.p: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
1/11.—lf the foreigner would pay a tax on wheat or meat, why would he not pay a tax on bacon or maize P

Mr. Chamberlain, when he produced his "prac- tical " proposals for Tariff Reform at Glasgow, in October, 1003, told us that, while he proposed to tax corn, be did not propose to tax maize ; and while he proposed to tax meat, he excepted bacon from taxation. As to maize, he said : "I propose to put no tax whatever on maize, partly because maize is a food of some of the poorest of the population, and partly, also, because it is a raw material for the farmers, who feed their stock with it." And to the bacon, he said "I propose to exclude bacon because, once more, bacon is a popular food with some of the poorest of the population. But if it is true that impart taxes are paid by the foreigner who sends us in tize or bacon, why make any exceptions ? If the foreigner pays a wheat tax he must also pay a maize tax. Indeed, if the foreigner pays import duties, the more import duties the better. L. C. C. M.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

Distress in Warrington. Sir,—l am instructed by my Branch to forward to the Town Clerk and the local Press, copies of the following resolution which was carried unanimously eta well-attended meeting held on the 21th instant : " The members of the Independent Labour Party respectfully direct the attention of the Town Council to the extreme gravity of the distress prevailing in ccarringtOn and suggest that immediate steps be taken to relieve the same by instituting works of utility which would provide employment for numbers of our fellow-toccnsmen who would otherwise he unable to obtain work during the present depression,—Youn truly, CHARLES WALKER.

The People Versus the Peers. Sir, —lt behoves every patriot, every lover of his kind, everyone 7ho sincerely prays " Thy Kingdom Come," who seeks the eradicati n of unemployment, who desires the general comfort end the moral well- being of our masses, to forthwith rally, at whatever sacrifice, to the support of the Government in its magnificent fight for the removal of the drink evil, by means of the finest legislative measure, all things considered, of the last half century. No consideration of personal interest or of public revenue could have justified the continuation oi the Tresent licensing system, so absolutely wrong an principle, suicidal in policy, and disastrous in results ; and one would have thought, as I had hoped, that rising above class, sec- tarian, or party considerations, all good. citizens would have combined everywhere in support of the moderate and just proposals of the Government. There has indeed been generally a marked union of the sects in support of the Bill, so much so that one could hardly have contemplated that, after the friendly reception accorded to the Bill by all that is best in the country, and the overwhelming support given to its -provisions in the elected Chamber, the irresponsible House of Lords would have dared to decide to wreck it even before they had given any time whatever to its discussion! In the coming and unavoidable con- flict between the ceople and the peers, largely between the struggling disinterested on the one aide, and on tile other, the sleek self-interested —whose horizon is confined to their own privileges and . .
every unbiased citizen

property institution —I hope will join. The issue must include the continuation of the House of Lords as a merely docile and ready tool of the leader for the time being of the Tory Party; rushing at his beck its reactionary legislation, or delaying at his call, and sometimes for a generation, the remedial measures of the party of progress. England must, and 1. believe will, realise that if she is to free herself from the drink cone which has hitherto

so seriously retarded her progress among the nations. her first task is to free herself from the incubus of the House of Lords, in. which conscianceless wealth, and selfish self-interest Coastitate the primary bases of nearly all of their legislative acts. I remember the General Election of 1&0 and every subsequent one, and I have ever taken a deep interest in public affairs. But I have never felt so intensely indignant at any of the many cliocreditable acts of the hereditary chamber as I have in regard to its treatment of this year's Licensing Bill. That on a measure so largely and so vitally concerning the daily comforts and the best interests of the common people, the House of Lords should have sunk so low, mainly at the instigation of Lord Rothschild, whom I know to be personally and through Companies of which he is the chairman, deeply interested in brewery shares, as to let itself be dominate(' by partizan intrigues and the callous greed of capitalism and interest would to me have been incredible, bad I not had experience of what self-interest will induce in men whatever their station. Sir, I have walked in Warrington over 30 years ; I have hitherto felt that on the whole it has not been necessary for me to take any public part in party politics. I have no ambition now in that direction, and I would gladly have closed a strenuous life, so far as party work is concerned, as a soldier in the ranks. But the discreditable course of the Tory Lords in regard to this Licensing Bill, so freighted with hope and promise for the people of England, has deter- mined me as I hope it will determine thousands more, to resolve that until this measure is enacted, and until the House of Lords has bad its teeth drawn, its power for mischief taken away, it mast be war to the knife, and the kniie to the hilt.—Yours etc, JAM ES DO DDS, President of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League.

div.head: LICENSING BILL. An Address to Liberal Women.
div.p: THE LICENSING BILL. An Address to Liberal Women.

Ender the auspices of the Werrington Women's Liberal Association a meeting was held at the Liberal Club on Thursday evening, when an address was given by Miss Thirza Potts, M.A. There was a a good attendance. The Rev. C. Harvey Cook presided, and was supported by Mrs. F. Meginn, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Lindley and Mrs. Clegg. The CHAIRMAN said he was glad to see men and women there who showed their gratitude for the Licensing Bill. Referring to the action of the Lords be said they as a party did not deserve to be returned to power if they did not take a strong attitude against the Lords. Were they, because the House of Lords turned into a House of Lions, going to turn their feet to them or their backs ? They had to gain for them- selves and for the English public the right to rule the drink, that wanted to rule them. (Applause.) Miss Purrs, in the course of her address, said the enemy to thrift in this country was the drink habit which permeated the whole of Society. If the drink bill were spent on clothing it would keep all the Cotton mills working overtime for 12 months and then the order would not be executed. It was not Free Trade that was going to ruin England, but the drink. The demonstration in London by the Brewers did not carry the weight that was desired. It was more than fair that II ,years should be the time limit. Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Salisbury said 5 years was sufficient, and Sir:R. Peel said 7 years was enough. The Bill was not extreme enough; but they would accept it. It did not go far enough with the clubs, and she was sorry it did not touch grocers' licensee. She reed not tell them what had happened this week. Their Bill had gone to the Lords. Their action was more detestable because it did not concern the House of Lords. It did not affect the peers' wives and families because they could get their drink in a club or at borne. It was really due to Lord Rothschild that the Bill had been rejected. It would affect them financially—again the birthright had been sold. If the Bill did pass eventually it did not mean that the peers would have to give up one luxury. She believed it was a critical time for tho Liberal party, which in the past bad always been stimulated by great ideals. It was for them of the rank and file, if the leaders would lead, to follow. There was more than the fate of the Liberal party at stake: tho fate of the country was at stake. (Hear, hear.) They must work for the cause of temper- ance for the sake of their country. (Applause). The discussion on Miss Potts' address was taken part in by Mrs. SIM PSON and Mr. EAST WOOD. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Miss Potts and the Rev. C. H. Cook. The following resolution was passed and sent to the Premier and Mr. Croseeld (the Borough Member) : "That this meeting of Warrington Liberal Women heartily approves the Licensing Bill now before the country and pledges itself to use every means in its power to get the Bill passed until it becomes the law of the land.'

A few particulars of Mr. Birrell's career will doubtless be read with interest. He was born near Liverpool on January 19th, 1850, being a son of the Rev. Charles Birrell, Nonconformist minister, and Harriet Jane, daughter of the Rev. Harry Grey, Edinburgh. lie was educated at Amersham Hall School and Trinity Hall, Cambridge, where he gradu- ated in 1871 He became a barrister in 1875, and Beneher of the Inner Temple in 1903. He was Quain Professor of Law at University College, London, from 185 G to 1895. He • holds the honorary degree of LL.D. conferred upon him by St. Andrew's University. Mr.Birrell was returned M.P. for Fifeshire W. in 1839, and represented that constituency until 1900 when he unsuccessfully con- tested N.E. Manchester. He Is- now member for North Bristol. When the late Sir Henry Campbell- Bannerman formed his ministry in 1905, Mr. Birrell was appointed President cf the Bcard of Education and the Education Bill which he introduced was a brave attempt to solve a difficult problem on moderate lines. Owing to the opposition of the /101138 of Lords, however, the Bill did not pass into law. Later Mr. Birrell succeeded to the office of Chief Secretary for Ireland and has fulfilled the duties with distinction. As all our readers know, he is a clever man of letters, his numerous publications including " Obiter Dicata," " Life of Charlotte Bronta," " Men, Women, and Books," " Lectnres on the duties and liabilities of trustees," "Sir Frank Lockwood," "Copyright in Brooks," " Collected Essays," " Miscellanies," "William Ilazlitt." In 1897 he edited Boswell's Life of Johnson." His chief recreations are pedestrianism, golf and book-hunting. Mr. W T. Stead's" Portrait gallery" of the Liberal Ministry, contains the following article on Mr. Birrell , written in 1905. There are two men in the Cabinet who were never baptised as infants. One is Mr. Augustine Birrell, the Minister of Education, the other is Mr. Lloyd- George, the 'President of the Board of Trade. Mr. Birrell's father was a Baptist minister. Mr. Lloyd- George was the son of a Baptist mother and a Unitarian schoolmaster, and was brought up by a Baptist uncle. Mr. Birrell is commonly reported to have strayed from the precincts of the conventicle into the colder and more arid plains of Agnosticism. Mr. Lloyd-George remains a Nonconformist to this day. He is indeed the typical Welsh Nonconformist and his presence in the Cabinet is regarded as a sruaranfee to the Church Militant whose weapon is Passive Desistance, that the new Ministry will not err from the strait and narrow path marked out for it by the Nonconformist conscience. He is a friend of Evan Roberts the Welsh Evangeliet,and brings to the House of Commons something of the fervour and the emotion of the popular religion of Wales. Mr. Augustine Birrell has for the last twelve years been the editor of the Liberal Publication Department, the , journalistic fighting man of the Liberal organisation. He is also the enthroned wit of the party. Now that 11r. Labouchere has departed and Sir Wilfred Lawson. is content to be merely Laureate of the Lobby, Mr. Birrell reigns alone. It may be that he will be no longer witty. Six years ago he wrote : This desire of being witty sneered,at as it always is, has in most cases an honorable, because a humane, origin. ft springs from pity for the audience—This desire to amuse just a little ought not therefore, to bean very contemptible, springing as it does from the pity that is akin to love. But now to me at all events it matters not to whom this desire is related or by whom it was begot. I have done with it. Ten years in the House of Commons and on the political platform have cured me of a weakness. mow feel to be unmanly : Ino longer

. - pity my audiences. I punish them. Nevertheless he will find it difficult not to be amus- ing. His new ()biter dicta will lose none of their point because be is seated on the Front Bench. Someone predicted that he will become a Radical Sir John Gorst but it is improbable—there is only one Sir John Gorst. Mr. Birrell has discoursed eloquently upon llazlit, Bagehot, Emerson, Cowper and many 11 other worthies. He has the hereditary bias against drunkenness, gambling, jingoism and other curse's of cur time. It is somewhat difficult to define his 'religious or ethical ideas. But he has told us that the test of progress was that the world should become day by day more fit for human habitation. Things material were great, but things spiritual belonging to the realms of thought were greater. The greatness of a nation did not depend upon the size of what was called empire, but upon the breed of it, people, upon their characteristics, upon the ideas they entertained, upon the tastes they cilia- • vated, upon the habits of their lives, and upon their possessing in all these matters a certain unity of thought and feeling. It is probable that he described himself fairly enough in the words which he used of Emerson.

Of theology strictly so called he had none ; but he was a fearless optimist, who rested on a belief in tile inviolate and unconir cable spirit of man, independent of time, place or circumstance. It was hard to be an optimist on June 2nd, 1003, but at no time did the luckless race of man stand more in need of Emerson's spirit than at this moment . H a , splendid courage, his determination to quake at nothing, his spiritual independence and individu- ality, his lofty sense of the brotherhood of man, his undying cheerfulness, his serenity and his peace were qualities of which we stood sorely in need. On the question of religious education in the public schools, Mr. Birrell Las spoken at various times with uncertain sound. But since his appointment as Minister of Education be has proclaimed his belief in a system of religious education embodying the wish of the average parent. This undenorninational religion i greatly daring, be proceeded to define as follows. It I consists of three articles :-1, The Fatherhood of God; 2, The Responsibilities of Man; 3, The rea!ity of a Future State. This is,at least, a distinct advance upon I the old Bible 'Reading without note or comment. Now I that Mr. Birrell has begun to define the common denominator of the religious belief of the British public he has embarked upon an enterprise in which he will be sorely buffeted by Lord Hugh Cecil on the one side and the logical Secularists on the other.Tle did not long maintain his first position. Speaking a few days later, Mr. Birrell said : He did not. want to separate secular education altogether from the religious instincts of the people. lie desired to see in all schools simple religions Christian teaching—simple elementary Christian Bible and New Testament teaching. But what Mr. Birrell seems now to desire is simple Protestant Bible teaching which is sectarian to the Anglican and the Catholic.
MR. BIRRELL'S PRESENT TASK.

Mr. Mirell entered on Monday night upon what Mr. Long described as a "very thorny "path. No one recognises that more strongly than Mr. Birrell himself, for the last words rf the speech in which he introduced his Irish Land Bill were : I have striven in the cause of land purchase as I have never striven for any cause before, public or private, for wife or child, for fame or fortune. I have done the Lest I could to extend it, to continue

These proposals have for their object,not the reversing of the policy of the right hon. gentleman opposite, but the continuing of that policy, because we believe that, long and diincult as the joureey may be,the path will lead us to a settled peace and an increased pros- perity which must inevitably redound to the credit and the safety of the United Kingdom.

div.head: CHRIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD. Sale of Work Opened by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield.
div.p: CHRIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD. Sale of Work Opened by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield.
SPEECH BY THE MEMBER.

The Parish Room in Grappenhall-road, Latchford, presented a pleasing scene on Thursday when the annual sale of work in connection with Christ Church,Latchford was held. Thanks to the efforts of a large band of workers, the stalls, which were well laden with all manner of useful and fancy wares, had been very attractively arranged and there was every inducement to purchase. The following is a list of the stall- holders : Ph its WoRK ST %Lt.—Miss Fanny Smith, Miss Smith, Mrs. Briggs, Mrs. John Fairclough and Mrs. Tinsley. REFRESHMENT STALL—Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Deacon, Mrs. James Fairclough and Mrs. Forshaw. FANCY WORK STALL—Miss Massy, Mrs. George Dakin, Mrs. R. T. Fairclough. TOY STALL—Mrs. Atkinson, Mrs. Edwin Woods,Mrs. Venn, Mrs. Skinner. FLOWRR STALL—Mrs. and the Misses Broadbent, Mrs, Waring. The sale was opened by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, who was accompanied by Mr. A. IL Crosfield, M.P. The Rev. G. C. Briggs (Vicar) presied over a large attendance which included the Revs. IT. B. Firth and H. H. Corsbie, Rev. R. E. and Mrs. Letheren, Mrs. John White, Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. Peter Rylands, Mrs. Frost, Mrs. Smethurst, Miss Bessie Dutton, Mrs. Willcocks, Mrs. John Coxrin, Mrs. John Reynolda,Mrs.Lister Kaye, . Mrs. Brereton Fairclough, Mrs. Henry Fairclough, Mrs. 1 flattori, ;la& st Browne. Mrs. Atkin, Misses Woods, I Miss Waring, litilatlie Waring, Mr. T: Broadbent, and I Mr. Firth (Police Court Missionary). The VissAß, in introducing Mrs. Crosfield, said they Iwere all most grateful to her for coming and he could assure her of a hearty welcome. He did not know what Mrs. Crosfleld's impresaions of Warrington were. To mast strangers the name of Warrington conveyed the same idea as Wigan, Oldham, or some of those places—(laughter)—but when they had been here a short time they found how hopelessly mistaken they were and what a delightful place Warrington was, mad what very charming people its inhabitants were. (Laughter.) He could assure Mrs. Crosfield of one thing—that she would always get a very hearty Lancashire welcome whenever she appeared an Warrington and not least at Christ Church, Latchford. (Applause.) Ho was delighted that Mrs. Crosneld had been able to persuade her husband to come with her. (Applause). He believed he was right in saying that in the long history of the sales of work at Latchford, that wart the first occasion on which they had been honoured with the presence of the Member for the Borough, and they cordially welcomed Mr. Crosfield. (Applause.) He did not know what Mr. Crosfield thcught about bazaars and sales of work. He (Mr. Briggs) was quite sure that if he were a member of Parliament he should have conscientious scruples about them. (Laughter.) He thought he should object to them on principle as being such an awful nuisance, but he was thankful to think Mr. Cros- field had no such scruples. He (Mr. Briggs) was not a politician, lant.he believed he had read somewhere that Mr. Crosfield was a Liberal. (Laughter.) He knew that all of them at Latchford, or nearly all of them, were Conservatives—(laughter)—but he could assure Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield that they were quite safe that after- noon—(laughter)—although he could not answer for their purses. (Laughter.) Alluding to the objects of the sale, Mr. Briggs said they organized it every year in order to finance, in the first place, their numerous parochial organizations which depended very largely upon grants which the Church Workers' Association very generously made to them, and also to increase the endowment of the living which at present was only £125 a year. They were trying to work that up to £2OO a year. It was a slow process, but during the pest eight years they had increased the endowment by £4B a year, so that showed what could be done by persistent work. The parish was already a large one, with over 4,000 inhabitants, and it was increasing at the rate of at least 250 people each year. They did not keep all the money they raised to themselves. They made grants to outside societies, including the Warrington District Nursing Association which he believed was one of the most useful and beneficent institutions in tho town. It only remained for him to express the very cordial thanks of the parish to the Church Workers' Association for all the work which they did, and to the stall-holders and numerous helpers. Special mention must he maile of its Fanny Smith to whose hard and unselfish work the success of their sales was largely due. The Mayor of Warrington was to have been present to propose a vote of thanks to Mrs. Crosfield, but he had been unexpectedly called to London, and asked him (Mr. Briggs) to express his regret. Mrs. CROSFIELD, who had a hearty reception, said : I asi only going to say a very few words because I do not wish to eclipse my husband who is going to speak later. (Laughter.) This is really the very first time I have spoken in public, but I am very glad to have the opportunity of telling you how much interest I take in the gaod cause which it is the object of this bazaar to support. I hope the sale will be a very great success and I have very great pleasure in declaring it open. (Anplaurie). Captain WARING, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Crosfield, said they all knew Mr. Arthur Crosfleld, who was welcome at any time. That was Mrs. Crosfield's first visit to Latchford and they hoped she would be so pleased with her reception that she would wish to come again. (Applause). Mr. JAMES LowE seconded and the vote was heartily , accorded. Mr. A. IT. CEOSFIELD, 'M.P., in responding, said be wished in the few remarks he bad to make that he could hope to rival the eloquence and the happy address they had had from their friend Mr. Briggs. It was about ten days since he( Nlr.Crosileld)listened to a sermon from Mr. Briggs in the Parish Church and he was bound to say that both in tone and substance and in the forensic ability with which it was delivered, be thought the sermon was one of the very best he had ever listened to in his lifa. (Applause). He was not going to be led away by any spirit of rivalry to attempt to compete with Mr, Briggs—(laughter)—because, after all, his wife and he had come there not for the purpose of speaking so much as for that of spending. However, he was glad to have that opportunity of telling Mr. Brigm how very much struck they all were by the truly admirable and splen- did address he gave them in the Parish Church. The central note of the discourse might be described as "Civic progress" and he hoped that sale of work would assist the same kind of progress in Mr. Briggs's own parish in Latchford. (Applawe.) Th 3 cynic had a good deal to say in these days and perhaps he did not speak without reason. Ho (Mr. Crosfield) fancied that if they could peer back into the good old days—those golden days they were all happy to dream about but which he often thought possibly gained enchantment by distance—they would find the cynic had quite as good and perhaps even better opportunity in those times than 1113 had now. At any rate, let the cynic have his chanee, but let them always remember that what he had to tell them was, aftersall the less edifying and less important part of the truth, and there were some very much more important truths and facts which they saw before their eyes at the present time than anything their friend the cynic had to tell them. They had all got to keep their hope and faith in human progress, and in those endeavours which men and women wore making, and which were largely helped on by the good work of a parish like that, with the object of checking, so far as it Was given to human beings to check what had been called the cruelty of circumstance, economic wrong, physical misfortune, and those things which, when politicians had said their last word, were beyond the power of the statesman or the politician. Ile was an erring politician himself —(laughter)---but he was not going to treat them to politics that day. He could not, however, refrain from making that one little quotation from a very memorable speech delivered many years ago by Mr. John Morley in Dundee, when he told them that after statesmadship had said its last word, there must still remain for good men and women that work in the world which lay beyond the power of any statesmanship to reach. In conclusion Mr. Crosfield said that looking ahead to the formidable task that lay before men in this and other nation., to the great problems that had to be tackled, he felt with all his heart that the work that confronted the nations of the world, and above all, those civilized people whose duty it was not only to work out their own salvation but to hold high a fine example to other and less fortunate races following in the wake of civilization, could not be accomplished unless the spirit that inspired the Gospel of Christianity was kept alive in our midst. (Applause.) fie therefore, on behalf of his wife and on his own account,wished all possible success to that undertaking which was going, if he might so express it,to add more power to the elbow of their friend Mr. Briggs, and strengthen the position of that parish and its good influence in Latchford and the whole of that part of Warrington. (Applause.) In the evening enjoyable entertainments were given, the items including songs by Mrs. Adams and Miss Gorton, pianoforte solos by Mrs. Jackson Holmes, violin solos by Mrs. Waring and recitations by Miss Broadbent, The proceeds of the sale amounted to £llO.

Said Darby, to his old wife, Joan, "We. side by side, have aged and grown, But here I tell you plump and plain, You shall not poultice me again ! There's something now to cure one faster Of cough or cold than mustard plaster, No more these blisters I'll endure, I'll purchase Woods' Great Peppermint Cure."—Advt.
