NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
"By Gvalist."

There is no lack of football news just now —with league matches, county matches, cup ties and protests almost every other day. The Warrington men have been in the thick of the struggle for fame and profit, I and if they have not scooped in much of the latter they have earned plenty of the former since the last I issue of the "Examiner." It was no mean feat to I beard the Swinton Lion in his den and come off victorious, but the doings of Saturday were forgotten ,in the splendour and excitement of Monday's match I with Oldham.

Readers of this column will recollect that I predicted last week the likelihood of Oldham sustaining their first defeat at the hands of Warrington, and that I laid stress upon the fact that once before they came here with an untarnished record of ten successive victories behind them and met their masters. It was a significant coincidence that the circum- stances were exactly the same on Monday. The result, however, was electrifying. War- rington not only inflicted the first , defeat 1 upon their proud foes, but they crushed them to earth in an unprecedented fashion. Tlcenty•seren points to nil was the MITI total of Warrington's superiority, and they were full value for every unit. It seems hardly credible, that Oldham, the team of internationals who have never bowed the knee on their own ground for nearly three years, and who have swept all opposition aside in this season's matches should be pulverised by a side which had only won three League engagements out of ten. The most that an optimistic Warring- tonian could hope for was a narrow- victory, and the ' only justification for expectin so much was based on the somewhat sudden jump into form by Warrington in the Lancashire Cup ties.

When Oldham were last beaten by 27 points to nil is a question I have in vain tried to find an answer to. Possibly in the dim and distant past some such slaughter of the Spinners has been witnessed, but there seems to have been no record cf any such drastic licking during the last ten or twelve years. Ever since the formation of the N.U.—and long before —Oldham have been a power in the land of football, and the team that beat them at all usually felt a 'justifiable glow of pride. In my recollection they were never so soundly thrashed as on Monday. The victory paid off a lot of old scores from a Warrington point of view. Do not Oldham possess the honour of running up the record score which Warrington ever fell by —35 points to nil at Watersheddings ? Each side has now given the other a record whacking. In addition Warrington have defeated their old foes in the final for the N. 1.1. Cup, so that the balance of honours just about rests with the Wirepullers.

-- Warrington actually run up 20 points before half. time against the Oldham contingent—which was possibly the greatest achievement of the lot. But apart from the phenomenal scoring, the game was remarkable for the superbly skilful play of the War- ringtonians. At their best they have always had the reputation of being a clever side, but they surpassed their best on Monday. Every max was at the height of his form, and every man was superior to his ris a via on the Oldham side. Magnificent forward play was backed up by dashing and resourceful half- back tactics. The thremparter play was a triumph of speed and strength allied to 'brainy combination and resourcefulness. And at full back stood Tilley, as cool as an iceberg and as reliable as the tides. For once in a way a faultless exhibition of Rugby Foot- ball was given, and even W. L. Sinclair of the 'Sport- ing Chronicle "—who gets more football that he can digest said it was the fieest display be had seen for five years. The good ship Oldham struck an uncharted I rock and promptly foundered. Any other team would I have done the same.

While complimenting the Warrington men on the brilliance of their performance, I think a word of con- gratulation is due to the Committee and officials of the ChM. Little more than a month ago the team could do nothing right and the prospect was blue in the extreme. A bold policy waS pursued, new players of established reputation were secured, and a team of alent built up in an incredibly short space of time. At the present moment the Club is probably stronger in a playing Sense ti..ttn ever it was, and the men who now wear the primrose and blue ought to be equal to finishing the season in a blaze of glory such as will fully compensate for the earlier days of gloom.

Confidence and success usually beget one another. The Oldham men, with their fine record'behind them were confident of adding Warrington's scalp to the rest. They came on the field with a jaunty, "See us do it "kind of air. Warrington were encouraged by recent successes and did not lack faith in their own powers. For ten minutes after the start of the game Oldham gave a promising display. Their light-coated, boisterous Committee men were happy and patronising Then there came the first flash of Warrington's. brilliance and Taylor made the defence which had only give away 33 points in 10 matches, lrok rather cheap. Fish added a goal amid a roar of cheering. The visiting big-wigs still smiled —faintly. Next Fish cavorted round Tyson and sent Jenkins over,and Thomas goaled. Smile all gone ! In its place a high colour and vociferous explanations. In quick style Treharne and Thomas added ten more points to the home total. The interval arrived with the Oldham men pinching one another to be quite sure they slept not and endured some horrid dream. In the second half Warrington had their opponents tame and sub- missive, and-all the Oldham directors could do was to make frantic efforts to display a philosophic calm while quietly cursing the unfortunate fellows who, some 80 fleeting minutes before, were idols fit for the devoutest worship.

The battle of Wilderspool —to which Waterloo was a mere nothing—has somewhat altered the complexion of the League table. Oldham are jolted rudely from that seemingly secure place at the top, and Wigan step up. Wairington get merely a modest rise,which is nevertheless( welcome.
The League table, including Saturday's results, is as follows : For At. Per

It might be as well if I devoted some attention to the Cup-tie which Warrington won so well at Swinton, but really, beyond the actual success there is little to write about. Football was at a discount on the Chorley-road mud-heap and the match was anyone's until near threeguarter time. Swinton had led by a goal to nil right from the start, though Warrington had shown superior form. Scoring was a difficult matter, but Fish ran in a couple of beauties in quick succession. Taylor let up to the first with ore of those judicious cross-punts, which left Swinton help- less, and the second was shared in by Dickenson, who played the game of a giant. Much credit is due to the unflinching way the Warrington front rank stuck to their guns. They out-pointed Jack Preston's little band in the closing stages when breath was getting short and boots very heavy.

Warrington have certainly not been favoured with luck in the Lancashire Cup-ties, and if they should land the trophy it will be a real triumph. They have been drawn away every time, and even in the semi-
final the handicap is still kept on. Wigan away sounds attractive financially, but it doe 3 not offer the best prospects of success.
The semi-final draw is as follows : Oldham v. Runcorn. Wigan or Leigh v. Warrington. -- Oldham have had every tie at home. They may go down in the final!

On Wednesday, the chosen of Lancashire were cut up into very small pieces by the Australians, who have so far triumphed in every represeet4tive match. Leytham and Tyson were notable absentees from the County team, but a better show should have been made. However, they were slow and unenterprising from the start, and with W. G. Smith missing every pass and Hogg shaping like a nursemaid, the Kangaroos had an easy journey. They played fine football too, some of the passing being equal to any- thing shown by the All Blacks. Messenger was great. lOn the home side Brooks was a long way ahead of the other backs. The forwards apparently suffered from "that tired feeling." It was the Champion County's humiliation. Only a small crowd saw the sad affair, which is just as well, except for the Kangaroos!

Warrington resume their League programme to-day, when they visit Runcorn, and should have every prospect of success. The Linnets have a superior record to Warrington on the season's play, but I doubt if they are as strong a side at present. More- ever they are handicapped by injuries and illness which will cause the absence of Harrison, Padbury and Deakin, Warrington are fortunate in having all their men sound at last, and the team which slaughtered Oldham will do duty at Runcorn.
The side is Tilley, fall back ; Fish, Dickensoß, Taylor and Treherne, threequarters ; Jenkins and Brooks, half-backs; ONeill, D3well, Thomas, Chester, A. Boardman and P. Bolrdcaan, forwards.

The full strength of the" A team has also been assembled for the benefit of Runcorn "A " at Wilderspool. The selected thirteen are : —Mclntyre, full back; Landor, Jordan, Cartwright and Bradshaw, three-quarters ; Lees and Lambert, half hacks ; Naylor, Harmer, Belton,ilewitt, Gibbs and Bradshaw, ,frnwards.

Hockey. Latchford recorded another win last Saturday against Westbrook by 2-1, and had they not missed several chances, the margin would have been greater. The teams were on level terms at half time, Travis having scored for the home team. Banks subsequently obtained the winning goal. Westbrook pressed very hard in an endeavour to equalise but a resolute defence kept them out.

The Second Eleven played Stockport "A" at Heaton Moor and after being behind by a goal for three parts of the game eventually won 2-1. Wilkinson was largely responsible for the turning 3f the table in that he scored both goals for Latchford. Stockport are a very good side and the visitors win was a most creditable one.

To-day the Ist eleven oppose Altrincham St. George's at Altrincham with the following team :—W.Cnsworth, goal ; C. Plinston, T. Dixon, backs ; D. Trans. J. B. Wilkinson, J. Albinson, halves ; F. Newell, H. Parker, H. Scott, E. Banks,W. Spensley, forwards. Referee : Mr. W. B. Cobb. Train from Central Station 1.35 p.m.

The 2nd elevens meet at Latchford and the home team is Appleton, goal ; J. Wilkinson. W. H. Pickles, hacks; L. Kenworthy, F. Tole, A. Newton, halves ; F. Dunn, H. ;Jones, A. Knight, A. Starkey, C. Hackney, forwards. Referee —Mr. Harry Warburton. Bully-off 2.30 p.m.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There are many novel turns at the Hippodrome this week, chief among which is that of Ford and Barras, tato boys who were originally found perform- ing in the London streets with a barrel-organ and whose skill attracted the attention of a Loudon music hall mmnager. The boys appear isa white and gold, and while one rattles away at the original " hurdy gurdy," the other dances. Ford did some wonderful break-downs, and wound up with his own special hurricane dance in which his limbs flickered as quickly as a biograph film. Frank Cass, described ,as the favourite vocal cotnedion, earned, hearty applause for his song "which is the sinner and which is the saint." Frank was resplendent in a bright green suit, lemon-coloured waistcoat and patent leather boots. The Lyons Trio also had ' a big reception for their really clever dant% show and dancing. The waiter was exceedingly funny and introduced queer business as well as queer dishes. It takes artistes a little,above the ordinary to present a sketch which amuses every- one, without saying a word. Charles Banks appears as comedian and introduces his clever dog " Woof " which performs all sorts of little duties at a syllable. Elroy, the armless wonder, is rightly named. For a person who lost both arms at the tender age of three years, he has got on well in life and can look after himself very comfortably. Elroy's feet would make a monkey envious. He can carry things about, fire a gun, light cigarettes, and paint pictures with his pedal extremities. Woodhouse and Wells are very successful as )aatter vocalists comedians and dancers. We wonder who introduced the smell and the buffoon combination seen so often on the halls nowadays? Cissie Esdaile and Gracie Hunt are two dainty comediennes with a liking for masculine attire The fixtures —Mr. Widdop's orchestra and the biograph —never fail to please. In connection with the Ford and Barra s turn, a dancing competition has been held each evening —for juveniles at the first house and adults at the second. The local talent displayed has been surprisingly good.

div.head: SECOND SUNDAY CONCERT.
div.p: SECOND SUNDAY CONCERT.

The programme of the second sacred concert, at the instance of the Warrington Branch of the Ainalgamatkd 'Musicians' Union, was of a varied and interesting character and attracted a much larger audience than attended at the first concert a few weeks ago. In addition to the orchestral pieces there were items given by the Warrington Male Voice Choir, songs by Miss Lucy Davies and a violin solo by Mr. Tom. Boothroyd. The first mentioned,—particularly the "Glow-worm" idyll and the "Semiramide" overture, marked a distinct advance in the playing of the associated instrumentalists, indicating latent resources which may under favourable circumstances materialise into even better things in the future. Mr. Wilde, in the post of condactor, was, however, not of much more use than a metronome. Consequently the bands- men lacked both the spur and the controlling hand that would have brought out more fully the possi- bilities of the various pieces set down in the pro- gramme. • Still there was much to admire and to enjoy in the band pieces and praise is due to the orchestra for the manner in which they presented them with probably very slight rehearsal. Mr. Tom Boothroyil played Goclaid's `!Bercense " with nice feeling and exact, though somewhat weak,intonation. After getting through the introductory and recitative like p rtions the principal theme might with advantage have been more lovingly lingered upon, but this is perhaps so pinch a matter of the performer's personal idicsyncracies that the idea can only be put forward as a suggestion. Miss Lucy Davies sang The promise of life " (Cowen) and " Sunshine and rain " (Blum' enthal) sweetly and with intelligent insight, but her voice lacks the roundness and resonance necessary to anything like dramatic effectiveness. Of the male- voice choruses " The destruction of Gaza " stood out with monumental prominence, and the choir is to be congratulated upon a finished and virile interpretation of this picturesque work. Mr. N. Latham played the pianoforte accompaniments nuobstrusively, yet with admirable skill and judgment. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The management announce a capital progra name for next week, the bill being headed by Gunner Moir, the premier British Champion, the only man in the three Kingdoms who has given. Tommy Burns a fight." He will box twice ti ightiv, and will in addition meet all local champions The gunner will fight any man in the world for £5OO a-side. Each evening hioscope views of the 11.irs and Dnrns contest will be exhibited and lectured on by Major Best. Other attractions will be :—Chris Richards, the eccentric comedian of the day ; The Two Rubies, duettists and dancers ; Cha.ss Lewis, novel ventriloquist ; Sidy Nirvana presenting artistic poses in colours, introducing her statue horse ; the Two hays in vocal scena entitled "The Cuckoo" ; flabusio Brothers, phenomenal head to head acrobats ; Mr. Yettmab, Japanese impressionist.
Died at His Work.

James Toddy, aged thirty, residing in Philip-street, dropped dead whilst following his employment at Messrs Pearson and Knowles' ironworks, Dallarn, at 4.30 on Tuesday afternoon. Heart failure was tLe cause.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
RAILWAY NATIONALIZATION DISCUSSED.

Notwithstanding last week's defeat, the Gavernment I is as keen as ever on the progressive programme out- lined at the beginning of the Session, and on Thursday evening the local Parliament discussed another most important measure in the shape of a Bill for the Nationalization of the Railways, Light Railways, and Canals of Great Britain. It was a rather remarkable fact that when a scheme so dear to the hearts of Socialists was being proposed, the Socialist Benches were almost empty, only two members of that party being present. The hope was expressed that the Soaialists would see their way to accord more enthu- siastic support to the Society by attending and endeavouring to make the debates as interesting as possible. Mr. J. JARMAN (President of the Board of Trade) Introduced the Bill which, briefly, proposes:— That on and after January Ist, 1910, the whole of the railways, light railways and canals, together with rights (..f way, rolling stock, station terminals, wharves and sidings, and all other property and possessions now owned and controlled by every railway and canal com- pany, including all steamships or other vessels o weed by such companies, shall be transferred to and become the property of the State. That all the existiog share- holders in the Companies shall receive for their present stock certificates, Government Sarip, to, be termed "Government Railway Stock "which shall bear interest at the rate of 3 per cant, per annum, such interest to be guaranteed by Government and be a first charge upon the revenues of the State Bail trays and Canals, such Scrip to be issued at the average rate of railway stock for the past five years. The State shall not for a period of three years make any reductions in salaries or staff without the matter has been previously submitted to, and agreed upon by a two-thirds majority of the Conciliation Board appointed under this Bill. The government of the State Railways shall be vested in a Permanent Committee consisting of 20 managers elected by the present railway com- panies, five by the canal companies, and 23 representa- tives norainated,by the Board of Trade, the salaries of the nominated representatives to be voted by Parlia- ment. It shall also have a permanent Secretary appointed by the Board of Trade and a President who Shall molt 91 9 cabinet Mini*r with tip) title of Trafdo Minister a a salary of 22000 per annum. The Committee shall appoint horn themselves a Sub- Committee of 10 persons, who shall act as Government Representatives with fr like number appointed by the employees on a Conciliation Board, to enquire into and settle all differences or questions that may arise as to wages, hours of labour, &a. They shall also enquire into and report upon the existing Pension Funds of the , companies, with a view to a Government Pension Scheme being embodied for the employees. Separate accounts of receipts and expenditure shall be kept, and any profits arising from the State Railways, after full provision has been made for interest, upkeep, &a., shall be utilized for the purpose of increasing facilities for cheap transit and reduction of rates on goods traffic. Mr. JARMAN made an interesting and well-reasoned LI speech in which he contended that the present system was unsatisfactory to the shareholders, the traders and , the employees of the companies. The railways had , been excessively over-capitalised and consequently there was an inadequate return to the shareholders on the money invested. The railways in England had cost £59,000 per mile as against Cermauy £20,000 and Belgium £29,000. There wore 111 railway companies in the United Kingdom as against six companies in France and that meant muddle in every direction. Ile calcu- lated that centralization would save £10,000,000 a year. Mr. Jarman also referred to the anomalies in railway rates which he contended would be abolished by nationalization. It was not the intention of the

Government that the money should be -saved at the expense of the men at present employed, many of whom worked excessively long hours and received very low pay. The country was not deriving the benefit it ought to from the canals the reason being that one third of them were owned lite the railway companies and the majority were kept closed so as not to compete with the railways. "Mr. W. CLEGG (Postmaster-General) seconded. Mr. S. F. LLOYD (Windsor) moved the rejection of the Bill which he characterised as premature and ill- timed. Why did not the Government throw away their Socialistic cloak and give the House a bit of their own policy ? (Laughter). In his opinion Liberalism was practically dead, and what they bad to fight in the future was Socialism. (Laughter). State ownership of railways would increase unemployment, for the present competition caused a large amount to be spent in rolling stock Ste. and found work for many outside the service. It would also kill enterprise and stop progress. If there were no competition, State manage- ment would not move in the direction of improve- ments except under compulsion. Mr. F. G. TAYLOR (Petersfield) seconded. Mr. PETER PEACOCK (Secretary for War) said the present system was a curse to the country and was becoming a gigantic monopoly. Amalgamation and agreements were being erranged with the result that competition would be stifled and the traders strangled out of existence by unfair rates. In Warrington to-d ty I large industries were suffering from the way in which 1 the railway companies treated them. Mr. Peacock gave instances of the heavy rates imposed on traffic in England as compared with that from abroad and con- tended that under nationalization there would be some- thing like remonabletness and uniformity. Far from being premature, the Bill was ail urgent necessity. Alderman BRNNETT (W. Birmingham) strongly sup- ported the Bill and said the objection that it was Socialistic had no point whatever. The case in favour of nationalization rens absolutely unanswerable. There were only three leading countries in the world which did not own their own railways—the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States. There was no logic, symmetry or fairness in the present rating system in England which often greatly handicapped the British trader in his competition with foreign counties. The waste under the private ownership of railways was really stupendous. The highly-paid boards of direCtors were to some extent ornamental excrescencies, and he was inclined to think the managers could do the work almost as well without them. Ile sometimes thought the affairs of the Corporation would be run as well by paid officials as by members of the Council, though he supposed it was rink heresy to say so. (Laughter.) Nationalization of. railways would help the Liberal Government to finance their extravagant proposals, but it would not stave off tariff reform. (Laughter.) find r nationalization we should have a better and cheaper service, better wages and shorter hours for the employees, and one might expect that the railways would be managed with a little more regard to methetic consideration. With State railways, it would not be possible to perpetrate- such an abomination as the Arpley railway bridge. (Langht9r). Mr. NIGHTINGALE (Normanton) regarded the present system as obsolete and strongly urged the House to combat the amalgamation of railways which he likened . . .
:a a great o. ctopu-s.. liTe .thou.ght tge Member for West

Birmldljham (might to take hi; place on the Socialist beneles. (Laughter and applause). Mr. F. a. TAYLOR (Petersfield) contended that private control was, on the whole, better for the country. He admitted that the present system left much to be desired but he saw no raason w`iy Parlia- ment should not alter it without going to the length of nationalization. He suggested a Board under the con- trol of Parliament to regulate railway rates, and it should also be enacted that no railwaylcompany should be entitled to own a canal. In this measure the

Government had gone out of their way to give generous compensation, and how they reconciled that with their procedure in the Licensing Bill he failed to understand (Laughter and applause). Mr. E. ENGLAND (Chancellor of the Exchequer) welcomed the memmre as providing a great source of revenue, lie was informed that the income from the State railways would be at least £30,000,000 a year, so there would be no necessity for tariff reform. (Applause,) He hoped that under nationalization all the railways would be electrified, as that would mean a great saying and extra comfort and convenience. The debate was adjourned until next Thursday.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

Replying to Mr. Johnstone (Dumfries), the Prtmarna (Mr. John Upson) said the Government recognized the great evil which had arisen and constantly did arise when a progressive Government was in power, by the unconstitutional action o: the House of Lords. It waa a matter for regret that the Government would shortly go out of power; otherwise they had hoped to intro- duce very strong proposals for the removal of the intolerable conditions at present obtaining. (Applause.) FUTURE BUSINESS.

Mr. J. F. AMERY (Secretary for Ireland) announced that the it vision on the Railway Nationalization Bill would be Wren next week. On December 10th a Bill would be introduced by the Chief Secretary for Scot- land dealing with the taxation of land values. The division would be taken on December 17th, and that would ring down the curtain on the career of the first Liberal administration in the Warrington Parliament.

ECOTT WARD'S DEPARTITRE.—On Wednesday night a farewell meeting was held in Risley Chapel in order to make a presentation to Mr. Scott Ward, of Fearnhend, the son of Mr. Thomas Ward, a former editor of this paper. Mr. Scott Ward is sailing for New Zealand next Wednesday, and we understand that it is his intention to settle in the district of Auckland,in the northern part of New Zealand, where already members of the Ward family resici.e. Mr. Scott Ward has made himself very useful in various offices in connection with Risley Church, and his services will be much missed.

div.head: ORFORD WARD ELECTION.
div.p: ORFORD WARD ELECTION.

div.head: Unsuccessful Candidate's Petition.
div.p: Unsuccessful Candidate's Petition.

Mr. James Armitage Rushworth, the unsuccessful C mservative candidate in the recent election in Orford Ward, has petitioned against the return of Councillor Peter Peacock (L), on the ground of alleged corrupt practices. The official poster, issued by the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) states that the petition is presented to the High Court of Justice King's Bench Division, under the Municipal Cor- porations Act, 1882, and the Municipal Elections (Corrupt and Illegal Practices) Act, I?.84. It sets forth the fact that the election took place in Orford Ward on November 2nd and Peter Peacock was" in the usual manner declared to be duly elected." The petitioner (James Armitage Rushworth, licensed victualler, 212, Winwick-road) says "That before, during and after the said election, the said Peter Peacock was by himself and by his agents guilty of the corrupt practices of bribery, treating, and undue influence.
Wherefore your petitioner prays that it ray be determined that the said Peter Peacock was not duly elected and that his election was void."
The petitioner's agents are Henry Greenall and Co., Warrington. WHO WILL BEAR TUE EXPENSE

The procedure to be observed in presenting att election petition is as follows : —The petition must be lodged within t r enty-one days of the election in the master's office in the Kings's Bench Division. Within five days afterwards the petitioning side must enter into recognisances for such a sum as may be fixed, being* not less than £3OO and not exceeding £5OO. The other side may object to the recognisances if they think fit. These preliminaries over, the person petitioned against is entitled to inquire for particulars of the actual acts alleged to have taken place, which will be ordered to be given. When the election petition list is filled up it is sent to the two judges on the Circuit who appoint a Commissioner to hold an elec- tion Court to inquire into the case. The Commissioner must be a barrister of not lees than fifteen years' standing, and he must give the Town Clerk fifteen days' notice of the holding of his Court. The pro- ceedings will take place in Warrington and the public will have right of access. The Public Prosecutor will be represented. The expenses of the Commissioner are paid direct, by the Treasury but are recoverable from the Borough rates. The Town Clerk's expenses in receiving the Court, which comprise finding the necessary accom-. modation, payment of shorthand writer, &c., are also, payable from the Borough fund in the first place. However, in the event of the petition being decided try be frivolous or the respondent being proved person- ally guilty of the offences alleged, the whole of the costs will be borne by the petitioner or the respond- ent respectively. If the petition fails but the com- missioners are of opinion that 'there were good grounds for bringing it, the costs will be borne by the ratepayers, and we understand the town would also have to bear the expense if it were decided that only the agents of the respondent were responsible. The legal costs of either Fifty will be borne in such a, manner as the Court may direct, but not by the town,. It is not probable that the Court will be held before Christmas.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN LIVERPOOL. Mr. Crosfield and the Lords' Veto.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN LIVERPOOL. Mr. Crosfield and the Lords' Veto.

The three days' bazaar at Hardman-stret Assembly Rooms, Liverpool, promoted by the Liberals of Aber-- cromby Division with the object of raising funds for an extended political campaign, concluded last evening. Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, M.P. for Warrington, was the principal Speaker at the opening proceedings in the afternoon, and a hearty welcome was accorded to him and to Mrs. Crosfield, who accompanied him. Mr. J. L. Mills presided. Mr. Crosfield said it was an immense pleasure to him to assist in such a cause as that of advancing Liberalism in the division represented by his friend Colonel Seeley. Tt was sometimes said that Liberals were people with small imaginations, that their politics were the politics of the parish pump, and that they had no idea of the responsibilities of the empire. No better answer to that statement could be found than was afforded by the personality of Col..nel Seely who had- not only shown how to fight for Empire, but with con- spicuous ability had shown how to bear a part in governing the empire. Colonel Seely had done riplendid service in the beating down of ttre- ill-ornened attempt to introduce Chinese labour into South Africa and he was at the present time engaged in trying to check the excesses of the disastrous opium traffic in the Far East. At different times in national history, M. Crosileld went on, a good deal had been heard of the formation of a great central national party. That object had now been achieved in Liberalism. On the one hand there was a rather extreme and irresponsible set of people, whose notion of reform tires to turn the world topsy-turvy, and on the other side there was the good old Tory brigade, which in these days stood very largely for political selfishness. Between the party of reaction and the party of recklessness, there was the central party of Liberalism,. which stood for progress, sanity and equity. The whole country had been astonished by the liberty which had been taken by the Tory peers in rejecting, without any care- ful consideration of details but purely on party lines. the Licensing Bill to which the House of Commons had given six weeks of thoughtful deliberation and hard work. This was not going to do any harm to Liberalism either in Liverpool or in any other part of the country. From a party point of view it was certain to strengthen Liberalism all through the kingdom.- He was certain that neither in Liverpool nor in his own constituency would any injury be done to the Liberal cause by the absurd charges of "confiscation" and "bare-faced robbery" which had been levelled wholesale at the Bill. When they considered what labour and anxiety it cost a man to produce a patent which would be a real benefit to his country, and bore in mind that her was allowed to enioy the monopoly value of his invention for only fourteen years, they would appreciate very clearly that the time limit of 21 years which the Government would have been prepared to give to the licensed trade, by way of recognising-not a legal right, but a custom, was generosity itself. (Hear, hear.) There might have been a little too much frilling in the- Bill—which was perhaps put in so that the Gilded Chamber might have an opportunity to do a little trimming (laughter)—but the fundamental principles of the time limit and the reasonable reduction of redundant licenses constituted a cause which was impregnable. He hoped that Liverpool would be able to do what had been done in Warrington—to educate the electors up to the proper understanding of these facts, and so secures strong and solid backing of public opinion. A vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfleld and his wife was warmly passed on the proposition of Dr. PERIIEWAN, seconded by Mr. DEACON.

MISCELLANY. rumors In Ashcroft, British Columbia, are several 'emall lakes whose shores and bottoms are -covered with a crust containing borax and soda in such quantities that, when cut out, it serves as a washing-compound. The crust 15 cut into blocks, slid handled in the same manner as ice. It is estimated that one of 'the lakes contains twenty thossand tons of this material. TRADING IN HUMAN SKIN. As skin grafting on a large scale comes info more extensive use in surgery, it becomes 'snore difficult to procure the best material for the purpose. The difficulty has recently been met in America by treating the skin as an article of commerce, and buying the amount required. Five dollars (about El • sterling) was the price paid by a doctor for sufficient skin to put on the limb of a little •Lo y who had been badly scalded, A DISEASED GLASS. The authorities of the Royal Museum at bmsden have discovered a glass vase in one of their show-cases, dating from the eigh- teenth century, which shows every sign of suffering from a wasting disease, and not Only is it wasting away, but the authorities t declare it has infected the other glass vessels in its immediate neighbourhood. The vase has been carefully examined by experts and various medicines, externally applied, ha N c 'been prescribed to stay the progress of the latalady, but all to „go purpose. KETTLES THAT SING. The Japanese, who know so well how to ,add little unexpected attractions to every-day life, manufacture, in a great variety of forms, iron teakettles which break into song when the water boils. The song may not be a very Perfect melody, but it is perhaps as agreeable •as the notes produced by some of the insects Which the Japanese also treasure for their 'music. The harmonious sounds of the tea- -1 isettles are produced by steam bubble eseap- iLe from beneath thin sheets of iron fastened Close together nearly at the bottom of the kettles. These singing kettles have been used sfor many centuries.

POSTAL AND SAVINII3 BANK REGULATIONS For further particulars see " Post Office Guide," at any Post Office. POSTAGE STAMPS. Books containing 12 penny and 23 halfpenny stamps are now on sale at each post office. Price 2s. INLAND CORRESPONDENCE. - The term " Inland Correspondence " means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. " Inland Correspondence " is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (4) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size. LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows : Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... ... Id. A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth. POST-CARDS. The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 31 incises in width, or be less than 31 inches iu length by 2± inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and 2-inch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. HALFPENNY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post CAM be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, dm., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is id. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter. PARC'EL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For aparcel ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 exceeding 1 lb. 2 lb. 0 4 PI „ 2 lb. PP 3 lb. 0 5 3 lb. If 5 lb. 0 6 2P „ 5 lb. 7 lb. 0 7 ft ft 7 lb. fl 8 lb. 0 8 91 „ 8 lb. 9 lb. 0 9 „ 9 lb. ft 10 lb. 0 10 10 lb. 11 lb. 0 11 No parcel may exceed 111 b. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel la : Greatest length... ... ... 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. ein, in its longest dimensions as much as 21t. Gin, round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker ; thus, if it measure no more than Oft. in length, it may measure as much as 315. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FottErcal AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 6d. ; £33, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A feo of Gd. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by 6d., from 6J. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are up to 2s. 6d.; ld. tin to 155.; I Ad. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after no order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postinaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege ofstranstnitting,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d., which covers 12 words, and an additional id. for each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All • charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply rosy be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handyd to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The &st of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 is. TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are assepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK. • These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person call have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only, under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. Any amount up to and including £1 may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can bee xpedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELF.PIIONE AND TRUNK LINE CrIARGES. The fees for the use of the Trunk lines are as follows:— For 25 miles or under 3d. 50 -s- „ /I PP Cd. PI 4 ft „ 100 „ „ every additional 40 miles or fraction thereof... ... gd. Between the hours of 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., six minutes conversation is allowed for the same price as three minutes between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., and a reduced charge is made for three minute calls. -- MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REGULATIONS. Each one must be registered with the council of a county or county borough, the fee being £1 bored motor car, and Is. for a motor cycle. A register a number is assigned to each, which it is' an offence not to keep affixed whcu driving. Each driver must possess a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 13 months, and obtainable Irons tho county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dargerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to his presence of the motor car on the road, the river must supply his name and address, and the twner and number of the car, under heavy penal- odie The driver must produceh is licence at the sequest of a police constable.

MR. BIRRELL'S VISIT. ARRANGEMENTS FOR TO-NIGHT'S DEMONSTRATION. -- Character Sketch. The Bight lion. Augustine T3irrell, K.C., M.PI (Chief Secretary for Ireland), will be the chief speaker at a ! great Liberal demonstration in Parr Hall this evening. I His approaching visit has aroused the greatest interest in the town, and a hearty welcome is assured Mr. Birrell. He is the third Member of the present Cabinet to visit Warrington, and is certainly one of the most talented Liberal Ministers of the day. In addition to the guest of the evening, the speakers will include our own Member for Warrington (Mr. Crosfield), Mr. W. J. Crossley, M.P. (Altrincham Division), Mr. A. J. King, M.P. (Knutsford Division), and Mr. George Harwood, M.P. (Bolton). Doors will open at 6.30. p.m. and seats will be reserved for ticket-holders. The chair will be taken at 7.30 prompt by Mr. Charles E. Parker (President of the Warring- ton Liberal Association).

Parish Church Parochial Tea. This popear annual gathering. in connection with the Warrington Parish Church, took place at the Parr Hall on Thursday evening and proved a great success'. Over 600 sat down to tea, the following ladies pre- siding at the tables : —Mrs. J. G. Craik, Miss Shaw, Miss Sankey, Miss Taylor, Mrs. Collin, Mrs. S. Taylor,. Mrs. Walton, Mrs. Scott, Mrs. J. Hill, Mrs. Barber, Miss White, Mrs. James Fairelough, Mrs. Willis, Miss Brooks, Mrs. Farrall. After tea pleasing entertain-• ments were given ky Mrs. Collin, Miss White and they Girls' Friendly Society. Dancing was indulged in from 8 p.m. till 12 p.m. to music supplied by Mr. Starkey's hand. The following acted as M.C's. : Mr. R. W. Collin, Mr. R. W. Antwis and Mr. G. W. A. Brown. The catering was admirably carried out by the Wininarleigh Cafe Company, Limited. The Rector (Rev.
